The purpose of these provisions is to establish the liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage, outlining the obligations of both the carrier and the passenger. The carrier is liable for loss or damage resulting from the death of, or personal injury to, passengers, as well as for loss or damage to registered luggage. However, the carrier may be relieved of this liability if the loss or damage was caused by a fault of the passenger, an inherent defect in the luggage, or circumstances that the carrier could not avoid. The provisions also apply to cases where railway vehicles are carried by ferry, and the carrier shall be liable for loss or damage caused by an accident arising out of the operation of the railway.

Passengers have certain obligations, including the requirement to be in possession of a valid ticket and to produce it upon inspection. Failure to do so may result in the passenger being required to pay a surcharge or being excluded from carriage. Passengers who present a danger to safety or inconvenience other passengers may also be excluded from carriage. The carrier may also be liable for loss or damage resulting from cancellation, late running of a train, or a missed connection, and shall provide reasonable costs of accommodation and notification to persons expecting the passenger.

The provisions also outline the basis of liability for registered luggage, which includes the carrier's liability for loss or damage resulting from the total or partial loss of, or damage to, registered luggage. The carrier may be relieved of this liability if the loss or damage was caused by a fault of the passenger or an inherent defect in the luggage. The provisions also establish the principle that the carrier shall be liable for his servants and other persons whose services he makes use of for the performance of the carriage.

In terms of asserting rights, claims relating to the liability of the carrier must be addressed in writing to the carrier, and the person entitled may be required to produce documents to support their claim. A carrier who has paid compensation may have a right of recourse against other carriers who have taken part in the carriage, and the compensation shall be apportioned between them in accordance with the provisions. Overall, these provisions aim to provide a framework for the liability of railway undertakings and the rights and obligations of passengers, ensuring that passengers are protected and that carriers are held accountable for their actions.

This Regulation establishes rules for the liability of railway undertakings towards passengers and their luggage. The Regulation applies to all rail journeys and services throughout the Community provided by one or more railway undertakings licensed in accordance with Council Directive 95/18/EC. However, it does not apply to railway undertakings and transport services which are not licensed under Directive 95/18/EC. Member States may grant exemptions from the application of the provisions of this Regulation to domestic rail passenger services, urban, suburban and regional rail passenger services, or particular services or journeys operated outside the Community, provided that such exemptions are granted on a transparent and non-discriminatory basis.

Passengers must be in possession of a valid ticket from the start of their journey and produce it on the inspection of tickets. The General Conditions of Carriage may provide for a surcharge to be paid by a passenger who does not produce a valid ticket, and for the passenger to be required to discontinue their journey if they refuse to pay the carriage charge or the surcharge. Passengers who present a danger to safety or inconvenience other passengers may be excluded from carriage or required to discontinue their journey, and shall not be entitled to a refund of their carriage charge or any charge for the carriage of registered luggage.

The carrier shall be liable to the passenger for loss or damage resulting from the fact that, by reason of cancellation, late running of a train or a missed connection, their journey cannot be continued the same day. The damages shall comprise the reasonable costs of accommodation as well as the reasonable costs occasioned by having to notify persons expecting the passenger. However, the carrier shall not be liable to the passenger for loss or damage arising from the fact that the passenger does not conform to the formalities required by customs or other administrative authorities.

The carrier shall be liable for loss or damage resulting from the total or partial loss of, or damage to, registered luggage between the time of taking over by the carrier and the time of delivery, as well as from delay in delivery. The carrier shall be relieved of this liability to the extent that the loss, damage or delay in delivery was caused by a fault of the passenger, by an order given by the passenger, by an inherent defect in the registered luggage, or by circumstances which the carrier could not avoid and the consequences of which he was unable to prevent. The provisions relating to the liability of the carrier in case of death of, or personal injury to, passengers shall apply to loss or damage caused by an accident arising out of the operation of the railway and happening while the passenger is in, entering or alighting from railway vehicles carried by ferry. When the operation of the railway is temporarily suspended and passengers are carried by another mode of transport, the carrier shall be liable pursuant to these Uniform Rules.

The Regulation applies to all rail journeys and services throughout the Community provided by one or more railway undertakings licensed in accordance with Council Directive 95/18/EC. Member States may grant exemptions from the application of the provisions of this Regulation to domestic rail passenger services, urban, suburban and regional rail passenger services, or particular services or journeys operated outside the Community, under certain conditions and for a limited period.

Passengers must be in possession of a valid ticket from the start of their journey and produce it on the inspection of tickets. The General Conditions of Carriage may provide for a surcharge to be paid by a passenger who does not produce a valid ticket, and for the passenger to be required to discontinue their journey if they refuse to pay the carriage charge or the surcharge. Passengers who present a danger to safety or inconvenience other passengers may be excluded from carriage or required to discontinue their journey, without being entitled to a refund of their carriage charge.

The carrier is liable for loss or damage resulting from the total or partial loss of, or damage to, registered luggage between the time of taking over by the carrier and the time of delivery, as well as from delay in delivery. However, the carrier is relieved of this liability to the extent that the loss, damage or delay was caused by a fault of the passenger, an inherent defect in the registered luggage, or circumstances which the carrier could not avoid and the consequences of which he was unable to prevent. The carrier is also liable to the passenger for loss or damage resulting from the fact that, due to cancellation, late running of a train or a missed connection, the passenger's journey cannot be continued the same day.

The Regulation also provides that the carrier shall not be liable to the passenger for loss or damage arising from the fact that the passenger does not conform to the formalities required by customs or other administrative authorities. In cases where the operation of the railway is temporarily suspended and passengers are carried by another mode of transport, the carrier shall be liable pursuant to these Uniform Rules. Additionally, when railway vehicles are carried by ferry, the provisions relating to liability in case of death of, or personal injury to, passengers shall apply to loss or damage caused by an accident arising out of the operation of the railway and happening while the passenger is in, entering or alighting from the said vehicles.

The Regulation on rail passengers' rights and obligations aims to safeguard users' rights and improve the quality and effectiveness of rail passenger services. It applies to all rail passengers, including those with disabilities or reduced mobility, and requires railway undertakings to provide accessible information and services. Passengers have the right to be carried, provided they possess a valid ticket, and railway undertakings may exclude passengers who pose a danger to safety or inconvenience other passengers. In cases of cancellation, late running, or missed connections, passengers are entitled to compensation, including reasonable costs of accommodation and notification. Railway undertakings are liable for loss or damage to registered luggage, unless the loss or damage is caused by the passenger's fault, an inherent defect in the luggage, or circumstances beyond the carrier's control. The Regulation also requires railway undertakings to be insured for their liability to passengers and to take measures to ensure passengers' personal security. Member States may grant exemptions from certain provisions for specific services, but these exemptions do not apply to key provisions such as accessibility for disabled persons, the right to purchase tickets without undue difficulty, and liability for passengers and their luggage. Overall, the Regulation seeks to strengthen passengers' rights and improve the rail passenger experience, while also taking into account the needs of railway undertakings and the specific characteristics of different types of rail services.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish specific requirements for advanced therapy medicinal products, which are products that contain or consist of cells or tissues that have been subject to significant manipulation. The regulation applies to the marketing authorisation of these products, which must be granted by the Agency after a thorough evaluation of their quality, safety, and efficacy. 

In order to obtain marketing authorisation, the application must include a description of the physical characteristics and performance of the product, as well as the product design methods, in accordance with the relevant directives. For combined advanced therapy medicinal products, which contain medical devices, bio-materials, scaffolds, or matrices, the application must also include evidence of conformity with the essential requirements referred to in the relevant article. The Agency may request the relevant notified body to transmit any information related to the results of its assessment, and the notified body must transmit the information within a period of one month.

The holder of a marketing authorisation for an advanced therapy medicinal product must establish and maintain a system ensuring that the individual product and its starting and raw materials can be traced through the sourcing, manufacturing, packaging, storage, transport, and delivery to the hospital, institution, or private practice where the product is used. The hospital, institution, or private practice where the advanced therapy medicinal product is used must also establish and maintain a system for patient and product traceability, which must contain sufficient detail to allow linking of each product to the patient who received it and vice versa.

The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a crucial role in the evaluation of advanced therapy medicinal products, providing advice on the quality, safety, and efficacy of these products, as well as on any question related to them. The Committee must also contribute to the scientific advice procedures and provide scientific expertise and advice for any Community initiative related to the development of innovative medicines and therapies.

The regulation also sets out specific requirements for the traceability of advanced therapy medicinal products, including the need for the marketing authorisation holder to keep data for a minimum of 30 years after the expiry date of the product. In case of bankruptcy or liquidation of the marketing authorisation holder, the data must be transferred to the Agency. The Commission may draw up detailed guidelines relating to the application of the traceability requirements, and the regulation provides for the amendment of certain annexes to include advanced therapy medicinal products.

Overall, the regulation aims to ensure the safe and effective use of advanced therapy medicinal products, while also promoting innovation and the development of new treatments. It applies to all advanced therapy medicinal products, including those that are prepared on a non-routine basis according to specific quality standards and used within the same Member State in a hospital under the exclusive professional responsibility of a medical practitioner.

This Regulation sets out specific rules for the authorisation, supervision, and pharmacovigilance of advanced therapy medicinal products. The marketing authorisation procedure for these products involves the submission of an application that includes a description of the product's physical characteristics and performance, as well as its design methods. For combined advanced therapy medicinal products, which contain medical devices, bio-materials, scaffolds, or matrices, the application must also include evidence of conformity with essential requirements and, where available, the results of an assessment by a notified body. The Agency will recognise the results of such assessments in its evaluation of the product.

The holder of a marketing authorisation for an advanced therapy medicinal product must establish and maintain a system to ensure the traceability of the product and its starting and raw materials throughout the sourcing, manufacturing, packaging, storage, transport, and delivery process. Hospitals, institutions, and private practices where these products are used must also establish a system for patient and product traceability. The marketing authorisation holder must keep the traceability data for at least 30 years after the product's expiry date and may be required to transfer the data to the Agency in certain circumstances.

The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a crucial role in the evaluation of advanced therapy medicinal products, providing advice on their quality, safety, and efficacy, as well as on whether a product falls within the definition of an advanced therapy medicinal product. The Committee also assists in the elaboration of documents related to the fulfilment of the Regulation's objectives and provides scientific expertise and advice for Community initiatives related to innovative medicines and therapies.

The Regulation applies to advanced therapy medicinal products as defined in Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007, and its provisions are complementary to and compatible with the requirements laid down in other Directives, such as those related to human cells and tissues. The Commission may present proposals to amend certain provisions of the Regulation, and the European Parliament and the Council will take decisions on such proposals in accordance with the Treaty. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and effective use of advanced therapy medicinal products, while also promoting innovation and development in this field.

The marketing authorisation procedure for these products involves the submission of an application that includes a description of the product's physical characteristics and performance, as well as its design methods, in accordance with relevant directives. For combined advanced therapy medicinal products, the whole product is subject to evaluation by the Agency, and the application must include evidence of conformity with essential requirements and, where available, the results of assessments by notified bodies. The Agency may request additional information from notified bodies and may seek their opinion on the conformity of the device part with relevant directives.

The holder of a marketing authorisation for an advanced therapy medicinal product must establish and maintain a system to ensure the traceability of the product and its starting and raw materials, including all substances that come into contact with the cells or tissues it may contain. This system must be complementary to and compatible with the requirements for human cells and tissues laid down in relevant directives. The marketing authorisation holder must keep the traceability data for a minimum of 30 years after the expiry date of the product and must transfer the data to the Agency in the event of bankruptcy or liquidation.

The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a key role in the evaluation of advanced therapy medicinal products, providing advice on their quality, safety, and efficacy, as well as on whether a product falls within the definition of an advanced therapy medicinal product. The Committee also provides scientific expertise and advice on the development of innovative medicines and therapies. The Regulation applies to advanced therapy medicinal products as defined in Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007, and the Commission may present proposals to amend the Regulation as necessary. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and effective development and use of advanced therapy medicinal products in the European Union.

The Regulation on advanced therapy medicinal products aims to ensure the free movement of these products within the European Union while safeguarding public health. It applies to advanced therapy medicinal products that are prepared industrially or manufactured by a method involving an industrial process, and are intended to be placed on the market in Member States. These products include gene therapy, somatic cell therapy, and tissue engineering products, which are considered biological medicinal products. The Regulation introduces specific requirements for the authorisation of these products, including the need for a description of the physical characteristics and performance of the product, as well as the product design methods.

For combined advanced therapy medicinal products containing medical devices, the whole product is subject to final evaluation by the Agency, and the application for a marketing authorisation must include evidence of conformity with the essential requirements. The Agency may also seek an opinion from a notified body on the conformity of the device part with the relevant Directives. The Regulation also establishes requirements for the traceability of advanced therapy medicinal products, including the need for a system to trace the individual product and its starting and raw materials, as well as a system for patient and product traceability at the hospital, institution, or private practice where the product is used.

The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a key role in the evaluation of advanced therapy medicinal products, providing advice on the quality, safety, and efficacy of these products, as well as on whether a product falls within the definition of an advanced therapy medicinal product. The Regulation also amends Directive 2001/83/EC and Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 to include advanced therapy medicinal products within their scope. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a harmonised framework for the regulation of advanced therapy medicinal products, while ensuring the protection of public health and respecting the fundamental rights and principles reflected in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

This Regulation aims to establish a framework for the production of Community statistics in the field of education and lifelong learning. It defines key terms such as "Community statistics", "production of statistics", "national authorities", "education", "lifelong learning", "micro-data", and "confidential data". The Regulation applies to the production of statistics in three domains: Domain 1 covers statistics on education and training systems, Domain 2 covers statistics on the participation of adults in lifelong learning, and Domain 3 covers other statistics on education and lifelong learning, such as statistics on human capital and on the social and economic benefits of education.

The production of Community statistics in these domains shall be carried out in accordance with the Annex and shall be implemented by individual statistical actions, including the regular delivery of statistics by Member States, the use of other statistical information systems and surveys, and the development and improvement of standards and manuals on statistical frameworks, concepts, and methods. The Commission shall seek cooperation with international organisations to ensure international comparability of data and avoid duplication of effort.

The Regulation also sets out requirements for the quality of the data, including relevance, accuracy, timeliness, accessibility, comparability, and coherence. Available capacities within Member States for data collection and processing shall be taken into account, and special attention shall be given to the regional dimension of the data and the breakdown of data by gender where appropriate.

Implementing measures may be adopted to amend non-essential elements of the Regulation, including measures to take account of economic and technical developments concerning data collection, transmission, and processing. These measures shall be based on a cost-benefit analysis and shall take into account the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals, the results of pilot studies, and the latest agreements between international organisations.

The Regulation also sets out specific requirements for the collection of data on participation in learning activities, characteristics of these activities, self-reported skills, and socio-demographic information. Data on participation in social and cultural activities may also be collected on a voluntary basis. The data source shall be a sample survey, and administrative data sources may be used to reduce the burden on respondents. The sample size shall be established on the basis of precision requirements, and specific subpopulations shall require particular sampling considerations.

Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a framework for the production of high-quality Community statistics in the field of education and lifelong learning, while taking into account the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals and the need for international comparability of data.

The production of statistics in these domains shall be carried out in accordance with the Annex.

The Regulation defines various terms, including "Community statistics", "production of statistics", "national authorities", "education", "lifelong learning", "micro-data", and "confidential data". It also sets out the statistical actions to be implemented, including the regular delivery of statistics on education and lifelong learning by the Member States, the use of other statistical information systems and surveys, the development and improvement of standards and manuals on statistical frameworks, concepts, and methods, and the improvement of data quality.

The Commission (Eurostat) shall seek cooperation with international organisations to ensure international comparability of data and avoid duplication of effort. The Regulation also provides for pilot studies to be carried out on a voluntary basis by the Member States to assess the feasibility of data collection and the benefits of the availability of the data in relation to the collection costs and the burden on respondents.

Implementing measures may be adopted to amend non-essential elements of the Regulation, including measures to take account of economic and technical developments concerning the collection, transmission, and processing of data. These measures shall be based on a cost-benefit analysis and shall take into account the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals, the results of pilot studies, and the latest agreements between international organisations on concepts, definitions, data collection format, and deadlines for transmission of results.

The Regulation also sets out the subjects to be covered by surveys, including participation and non-participation in learning activities, characteristics of these learning activities, information on self-reported skills, and socio-demographic information. Data on participation in social and cultural activities may also be collected on a voluntary basis. The data source shall be a sample survey, and administrative data sources may be used to reduce the burden on respondents. The sample size shall be established on the basis of precision requirements, and shall not require effective national sample sizes to be larger than 5,000 individuals.

The Regulation concerning the production and development of statistics on education and lifelong learning aims to establish a framework for the collection and production of comparable statistical information at the Community level. This framework is essential for the development of education and lifelong learning strategies and for monitoring progress in their implementation. The Regulation applies to the production of statistics in three domains: statistics on education and training systems, statistics on the participation of adults in lifelong learning, and other statistics on education and lifelong learning, such as statistics on human capital and on the social and economic benefits of education.

The Regulation also provides for the adoption of implementing measures to amend non-essential elements of the Regulation, including measures to take account of economic and technical developments concerning the collection, transmission, and processing of data. These measures are adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure with scrutiny and take into account the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals, the results of pilot studies, and the latest agreements between international organisations on concepts, definitions, and data collection formats.

The Regulation is based on the Treaty establishing the European Community and is the result of a long process of cooperation between the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission. It takes into account the Council Resolution of 1994 on the promotion of education and training statistics, the European Council's conclusions on the Lisbon Strategy, and the Integrated Guidelines for Growth and Jobs. The Regulation aims to contribute to the development of education and training systems in the Member States, to promote lifelong learning, and to provide a basis for political decisions.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a common legal framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the aquaculture sector, which has become increasingly important for the Common Fisheries Policy. To achieve this, Member States are required to submit statistics on all aquaculture activities conducted in freshwater and saltwaters on their territory. The Regulation defines key terms such as "aquaculture", "capture-based aquaculture", and "production", and sets out the obligations of Member States in relation to the compilation and submission of statistics.

Member States must use surveys or other statistically validated methods to cover at least 90% of the total production by volume, or by number for the production of hatcheries and nurseries. The remaining part of the total production may be estimated, but a request for derogation must be submitted if more than 10% of the total production is to be estimated. The data to be submitted includes the annual production of aquaculture, the annual input to capture-based aquaculture, the annual production of hatcheries and nurseries, and the structure of the aquaculture sector.

The submission of data must be made to the Commission within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year, with the first reference calendar year being 2008. Member States must also provide a yearly report on the quality of the data submitted and a detailed methodological report on how the data were collected and compiled. The Commission will examine these reports and present its conclusions to the relevant working group of the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics.

In cases where the inclusion of a particular sector of aquaculture activities would cause difficulties to the national authorities, a derogation may be granted, permitting the Member State to exclude data covering that sector or to employ estimation methods for more than 10% of the total production. Such derogations must be requested prior to the deadline for the first submission of the data, and must be supported by a report on the problems encountered in applying the Regulation. The Regulation also allows for a transitional period of up to three years to be granted to Member States where its application to their national statistical systems would require major adaptations and would be likely to cause significant practical problems.

The Regulation requires Member States to submit statistics on all aquaculture activities conducted in freshwater and saltwaters on their territory, including data on annual production, input to capture-based aquaculture, production of hatcheries and nurseries, and the structure of the aquaculture sector. The data shall relate to the reference calendar year and shall be submitted to the Commission within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year.

Member States are obliged to use surveys or other statistically validated methods to compile the statistics, covering at least 90% of the total production by volume, or by number for the production of hatcheries and nurseries. The remaining part of the total production may be estimated, but a request for derogation may be submitted if more than 10% of the total production needs to be estimated. Member States shall also identify the production by species, although the production of certain species may be estimated and aggregated.

The Regulation applies to all Member States, and they shall submit the required data to the Commission, which shall examine the quality of the data and present its conclusions to the relevant working group of the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics. The Commission is empowered to adopt technical changes to the Annexes to this Regulation, and shall be assisted by the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics.

The Regulation also provides for a transitional period of up to three years to be granted to Member States where its application to their national statistical systems would require major adaptations and would be likely to cause significant practical problems. Furthermore, the Regulation requires Member States to provide a yearly report on the quality of the data submitted, as well as a detailed methodological report describing how the data were collected and compiled.

Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic framework for the collection and submission of statistical data on the aquaculture sector, which is essential for the sound management of the Common Fisheries Policy. By establishing a common framework for the production of Community statistics, the Regulation seeks to ensure that the data collected is reliable, relevant, and comparable across Member States, and that it can be used to inform policy decisions and support the development of the aquaculture sector.

The purpose of this Regulation is to enable the European Community to collect and compile comparable and comprehensive statistics on population and housing, which are necessary for the study and definition of regional, social, and environmental policies. To achieve this, the Regulation requires Member States to submit data on the population and housing at a national, regional, and local level, covering determined demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households. The data must be submitted to the Commission (Eurostat) within 27 months of the end of the reference year, which shall fall in a year specified on the basis of this Regulation, with the first reference year being 2011.

Member States may base their statistics on different data sources, including conventional censuses, register-based censuses, and sample surveys, and must take all measures necessary to meet the requirements of data protection. They must also inform the Commission (Eurostat) of any revision or correction of the statistics supplied, as well as of any changes in the chosen data sources and methodology. The Commission (Eurostat) shall establish subsequent reference years and adopt a programme of the statistical data and metadata to be transmitted, in accordance with the regulatory procedure with scrutiny.

The Regulation also sets out quality assessment dimensions, including relevance, accuracy, timeliness, accessibility, comparability, and coherence, which shall apply to the data to be transmitted. Member States must provide the Commission (Eurostat) with a report on the quality of the data transmitted, and the Commission (Eurostat) shall assess the quality of the data transmitted and provide methodological recommendations to ensure the quality of the data and metadata produced.

The implementing measures necessary for the implementation of this Regulation shall be adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure referred to in Article 8(2) or the regulatory procedure with scrutiny referred to in Article 8(3), depending on whether they amend essential or non-essential elements of the Regulation. Consideration shall be given to the principles that the benefits of the measures taken must outweigh their costs and that additional costs and burdens must remain within a reasonable limit. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that the data collected are sufficiently reliable, detailed, and comparable, and that the Community can fulfil its tasks, in particular by enabling the study and definition of regional, social, and environmental policies.

The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure that the European Community has access to reliable, detailed, and comparable data on population and housing, which is necessary for the development and implementation of regional, social, and environmental policies. To achieve this, the Regulation requires Member States to submit data on population and housing to the Commission (Eurostat) at a national, regional, and local level, covering demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households. The data must be submitted in accordance with a programme of statistical data and metadata established by the Commission, and must meet certain quality assessment dimensions, including relevance, accuracy, timeliness, accessibility, comparability, and coherence.

Member States have flexibility in choosing the data sources for the statistics, which can include conventional censuses, register-based censuses, sample surveys, or a combination of these methods. However, they must ensure that the chosen data sources and methodology meet the essential features of population and housing censuses, which include individual enumeration, simultaneity, universality within a defined territory, availability of small-area data, and defined periodicity. Member States must also take measures to protect data protection and ensure the physical and logical protection of confidential data.

The Regulation applies to all Member States, which must determine a reference date and submit the data to the Commission within 27 months of the end of the reference year. The Commission will assess the quality of the data transmitted and provide methodological recommendations to ensure the quality of the data and metadata produced. The Regulation also establishes a framework for the transmission of data subject to statistical confidentiality, which is governed by existing Regulations. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a common framework for the collection and compilation of comparable and comprehensive Community statistics on population and housing, which will enable the Community to better achieve its objectives.

The European Parliament and the Council have adopted a regulation on population and housing censuses, which aims to provide the European Community with reliable, detailed, and comparable data on population and housing. The regulation requires Member States to submit data on the population, covering demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households, as well as on housing at national, regional, and local levels. The data must be submitted to the Commission (Eurostat) within 27 months of the end of the reference year, which falls at the beginning of every decade, with the first reference year being 2011.

Member States may base their statistics on different data sources, including conventional censuses, register-based censuses, and sample surveys, and must take measures to meet the requirements of data protection. They must also inform the Commission of any revisions or corrections to the statistics and ensure that their data sources and methodology meet the essential features of population and housing censuses, which include individual enumeration, simultaneity, universality, availability of small-area data, and defined periodicity.

The Commission is responsible for establishing the conditions for the establishment of subsequent reference years and the adoption of the programme of statistical data and metadata. It must also adopt technical specifications for the topics and their breakdowns, as well as the appropriate technical format for the transmission of the required data. The regulation also establishes quality assessment dimensions, including relevance, accuracy, timeliness, accessibility, comparability, and coherence, and requires Member States to provide a report on the quality of the data transmitted.

The regulation applies to all Member States, and its implementation is subject to the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. The Commission, in cooperation with the competent authorities of the Member States, must provide methodological recommendations to ensure the quality of the data and metadata produced. The regulation also takes into account the principles set out in the European Statistics Code of Practice and the need to protect statistical confidentiality, as governed by Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Council Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a common statistical framework for the collection and compilation of comparable and comprehensive Community statistics on population and housing.

This Regulation governs the admission to and pursuit of the occupation of road transport operator within the European Community. It applies to all undertakings established in the Community that are engaged in or intend to engage in the occupation of road transport operator. However, certain undertakings are exempt from the application of this Regulation, such as those engaged in road haulage operations with vehicles not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, those engaged in non-commercial road passenger transport services, and those using vehicles with a maximum authorised speed not exceeding 40 km/h. Member States may also exempt road transport operators engaged exclusively in national transport operations with a minor impact on the transport market.

To be authorised to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, undertakings must have an effective and stable establishment in a Member State, be of good repute, have appropriate financial standing, and have the requisite professional competence. The requirement of good repute is assessed by considering the conduct of the undertaking, its transport managers, and any other relevant persons, and includes the absence of convictions or penalties for serious infringements of national rules in force in various fields, such as commercial law, insolvency law, and road traffic.

The competent authorities in each Member State are responsible for ensuring the correct implementation of this Regulation. They examine applications, grant authorisations, and carry out checks to verify whether undertakings continue to fulfil the requirements. Undertakings that comply with the requirements are authorised to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, and their data is recorded in a national electronic register. The competent authorities monitor undertakings that pose an increased risk and carry out individual checks when requested by the Commission.

Member States may adapt the conditions for pursuing the occupation of road transport operator in certain regions, and they may also lower the limit for the permissible laden mass of vehicles used by undertakings engaged in road haulage operations. The Regulation also provides for the exchange of information between Member States and the Commission to ensure the effective implementation of its provisions. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonised framework for the occupation of road transport operator within the European Community, ensuring that undertakings engaged in this occupation meet certain standards of professionalism, financial stability, and good repute.

This Regulation governs the admission to and pursuit of the occupation of road transport operator, applying to all undertakings established in the Community that are engaged in or intend to engage in this occupation. The Regulation sets out the key requirements that undertakings must meet to be authorized to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, including having an effective and stable establishment in a Member State, being of good repute, having appropriate financial standing, and having the requisite professional competence. The requirement of good repute is further detailed, with Member States determining the conditions to be met, including the consideration of convictions, penalties, or infringements related to commercial law, insolvency law, pay and employment conditions, road traffic, and other relevant areas.

The Regulation also provides for exemptions and derogations, such as for undertakings engaged in road haulage operations with vehicles not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, or for undertakings engaged in road passenger transport services exclusively for non-commercial purposes. Additionally, Member States may exempt road transport operators engaged exclusively in national transport operations with a minor impact on the transport market.

To ensure compliance with these requirements, each Member State must designate one or more competent authorities to examine applications, grant authorizations, and carry out checks to verify whether an undertaking satisfies the requirements. The competent authorities must publish all conditions, procedures, and explanations, and undertakings with an authorization must notify the competent authority of any changes to the relevant data.

The Regulation also outlines the procedures for the examination and registration of applications, including the time limit for the examination of an application, which shall not exceed three months. The competent authority must verify the good repute of the undertaking and its transport manager, and may extend the time limit for one additional month in duly justified cases.

Overall, this Regulation aims to establish a harmonized framework for the occupation of road transport operator, ensuring that undertakings meet certain requirements to provide safe and reliable transport services, while also allowing for some flexibility and exemptions for specific cases.

This Regulation governs the admission to and pursuit of the occupation of road transport operator, which includes both road haulage and road passenger transport operators. It applies to all undertakings established in the Community that are engaged in or intend to engage in this occupation. However, there are certain exceptions and derogations, such as for undertakings that only use vehicles with a permissible laden mass not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, or for those that provide road passenger transport services exclusively for non-commercial purposes. Member States may also exempt certain road transport operators that only engage in national transport operations with a minor impact on the transport market.

To be authorized to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, an undertaking must meet certain requirements, including having an effective and stable establishment in a Member State, being of good repute, having appropriate financial standing, and having the requisite professional competence. The requirement of good repute is assessed by considering the conduct of the undertaking, its transport managers, and any other relevant persons, and includes factors such as convictions or penalties for serious infringements of national or Community rules.

If an undertaking does not satisfy the requirement of professional competence, it may still be authorized to engage in the occupation of road transport operator if it designates a natural person who satisfies the requirements of good repute and professional competence to act as a transport manager on its behalf. This transport manager must be entitled to carry out duties on an effective and continuous basis and must be independent of any undertakings for which the undertaking carries out transport operations.

The competent authorities in each Member State are responsible for ensuring the correct implementation of this Regulation and for granting authorizations to undertakings to engage in the occupation of road transport operator. They must also publish all the conditions and procedures for interested applicants and carry out checks to verify whether an undertaking satisfies the requirements laid down in the Regulation. Undertakings that are authorized to engage in the occupation of road transport operator must notify the competent authority of any changes to their data within a specified period.

The Regulation also provides for the exchange of information between Member States regarding serious infringements of the Regulation or Community road transport legislation, and for the imposition of administrative penalties. Additionally, the Commission must draw up a report every two years on the application of the Regulation and developments in the fields in question, which must be forwarded to the European Parliament and the Council.

This Regulation establishes common rules concerning the conditions to be complied with to pursue the occupation of road transport operator, with the aim of achieving a higher level of professional qualification, rationalising the market, and improving road safety. The Regulation applies to all undertakings established in the Community that are engaged in the occupation of road transport operator, as well as to those that intend to engage in this occupation. However, it does not apply to undertakings that engage in road haulage operations solely by means of motor vehicles with a permissible laden mass not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, or to those that engage in road passenger transport services exclusively for non-commercial purposes. 

To be authorised to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, an undertaking must have an effective and stable establishment in a Member State, be of good repute, have appropriate financial standing, and have the requisite professional competence. The requirement of good repute is met if there are no compelling grounds for doubting the good repute of the transport manager or the transport undertaking, such as convictions or penalties for serious infringements of national rules in force in fields like commercial law, insolvency law, and road traffic. 

The competent authority in each Member State is responsible for examining applications, granting authorisations, and carrying out checks to verify whether an undertaking satisfies the requirements. The authority must also publish all the conditions laid down pursuant to this Regulation, as well as the procedures to be followed by interested applicants. Undertakings that are authorised to engage in the occupation of road transport operator must notify the competent authority of any changes to the required data within a specified period. 

In cases where an undertaking does not satisfy the requirement of professional competence, the competent authority may authorise it to engage in the occupation of road transport operator without a transport manager, provided that the undertaking designates a natural person who satisfies the requirements and is entitled to carry out duties as transport manager on behalf of the undertaking. This person may manage the transport activities of up to four different undertakings with a combined maximum total fleet of 50 vehicles. 

The Regulation also allows Member States to exempt certain road transport operators from its application, provided that they are engaged exclusively in national transport operations with only a minor impact on the transport market. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a uniform set of rules for the occupation of road transport operator, facilitating the effective exercise of the right of establishment and improving road safety and market transparency.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to regulate the authorisation and placing on the market of plant protection products, ensuring the protection of human and animal health and the environment. Member States may authorise the provisional placement on the market of plant protection products containing an active substance not yet approved, provided that certain conditions are met, including that the decision on approval could not be finalised within a specified period, the dossier on the active substance is admissible, and the Member State concludes that the active substance can satisfy the necessary requirements. 

The authorisation of plant protection products must define the plants or plant products and non-agricultural areas on which the product may be used, as well as the purposes for which it may be used. The authorisation must also set out the requirements relating to the placing on the market and use of the product, including conditions of use necessary to comply with the conditions and requirements provided for in the Regulation approving the active substances. Additionally, the authorisation must include a classification of the plant protection product for the purpose of Directive 1999/45/EC.

Applicants for authorisation must submit a complete and summary dossier for each point of the data requirements of the plant protection product, as well as justifications for the steps taken to avoid animal testing and duplication of tests and studies on vertebrate animals. In the case of low-risk plant protection products, the applicant must demonstrate that the product meets specific requirements, including that all active substances contained in the product are low-risk active substances, the product does not contain a substance of concern, and it is sufficiently effective.

Member States must perform a comparative assessment when evaluating an application for authorisation of a plant protection product containing a candidate for substitution, weighing up the risks and benefits of the product against existing authorised products or non-chemical control or prevention methods. In exceptional cases, Member States may also apply this comparative assessment to products not containing a candidate for substitution or a low-risk active substance.

In special circumstances, a Member State may authorise the placing on the market of plant protection products for limited and controlled use, where such a measure appears necessary due to a danger that cannot be contained by any other reasonable means. Member States must keep and make available to interested parties upon request a list of test and study reports concerning the active substance, safener or synergist, adjuvant, and the plant protection product necessary for first authorisation, amendment of the authorisation conditions, or renewal of the authorisation. 

To avoid duplicative testing, prospective applicants must consult the information available to ascertain if and to whom an authorisation has already been granted for a plant protection product containing the same active substance, safener or synergist, or for an adjuvant, before carrying out tests or studies. The competent authority must provide the prospective applicant with the list of test and study reports prepared for that product, and the applicant must submit all data regarding the identity and impurities of the active substance they propose to use.

This Regulation aims to ensure a high level of protection for human and animal health and the environment by laying down rules for the authorisation of plant protection products in commercial form and their placing on the market, use, and control within the Community. The Regulation applies to Member States and requires them to authorise plant protection products before they can be placed on the market or used, with certain exceptions. For instance, no authorisation is required for the use of products containing exclusively one or more basic substances, or for the placing on the market and use of plant protection products for research or development purposes. 

Member States may authorise the provisional placement on the market of plant protection products containing an active substance not yet approved, provided that the decision on approval could not be finalised within a specified period, the dossier on the active substance is admissible, the active substance can satisfy certain requirements, and maximum residue levels have been established. The authorisation shall define the plants or plant products and non-agricultural areas on which the plant protection product may be used, as well as the requirements relating to its placing on the market and use, including conditions of use necessary to comply with the conditions and requirements provided for in the Regulation approving the active substances.

Applicants for authorisation must submit a complete and summary dossier for each point of the data requirements of the plant protection product, as well as justifications for the steps taken to avoid animal testing and duplication of tests and studies on vertebrate animals. The application shall also be accompanied by a draft label and, where relevant, a copy of the application for a maximum residue level. In the case of low-risk plant protection products, the applicant must demonstrate that the product meets certain requirements, including that all active substances contained in the product are low-risk active substances, the product does not contain a substance of concern, and it is sufficiently effective.

A comparative assessment shall be performed by Member States when evaluating an application for authorisation for a plant protection product containing an active substance approved as a candidate for substitution. This assessment shall weigh the risks and benefits of the product and consider whether an authorised plant protection product or non-chemical control or prevention method already exists which is significantly safer for human or animal health or the environment. The Regulation also provides for the renewal of authorisations and the submission of new information required as a result of amendments in data requirements or criteria. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that plant protection products placed on the market do not adversely affect human or animal health or the environment, and that the internal market functions smoothly through the harmonisation of rules on the placing on the market of these products.

This Regulation aims to ensure a high level of protection for human and animal health and the environment by laying down rules for the authorisation of plant protection products. It applies to the authorisation of plant protection products in commercial form and their placing on the market, use, and control within the Community. The Regulation covers rules for the approval of active substances, safeners, and synergists, as well as adjuvants and co-formulants. 

Member States may authorise the provisional placement on the market of plant protection products containing an active substance not yet approved, provided certain conditions are met, including that the decision on approval could not be finalised within a specified period, the dossier on the active substance is admissible, and the Member State concludes that the active substance can satisfy the necessary requirements. The authorisation shall define the plants or plant products and non-agricultural areas on which the product may be used, as well as the requirements relating to its placing on the market and use.

The authorisation shall include a classification of the plant protection product and may include restrictions on distribution and use, obligations to inform neighbours, and indications for proper use according to Integrated Pest Management principles. Applicants for authorisation must submit a complete and summary dossier for each point of the data requirements of the plant protection product, as well as justifications for the necessity of test and study reports and a draft label.

The Regulation also provides for the authorisation of low-risk plant protection products, which shall meet specific requirements, including that all active substances contained in the product are low-risk active substances and that the product does not contain a substance of concern. Member States shall decide on applications for authorisation of low-risk plant protection products within 120 days.

In addition, the Regulation requires a comparative assessment to be performed when evaluating an application for authorisation of a plant protection product containing a candidate for substitution. This assessment shall weigh the risks and benefits of the product and consider the existence of alternative products or methods that may be significantly safer for human or animal health or the environment.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that plant protection products placed on the market do not adversely affect human or animal health or the environment, and it provides a framework for the authorisation and control of these products within the Community.

The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure a high level of protection of both human and animal health and the environment, while also safeguarding the competitiveness of Community agriculture. To achieve this, the Regulation sets out rules for the placing of plant protection products on the market, including the approval of active substances, safeners, and synergists, as well as the authorisation of plant protection products. 

Member States may authorise the provisional placement on the market of plant protection products containing an active substance not yet approved, provided that certain conditions are met, including that the decision on approval could not be finalised within a specified period, the dossier on the active substance is admissible, and the Member State concludes that the active substance can satisfy the requirements for approval. The authorisation shall define the plants or plant products and non-agricultural areas on which the plant protection product may be used, as well as the requirements relating to its placing on the market and use.

The Regulation also sets out the contents of authorisations, which shall include a classification of the plant protection product, the maximum dose per hectare, the period between the last application and harvest, and other requirements necessary to comply with the conditions and requirements provided for in the Regulation. Applicants for authorisation shall submit a complete and summary dossier for each point of the data requirements of the plant protection product, as well as other information, such as the reasons why the test and study reports submitted are necessary and a draft label.

In addition, the Regulation provides for the authorisation of low-risk plant protection products, which shall meet specific requirements, including that all active substances contained in the product are low-risk active substances, the product does not contain a substance of concern, and it complies with certain requirements set out in the Regulation. The Member State shall decide within 120 days whether to approve an application for authorisation of a low-risk plant protection product.

The Regulation also introduces a comparative assessment for plant protection products containing candidates for substitution, which shall be performed by Member States when evaluating an application for authorisation. This assessment shall weigh up the risks and benefits of the plant protection product and consider whether an authorised plant protection product or non-chemical control or prevention method already exists which is significantly safer for human or animal health or the environment.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that plant protection products are placed on the market and used in a way that minimises risks to human and animal health and the environment, while also allowing for the use of effective products to protect plants and plant products against harmful organisms.

This Regulation establishes a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the placing on the market and use of plant protection products, which are a type of pesticide. The statistics will cover the annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, and will serve the purposes of Directive 2009/128/EC, particularly in relation to the sustainable use of pesticides. 

Member States are required to collect data necessary for the specification of the characteristics of pesticides on an annual basis for those placed on the market, and in five-year periods for those used. They will use surveys, information on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, administrative sources, or a combination of these means, including statistical estimation procedures, to collect the data. The data will be transmitted to the Commission (Eurostat) in electronic form, in a specified technical format, and will be presented in accordance with a given classification.

The Commission (Eurostat) will aggregate the data before publication, taking into account the protection of confidential data at the level of individual Member State. The confidential data will be used exclusively for statistical purposes. Member States will also provide reports on the quality of the data transmitted, and the Commission (Eurostat) will assess the quality of the data.

The Regulation also sets out quality criteria for the data, which are laid down in Regulation (EC) No 223/2009. The Commission may adopt implementing measures, including the technical format for the transmission of data and the definition of certain terms, in accordance with specified regulatory procedures. The Commission will also submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation every five years, evaluating the quality of the data, the data collection methods, and the usefulness of the statistics.

The Regulation applies to Member States, which are required to compile statistics on the use of pesticides for each selected crop within a reference period. The data will be transmitted to the Commission (Eurostat) within 12 months of the end of each five-year period and will be published, with a view to providing information to the public. The Regulation also sets out a harmonized classification of substances, including fungicides, herbicides, and other types of pesticides, which will be used for the purposes of the statistics.

This Regulation aims to establish a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, which are plant protection products. The statistics will cover the annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, as specified in Annexes I and II, respectively. These statistics will serve the purposes of Articles 4 and 15 of Directive 2009/128/EC, particularly in relation to the Thematic Strategy on the Sustainable Use of Pesticides.

Member States are required to collect the necessary data on an annual basis for the characteristics listed in Annex I and in five-year periods for those listed in Annex II. They can use various methods to collect this data, including surveys, information on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, administrative sources, or a combination of these methods. The data must be transmitted to the Commission (Eurostat) in electronic form, in accordance with a technical format to be adopted by the Commission, and presented according to the classification given in Annex III.

The Commission (Eurostat) will aggregate the data before publication, taking into account the protection of confidential data at the level of individual Member State. Confidential data will only be used for statistical purposes by national authorities and the Commission (Eurostat). Member States must also provide reports on the quality of the data transmitted, which will be assessed by the Commission (Eurostat) according to the quality criteria laid down in Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 223/2009.

The Commission is empowered to adopt implementing measures, including the technical format for data transmission and the definition of the 'area treated' as referred to in Annex II. The Commission will also adapt the list of substances to be covered and their classification in categories of products and chemical classes on a regular basis. Every five years, the Commission will submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council on the implementation of the Regulation, evaluating the quality of data transmitted, data collection methods, and the usefulness of these statistics. This report may contain proposals to improve data quality and collection methods, reducing the burden on businesses, agricultural holdings, and national administrations.

This Regulation establishes a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the placing on the market and use of plant protection products, which are pesticides intended for protecting plants or plant products against harmful organisms. The statistics will apply to the annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, and will serve the purposes of Directive 2009/128/EC, including the evaluation of the sustainability of pesticide use. 

Member States are required to collect data necessary for the specification of the characteristics of pesticides, using methods such as surveys, information on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, administrative sources, or a combination of these means. The data will be collected on an annual basis for the characteristics listed in Annex I and in five-year periods for the characteristics listed in Annex II. Member States will transmit the statistical results, including confidential data, to the Commission (Eurostat) in electronic form, in accordance with the schedules and periodicity specified in Annexes I and II.

The Commission (Eurostat) will aggregate the data before publication, taking into account the protection of confidential data at the level of individual Member State. The confidential data will be used exclusively for statistical purposes, in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 223/2009. The quality of the data transmitted will be assessed by the Commission (Eurostat), based on the quality criteria laid down in Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 223/2009.

The Commission is empowered to adopt implementing measures, including the definition of the 'area treated', the adaptation of the list of substances to be covered and their classification in categories of products and chemical classes, and the modification of requirements relating to the provision of quality reports. The Commission will submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council every five years, evaluating the quality of data transmitted, the data collection methods, the burden on businesses and national administrations, and the usefulness of these statistics in the context of the Thematic Strategy on the Sustainable Use of Pesticides.

The Regulation applies to plant protection products, which are products consisting of or containing active substances, safeners, or synergists, and intended for uses such as protecting plants or plant products against harmful organisms, influencing the life processes of plants, preserving plant products, destroying undesired plants, or checking undesired growth of plants. Active substances are substances, including micro-organisms, having general or specific action against harmful organisms or on plants, parts of plants, or plant products. Safeners are substances or preparations added to a plant protection product to eliminate or reduce phytotoxic effects, while synergists are substances or preparations that can give enhanced activity to the active substance(s) in a plant protection product.

This Regulation establishes a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, which are plant protection products. The statistics will cover the annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, and will serve the purposes of assessing policies on sustainable development and calculating indicators on the risks for health and the environment related to pesticide use. The Regulation applies to Member States, which are required to collect data on the characteristics of pesticides listed in Annexes I and II, using surveys, information on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, administrative sources, or a combination of these means. Member States will transmit the statistical results, including confidential data, to the Commission (Eurostat) in accordance with the schedules and periodicity specified in Annexes I and II. The Commission will aggregate the data before publication, taking due account of the protection of confidential data at the level of individual Member State, and will use the confidential data exclusively for statistical purposes.

The Regulation also sets out quality assessment requirements, with Member States providing reports on the quality of the data transmitted, and the Commission assessing the quality of the data. The Commission may adopt implementing measures, such as defining the technical format for the transmission of data, modifying requirements for quality reports, and adapting the list of substances to be covered and their classification. The Commission will submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council every five years, evaluating the quality of data transmitted, data collection methods, and the usefulness of the statistics.

The Regulation is based on the reference framework established by Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 on European statistics, which requires conformity to standards of professional independence, impartiality, objectivity, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and statistical confidentiality. The transmission and publication of data are governed by the rules set out in Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, which ensure the physical and logical protection of confidential data and prevent unlawful disclosure and non-statistical use. The Regulation applies without prejudice to other Community legislation and policies, and its implementation is subject to the principle of subsidiarity and proportionality.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a framework for the development, revision, and use of the EU Ecolabel, a voluntary label that identifies products with reduced environmental impact. The Regulation applies to all products that wish to bear the EU Ecolabel, regardless of their origin. The development and revision of EU Ecolabel criteria are initiated and led by the Commission, Member States, competent bodies, and other stakeholders, who must demonstrate expertise in the product area and lead the process with neutrality. The criteria development procedure involves the production of several documents, including a preliminary report, a proposal for draft criteria, and a final report, which are submitted to the Commission and the European Union Eco-Labelling Board (EUEB).

The Commission establishes specific EU Ecolabel criteria for each product group, taking into account the working plan and the comments of the EUEB. The criteria include requirements for assessing the compliance of specific products with EU Ecolabel criteria, as well as specifications for the period of validity of the criteria and the degree of product variability allowed. When establishing EU Ecolabel criteria, care is taken not to introduce measures that may impose disproportionate administrative and economic burdens on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Operators who wish to use the EU Ecolabel must apply to the competent bodies, providing full contact details, a description of the product, and all relevant documentation. The competent body checks the documentation, verifies that the product complies with the EU Ecolabel criteria and assessment requirements, and assigns a registration number to the product. The use of the EU Ecolabel is conditional upon the payment of fees, and operators must meet the costs of testing and assessment of conformity with EU Ecolabel criteria.

The competent bodies are responsible for market surveillance and control of the use of the EU Ecolabel, including verifying that products comply with the EU Ecolabel criteria and assessment requirements on a regular basis. They may undertake on-site verifications, request access to premises, and prohibit the use of the EU Ecolabel if a product does not comply with the relevant criteria. The Commission establishes a common register of products that have been awarded the EU Ecolabel, which is publicly available on a website dedicated to the EU Ecolabel. The EU Ecolabel may only be used on products that comply with the EU Ecolabel criteria and for which the EU Ecolabel has been awarded, and its use is without prejudice to environmental or other regulatory requirements of Community or national law.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a framework for the development, revision, and use of the EU Ecolabel, a voluntary label that identifies products with reduced environmental impact. The Regulation applies to all products that wish to bear the EU Ecolabel, regardless of their origin, and sets out the rules for the development and revision of EU Ecolabel criteria, the establishment of these criteria, and the award and use of the EU Ecolabel.

The development and revision of EU Ecolabel criteria are initiated and led by the Commission, Member States, competent bodies, and other stakeholders, following consultation with the European Union Eco-Labelling Board (EUEB). These stakeholders must demonstrate expertise in the product area and the ability to lead the process with neutrality. The purpose of this regulation is to establish a governance framework for freight corridors, which are designated rail routes for the transportation of goods. Each freight corridor is to be managed by two boards: an executive board and a management board. The executive board, composed of representatives of the authorities of the Member States concerned, is responsible for defining the general objectives of the freight corridor and supervising the measures taken by the management board. The management board, composed of representatives of the infrastructure managers, is responsible for taking measures to implement the freight corridor plan, including drawing up an implementation plan and an investment plan, and coordinating the use of interoperable IT applications.

The management board is also required to establish two advisory groups: one composed of managers and owners of terminals, and the other composed of railway undertakings interested in using the freight corridor. These advisory groups may issue opinions on proposals by the management board, which the management board must take into account. In the event of disagreement, the advisory groups may refer the matter to the executive board, which shall act as an intermediary.

The regulation applies to Member States and infrastructure managers concerned by a freight corridor, and requires them to cooperate within the boards to ensure the development of the freight corridor in accordance with its implementation plan. The executive board and the management board are to take their decisions on the basis of mutual consent of their respective members.

The implementation plan, which must be drawn up by the management board and approved by the executive board, is to include a description of the characteristics of the freight corridor, the objectives for the freight corridor, an investment plan, and measures to implement the provisions of the regulation. The investment plan is to include details of indicative medium and long-term investment for infrastructure in the freight corridor, and is to be submitted for approval to the executive board.

The regulation also sets out rules for the allocation of capacity to freight trains on the freight corridor. The executive board is to define the framework for the allocation of infrastructure capacity, and the management board is to evaluate the need for capacity to be allocated to freight trains. Infrastructure managers are to jointly define and organise international pre-arranged train paths for freight trains, and are to facilitate journey times, frequencies, and routings suitable for freight transport services. The regulation also provides for the reservation of capacity for international freight trains and for the promotion of coordination of priority rules relating to capacity allocation.
