The purpose of this EU legal act is to establish a framework for the participation of Member States in the North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC) Scheme, which aims to promote the sustainable management of fishery resources in the Regulatory Area. The act applies to Member States whose fishing vessels are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area. These Member States are required to send to the Commission a list of all vessels flying their flag and registered in the Union that are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area, including any amendments to the list, by 15 December each year or no later than 5 days before the vessel enters the Regulatory Area.

Member States are also obliged to inform the Commission by computer transmission before the 15th day of each month of the quantities of fishery resources caught in the Regulatory Area by vessels flying their flag, as well as the quantities of regulated resources caught in areas under the national fisheries jurisdiction of third countries and in EU waters of the Convention Area. The format for transmission of this data shall be determined in accordance with Article 50(2). The Commission shall compile the data for all Member States and forward it to the NEAFC Secretary within 30 days following the calendar month in which the catches were landed or transhipped.

In addition, Member States whose fishing vessels are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area shall assign inspectors to the Scheme to carry out surveillance and inspection. The Commission or the body designated by it shall coordinate the surveillance and inspection activities for the Union and draw up each year a joint deployment plan for Union participation in the Scheme. Inspectors shall carry out inspections in a non-discriminatory manner and in accordance with the Scheme, and shall avoid the use of force except in cases of legitimate self-defence.

Member States shall also designate and notify the Commission of ports where the landing or transhipment of fishery resources frozen after being caught in the Convention Area by fishing vessels flying the flag of another Contracting Party are permitted. Landings and transhipments of fish frozen after being caught in the Convention Area by fishing vessels flying the flag of another Contracting Party shall only be allowed in designated ports.

In the event of a serious infringement, the inspector shall promptly notify the infringement to the Commission or the body designated by it, the competent authorities of the flag state of the inspected fishing vessel, and the flag state or states of the donor vessels where the inspected vessel has engaged in transhipment operations. The flag Member State shall respond to the notification without delay and ensure that the fishing vessel concerned is inspected within 72 hours by an inspector duly authorised in relation to the infringement.

The act also provides for inspections at sea, where NEAFC inspectors may request permission to board and inspect non-Contracting Party vessels sighted or otherwise identified as engaging in fishing activities in the Convention Area. If the master consents to the boarding and inspection, the inspection shall be documented by the completion of an inspection report. If the master does not consent or does not fulfil any one of the obligations laid down, the vessel shall be presumed to have engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing activities.

Each Member State shall report to the Commission or the body designated by it by 15 February each year for the previous calendar year, providing information on the number of inspections of non-Contracting Party vessels conducted, the names of the vessels inspected, and the results of such inspections. The act aims to ensure the effective implementation of the NEAFC Scheme and promote the sustainable management of fishery resources in the Regulatory Area.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish a framework for the participation of European Union member states in the Northeast Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC) Scheme, which aims to conserve and manage fishery resources in the Regulatory Area. Member states are required to send a list of vessels flying their flag and registered in the Union, which are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area, to the Commission in a computer-readable form by 15 December each year or no later than 5 days before the vessel enters the Regulatory Area. The Commission will then forward this information to the NEAFC Secretary.

Member states must also inform the Commission by computer transmission before the 15th day of each month of the quantities of fishery resources caught in the Regulatory Area by vessels flying their flag, as well as the quantities of regulated resources caught in areas under the national fisheries jurisdiction of third countries and in EU waters of the Convention Area. The Commission will compile the data for all member states and forward it to the NEAFC Secretary within 30 days following the calendar month in which the catches were landed or transhipped.

In addition, member states whose fishing vessels are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area must assign inspectors to the Scheme to carry out surveillance and inspection. The Commission or the body designated by it will coordinate the surveillance and inspection activities for the Union and draw up a joint deployment plan for Union participation in the Scheme each year. Inspectors must carry out inspections in a non-discriminatory manner and in accordance with the Scheme, and member states must ensure that inspectors from another contracting party are permitted to carry out inspections on board vessels flying their flag.

Member states must also designate and notify the Commission of ports where the landing or transhipment of fishery resources frozen after being caught in the Convention Area by fishing vessels flying the flag of another contracting party are permitted. Landings and transhipments of fish frozen after being caught in the Convention Area by fishing vessels flying the flag of another contracting party shall only be allowed in designated ports.

In cases of serious infringements, inspectors must promptly notify the Commission, the competent authorities of the flag state of the inspected fishing vessel, and the flag state or states of the donor vessels, and transmit a copy to the NEAFC Secretary. The inspector must take all necessary measures to ensure the security and continuity of evidence while minimising inconvenience to the vessel and interference with its operation. Serious infringements include fishing without a valid authorisation, fishing without quota or after its exhaustion, use of prohibited fishing gear, and serious misrecording of catches, among others.

Overall, this regulation aims to ensure the effective implementation of the NEAFC Scheme and the conservation and management of fishery resources in the Regulatory Area, while also providing a framework for cooperation and enforcement among member states and contracting parties.

This EU regulation establishes a scheme of control and enforcement applicable to fishing vessels operating in the North-East Atlantic fisheries area, with the aim of ensuring compliance with conservation and management measures adopted by the North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC). The regulation applies to Member States whose fishing vessels are authorised to fish in the Regulatory Area, and requires them to assign inspectors to the Scheme to carry out surveillance and inspection. Member States must also inform the Commission of the quantities of fishery resources caught in the Regulatory Area by vessels flying their flag, as well as in areas under the national fisheries jurisdiction of third countries and in EU waters of the Convention Area. The Commission will compile the data and forward it to the NEAFC Secretary.

The regulation also sets out rules for the designation of ports where the landing or transhipment of fishery resources is permitted, and requires Member States to ensure that their inspectors comply with the inspection procedures laid down by NEAFC. In cases of serious infringements, inspectors must notify the Commission, the flag state of the inspected vessel, and the NEAFC Secretary, and take measures to preserve evidence while minimising inconvenience to the vessel. The regulation also provides for a new Port State Control system, which will effectively close European ports to landings and transhipments of frozen fish that have not been verified to be legal by the flag state of the fishing vessel.

The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts and implementing acts to implement the regulation, and to incorporate future amendments to the Scheme into Union law. The regulation repeals Council Regulation (EC) No 2791/1999, which laid down certain control measures applicable in the area covered by the Convention. Overall, the regulation aims to promote compliance by vessels flying the flag of a Contracting Party with the control and enforcement measures, and to ensure full respect of conservation and management measures adopted by NEAFC.

The purpose of this regulation is to ensure that disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility have equal access to bus and coach transport, and to provide them with assistance and protection against discrimination. Carriers, travel agents, and tour operators are prohibited from refusing to accept a reservation or provide a ticket to a person on the grounds of disability or reduced mobility, unless there are safety or operational concerns that cannot be overcome. In such cases, the carrier must inform the person of any acceptable alternative services. 

If a disabled person or person with reduced mobility is refused permission to board due to their disability or reduced mobility, they shall be offered reimbursement or continuation of their journey by alternative transport services. The regulation also allows for the accompaniment of a disabled person or person with reduced mobility by another person, who shall be transported free of charge. Carriers, travel agents, and tour operators must provide non-discriminatory access conditions and make them publicly available, including information on safety requirements and accessible formats.

Carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide assistance free of charge to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility at designated terminals and on board buses and coaches, subject to certain conditions. The conditions for providing assistance include notification of the need for assistance at least 36 hours in advance and presentation at a designated point at a stipulated time. If no notification is made, carriers and terminal managing bodies must make every reasonable effort to provide assistance. 

In cases of cancelled or delayed departures, carriers must offer passengers free snacks, meals, or refreshments, as well as hotel rooms or other accommodation if necessary, with particular attention to the needs of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility. Finally, carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide passengers with information regarding their rights under this regulation, including contact details of the enforcement body, and make this information available in accessible formats upon request.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish rules for bus and coach transport, including non-discrimination between passengers, rights of passengers in the event of accidents, non-discrimination and mandatory assistance for disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, and rights of passengers in cases of cancellation or delay. The Regulation applies to passengers travelling with regular services for non-specified categories of passengers where the boarding or the alighting point of the passengers is situated in the territory of a Member State and where the scheduled distance of the service is 250 km or more. It also applies to passengers travelling with occasional services where the initial boarding point or the final alighting point of the passenger is situated in the territory of a Member State, with some exceptions.

Carriers, travel agents, and tour operators are prohibited from refusing to accept a reservation from, to issue or otherwise provide a ticket to, or to take on board, a person on the grounds of disability or of reduced mobility, unless there are safety or operational concerns. Reservations and tickets must be offered to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility at no additional cost. In cases where a disabled person or person with reduced mobility is refused permission to board due to their disability or reduced mobility, they must be offered the choice between reimbursement and continuation of the journey or re-routing by reasonable alternative transport services.

Carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide assistance free of charge to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility at designated terminals and on board buses and coaches, subject to certain access conditions. The access conditions must be made publicly available in accessible formats, and tour operators must make available the access conditions that apply to journeys included in package travel. Carriers, travel agents, and tour operators must also ensure that all relevant general information concerning the journey and the conditions of carriage is available in appropriate and accessible formats for disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility.

To receive assistance, disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility must notify the carrier, travel agent, or tour operator of their need for assistance at least 36 hours in advance, and present themselves at the designated point at the stipulated time. If no notification is made, carriers, terminal managing bodies, travel agents, and tour operators must make every reasonable effort to ensure that the assistance is provided. The Regulation also requires that terminal managing bodies designate a point inside or outside the terminal where disabled persons or persons with reduced mobility can announce their arrival and request assistance.

The person may also request to be accompanied by another person of their own choosing who is capable of providing the assistance required, and the accompanying person shall be transported free of charge. The Regulation also requires that access conditions, including safety requirements, be made publicly available by carriers and terminal managing bodies in accessible formats.

The Regulation aims to ensure a high level of protection for passengers in bus and coach transport, comparable to other modes of transport. It establishes rules for the rights of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, ensuring they have opportunities for using bus and coach services that are comparable to those of other citizens. Carriers, travel agents, and tour operators are prohibited from refusing to accept a reservation or provide a ticket to a person on the grounds of disability or reduced mobility, except in cases where safety requirements or the design of vehicles or infrastructure make it physically impossible to transport them in a safe and operationally feasible manner.

In cases where a disabled person or person with reduced mobility is refused transport, they must be informed of the reasons for the refusal and offered alternative services. If a person is refused permission to board due to their disability or reduced mobility, they must be offered the choice between reimbursement and continuation of their journey or re-routing by alternative transport services. Accompanying persons who provide assistance to disabled persons or persons with reduced mobility must be transported free of charge and seated next to the person they are assisting.

Carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide assistance free of charge to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility at designated terminals and on board buses and coaches, subject to access conditions. The access conditions, including safety requirements and the design of vehicles or infrastructure, must be made publicly available in accessible formats. Passengers must notify carriers, travel agents, or tour operators of their need for assistance at least 36 hours in advance, and present themselves at the designated point at the stipulated time.

The Regulation also establishes rules for passenger rights in the event of cancellation or delay, ensuring that passengers are granted a minimum level of protection. Overall, the Regulation aims to promote non-discrimination and provide assistance to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, ensuring they have equal opportunities to use bus and coach services.

This Regulation sets out the rules for the labelling and marking of textile products, with the aim of ensuring that consumers are provided with accurate and reliable information about the fibre composition of these products. For the purposes of this Regulation, a textile product is defined as any product that is exclusively composed of textile fibres, regardless of the mixing or assembly process employed. The Regulation applies to all textile products, including raw, semi-worked, worked, semi-manufactured, manufactured, semi-made-up, and made-up products.

The Regulation requires that the fibre composition of textile products be labelled or marked, and it sets out specific rules for the labelling and marking of different types of textile products. For example, the names listed in Annex III may be used to describe wool contained in a textile fibre mixture if certain conditions are met, including that all the wool contained in the mixture satisfies the requirements defined in the Regulation, and that the wool accounts for not less than 25% of the total weight of the mixture.

The Regulation also sets out tolerances for the fibre composition of textile products, which are permitted to allow for minor variations in the fibre composition that may occur during the manufacturing process. For example, a manufacturing tolerance of 3% is permitted between the stated fibre composition and the percentages obtained from analysis carried out in accordance with the Regulation. The Regulation also sets out rules for the calculation of the mass of fibres contained in a textile product, including the use of agreed allowances to calculate the mass of fibres.

In terms of who the Regulation applies to, it applies to all manufacturers and suppliers of textile products, who are required to ensure that the products they supply comply with the labelling and marking requirements set out in the Regulation. The Regulation also sets out rules for the authorisation of higher tolerances in exceptional cases, where the manufacturing process requires tolerances higher than those laid down in the Regulation. In such cases, the manufacturer must submit a request for authorisation to the Commission, providing sufficient reasons for and evidence of the exceptional manufacturing circumstances.

Overall, the Regulation aims to provide consumers with accurate and reliable information about the fibre composition of textile products, and to ensure that manufacturers and suppliers of these products comply with the labelling and marking requirements set out in the Regulation.

This Regulation sets out the rules for the labelling and marking of textile products, with the aim of providing consumers with accurate information about the fibre composition of these products. For the purposes of this Regulation, a textile product is defined as any product exclusively composed of textile fibres, regardless of the mixing or assembly process employed. The Regulation applies to all textile products, including raw, semi-worked, worked, semi-manufactured, manufactured, semi-made-up, and made-up products.

The Regulation requires that the fibre composition of textile products be indicated on a label or by marking, and that this information be accurate and not misleading. The fibre composition must be expressed as a percentage of the total weight of the product, and must take into account the presence of extraneous fibres, which are fibres other than those stated on the label or marking. However, the presence of extraneous fibres does not need to be indicated if the percentage of those fibres does not reach certain thresholds, specifically 2% of the total weight of the textile product, or 5% of the total weight in the case of textile products which have undergone a carding process.

The Regulation also allows for certain tolerances in the fibre composition, specifically a manufacturing tolerance of 3% between the stated fibre composition and the percentages obtained from analysis. This tolerance applies to the total weight of fibres shown on the label or marking, and also to fibres which may be designated by the term 'other fibres'. The cumulative application of tolerances is permitted only if any extraneous fibres found by analysis prove to be of the same chemical type as one or more of the fibres shown on the label or marking.

In exceptional cases, the Commission may authorise higher tolerances for particular textile products, provided that the manufacturer submits a request with sufficient reasons and evidence of the exceptional manufacturing circumstances. The Regulation also sets out rules for the determination of fibre compositions, including the application of agreed allowances and the removal of certain items.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that consumers have access to accurate and reliable information about the fibre composition of textile products, and to prevent misleading or deceptive labelling practices. It applies to all textile products, including disposable products, and requires manufacturers to provide accurate and complete information about the fibre composition of their products.

This Regulation sets out the rules for the labelling and marking of textile products, with the aim of ensuring that consumers are provided with accurate information about the fibre composition of these products. The Regulation applies to all textile products, which are defined as any raw, semi-worked, worked, semi-manufactured, manufactured, semi-made-up or made-up product that is exclusively composed of textile fibres. The Regulation also defines various terms related to textile products, such as "textile fibre", "apparent width", "textile component", "extraneous fibres", "lining", "labelling", and "marking".

The Regulation allows for certain derogations from the standard labelling requirements, such as the use of specific names to describe wool contained in a textile fibre mixture, provided that certain conditions are met. For example, the wool must account for at least 25% of the total weight of the mixture, and the full percentage composition of the mixture must be given.

The Regulation also establishes tolerances for the fibre composition of textile products, which are allowed to vary from the stated composition by a certain percentage. For example, a manufacturing tolerance of 3% is permitted between the stated fibre composition and the percentages obtained from analysis. Additionally, the presence of extraneous fibres does not need to be indicated if the percentage of those fibres does not reach a certain threshold, such as 2% of the total weight of the textile product.

The Regulation also provides for the possibility of authorising higher tolerances in exceptional cases, where the manufacturing process requires it. In such cases, the manufacturer must submit a request for authorisation to the Commission, providing sufficient reasons and evidence for the exceptional manufacturing circumstances.

The fibre composition of textile products must be determined by applying the appropriate agreed allowance laid down in Annex IX, after having removed certain items set out in Annex VII. The Regulation also refers to various annexes, such as Annex I, Annex II, and Annex III, which contain specific information related to the fibre composition of textile products.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that consumers are provided with accurate and reliable information about the fibre composition of textile products, while also allowing for certain flexibility and exceptions in the labelling and marking requirements.

The Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 aims to harmonise the names of textile fibres and the indications appearing on labels, markings, and documents accompanying textile products throughout the European Union. It applies to textile products, which are defined as any raw, semi-worked, worked, semi-manufactured, manufactured, semi-made-up, or made-up product exclusively composed of textile fibres. The Regulation sets out definitions for various terms, including textile fibre, apparent width, textile component, extraneous fibres, lining, labelling, and marking.

The Regulation allows for certain derogations, such as the use of specific names to describe wool contained in a textile fibre mixture, provided that certain conditions are met. For instance, the wool must account for at least 25% of the total weight of the mixture, and the full percentage composition of the mixture must be given. The Regulation also establishes tolerances for the presence of extraneous fibres in textile products. For example, the presence of extraneous fibres does not need to be indicated if the percentage of those fibres does not reach 2% of the total weight of the textile product, provided that this quantity is technically unavoidable in good manufacturing practice.

The Regulation permits a manufacturing tolerance of 3% between the stated fibre composition and the percentages obtained from analysis. This tolerance applies to fibres that may be designated by the term 'other fibres' and to the percentage of wool referred to in the derogation provision. The cumulative application of tolerances is permitted only if any extraneous fibres found by analysis prove to be of the same chemical type as one or more of the fibres shown on the label or marking.

The Regulation also sets out rules for the labelling and marking of textile products, including the requirement to indicate the presence of non-textile parts of animal origin. It provides for the possibility of indicating the presence of small quantities of fibres requiring particular attention to keep the original quality of the textile product. The Regulation does not prevent economic operators from providing additional information on the label or marking, as long as it is not misleading.

The Regulation applies to all textile products placed on the market in the European Union, with certain exemptions, such as products contracted out to persons working in their own homes or to independent firms, and customised textile products made up by self-employed tailors. The market surveillance of products covered by this Regulation is subject to Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 and Directive 2001/95/EC. The Regulation lays down methods for the sampling and analysis of textile products to exclude any possibility of objections to the methods used, and it provides for the use of uniform methods of analysis of textile products composed of binary and ternary fibre mixtures.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a set of sanctions to be imposed on Member States that fail to comply with their budgetary policy obligations under the Stability and Growth Pact. The sanctions are designed to be effective, dissuasive, and proportionate to the nature, seriousness, and duration of the non-compliance. The Regulation applies to all Member States, and the sanctions are imposed by the Council, acting on a recommendation from the Commission.

The key obligations of the Regulation are that Member States must lodge interest-bearing deposits, non-interest-bearing deposits, or pay fines, depending on the nature and severity of their non-compliance. If a Member State fails to take action in response to a Council recommendation, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge an interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. If the Council decides that an excessive deficit exists in a Member State, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge a non-interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. If the Council decides that a Member State has not taken effective action to correct its excessive deficit, the Commission shall recommend that the Council impose a fine amounting to 0.2% of the Member State's GDP in the preceding year.

The Regulation also provides for the possibility of reducing or cancelling the sanctions in cases of exceptional economic circumstances or following a reasoned request by the Member State concerned. The Commission may conduct investigations into the misrepresentation of deficit and debt data, and the Council may impose fines on Member States that intentionally or by serious negligence misrepresent such data.

The Regulation is subject to review every five years, with the Commission publishing a report on its application, including an evaluation of its effectiveness and the progress made in ensuring closer coordination of economic policies and sustained convergence of economic performances of the Member States. The report may be accompanied by a proposal for amendments to the Regulation, and is forwarded to the European Parliament and the Council. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that Member States comply with their budgetary policy obligations, and to promote the proper functioning of the monetary union.

This Regulation establishes a system of sanctions to strengthen the enforcement of the Stability and Growth Pact in the euro area, applying to all Member States whose currency is the euro. The sanctions are designed to address situations where a Member State fails to take action in response to a Council recommendation or has an excessive deficit. In such cases, the Commission may recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge an interest-bearing deposit, amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. The deposit shall bear an interest rate reflecting the Commission's credit risk and the relevant investment period. If the situation giving rise to the Council's recommendation no longer exists, the Council may decide to return the deposit and the interest accrued to the Member State.

In addition to interest-bearing deposits, the Regulation also provides for non-interest-bearing deposits and fines. A non-interest-bearing deposit may be required if the Council decides that an excessive deficit exists in a Member State, or if the Commission identifies particularly serious non-compliance with budgetary policy obligations. The deposit shall be lodged with the Commission, and if the amount of an interest-bearing deposit lodged earlier exceeds the amount of the non-interest-bearing deposit, the excess shall be returned to the Member State. Fines may be imposed if the Council decides that a Member State has not taken effective action to correct its excessive deficit. The fine shall amount to 0.2% of the Member State's GDP in the preceding year, and if a non-interest-bearing deposit has been lodged, it shall be converted into the fine.

The Regulation also addresses the manipulation of statistics, allowing the Council to impose a fine on a Member State that intentionally or by serious negligence misrepresents deficit and debt data. The fine shall be effective, dissuasive, and proportionate to the nature, seriousness, and duration of the misrepresentation. The Commission may conduct investigations to establish the existence of misrepresentations and shall respect the rights of defence of the Member State concerned.

The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Council imposing fines. The Commission shall publish a report on the application of this Regulation every five years, evaluating its effectiveness and the progress in ensuring closer coordination of economic policies and sustained convergence of economic performances of the Member States. The report may be accompanied by a proposal for amendments to the Regulation. Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the enforcement of the Stability and Growth Pact and promote fiscal discipline among Member States in the euro area.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a system of sanctions to enhance the enforcement of the preventive and corrective parts of the Stability and Growth Pact in the euro area. The Regulation applies to Member States whose currency is the euro. In the event that a Member State fails to take action in response to a Council recommendation, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge an interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. The deposit shall bear an interest rate reflecting the Commission's credit risk and the relevant investment period. If the situation giving rise to the Council's recommendation no longer exists, the Council shall decide that the deposit and the interest accrued thereon be returned to the Member State concerned.

In cases where the Council decides that an excessive deficit exists in a Member State, or where the Commission identifies particularly serious non-compliance with budgetary policy obligations, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge a non-interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. If the Member State has already lodged an interest-bearing deposit, it shall be converted to a non-interest-bearing deposit. The Commission may recommend that the Council reduce or cancel the deposit on grounds of exceptional economic circumstances or following a reasoned request by the Member State.

Furthermore, if the Council decides that a Member State has not taken effective action to correct its excessive deficit, the Commission shall recommend that the Council impose a fine amounting to 0.2% of the Member State's GDP in the preceding year. The fine shall be imposed unless the Council decides by a qualified majority to reject the Commission's recommendation. If the Member State has lodged a non-interest-bearing deposit, it shall be converted into the fine. The Commission may recommend that the Council reduce or cancel the fine on grounds of exceptional economic circumstances or following a reasoned request by the Member State. The Regulation also provides for annual assessments by the Council to determine whether a Member State has taken effective action in response to a Council notice, and for the intensification of sanctions if the Member State has not complied. Any single deposit or fine imposed shall not exceed an upper limit of 0.5% of GDP.

The Regulation on the effective enforcement of budgetary surveillance in the euro area aims to strengthen economic governance and ensure the proper functioning of the economic and monetary union. It introduces a set of sanctions to enforce compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact (SGP), which includes interest-bearing deposits, non-interest-bearing deposits, and fines. If the Council decides that a Member State has failed to take action in response to a recommendation, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge an interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. The deposit shall bear an interest rate reflecting the Commission's credit risk and the relevant investment period. The Council may amend the Commission's recommendation and adopt the text so amended as a Council decision. 

In cases where the Council decides that an excessive deficit exists in a Member State, or where the Commission has identified particularly serious non-compliance with budgetary policy obligations, the Commission shall recommend that the Council require the Member State to lodge a non-interest-bearing deposit amounting to 0.2% of its GDP in the preceding year. The non-interest-bearing deposit shall be lodged with the Commission, and if the Member State has already lodged an interest-bearing deposit, it shall be converted into a non-interest-bearing deposit. 

If the Council decides that a Member State has not taken effective action to correct its excessive deficit, the Commission shall recommend that the Council impose a fine amounting to 0.2% of the Member State's GDP in the preceding year. The fine shall be imposed unless the Council decides by a qualified majority to reject the Commission's recommendation within 10 days. The Commission may recommend that the Council reduce the amount of the fine or cancel it on grounds of exceptional economic circumstances or following a reasoned request by the Member State concerned. 

The Regulation applies to Member States whose currency is the euro, and its provisions are designed to ensure fair, timely, graduated, and effective mechanisms for compliance with the preventive and corrective parts of the SGP. The Commission shall carry out surveillance missions and undertake broad evaluations of the economic governance system at regular intervals, complemented by relevant proposals if necessary. The Regulation also provides for a closer and more timely involvement of the European Parliament and national parliaments in the economic governance framework. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the credibility of the fiscal surveillance framework of the Union and ensure that Member States conduct economic policies that promote the proper functioning of the economic and monetary union. The sanctions introduced by the Regulation are designed to be effective, graduated, and fair, and to provide a strong incentive for Member States to comply with their budgetary obligations.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish a framework for the management of fishing activities in the GFCM Agreement area, with the aim of ensuring the long-term sustainability of fish stocks and the protection of the marine environment. To achieve this, the regulation sets out key obligations for Member States, including the requirement to issue fishing authorisations to vessels that meet certain criteria, such as having a record of fishing in the area prior to 31 December 2008. Vessels that do not meet these criteria are not authorised to start fishing in the area.

Member States are also required to communicate certain information to the Commission, including national legislation concerning fishing activities, such as the maximum number of hours per day a vessel is permitted to engage in fishing activity, and the maximum number of days per week a vessel is permitted to stay at sea. Additionally, Member States must submit reports on fishing activities carried out in the area, including the number of vessels involved, total landings, and transhipments of certain species.

The regulation applies to fishing vessels of more than 15 metres in overall length that are flying the flag of a Member State and are registered in its territory. These vessels must be included in a list sent to the Commission by each Member State, which includes information such as the vessel's EU Fleet Register number, external marking, and the period during which fishing and/or transhipment is authorised. Vessels that are not included in this list are not permitted to fish, retain on board, tranship, or land any type of fish or shellfish within the GFCM Agreement area.

Member States must also take measures to ensure that only vessels that are included in the list and hold a valid fishing authorisation are permitted to carry out fishing activities in the area. Furthermore, Member States must prohibit fishing, retention on board, transhipment, and landing of fish and shellfish caught in the area by vessels that are not on the GFCM register. In cases where there are strong reasons to suspect that a vessel is fishing or transhipping in the area without being on the register, Member States must communicate this information to the Commission without delay.

In addition to these measures, the regulation also sets out rules for the use of ports by third-country vessels. Member States are not allowed to permit these vessels to use their ports for landing, transhipping, or processing fisheries products caught in the GFCM Agreement area, unless they comply with the requirements of the regulation and have a valid authorisation to engage in fishing or fishing-related activities in the area. However, in situations of force majeure or distress, Member States may allow a third-country vessel to use their ports for services strictly necessary to remedy the situation. Overall, the regulation aims to promote sustainable fishing practices and prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing in the GFCM Agreement area.

This Regulation sets out the rules for the application of conservation, management, exploitation, monitoring, marketing, and enforcement measures for fishery and aquaculture products established by the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean. The Regulation applies to vessels authorised to fish in a designated area, which includes a fisheries restricted area established in the eastern Gulf of Lions. To fish in this area, vessels must be issued with a fishing authorisation by their Member State, in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009. Vessels without prior records of fishing in the area before 31 December 2008 are not eligible for authorisation.

Member States are required to communicate various information to the Commission, including national legislation concerning fishing activities, reports on fishing activities carried out in the area, and data on fisheries catch and fishing effort. They must also set up a system for collecting and treating fisheries data and report on the number of vessels involved in the fishery, as well as total landings and transhipments of common dolphinfish. The Commission may adopt implementing acts to specify the format and transmission of these reports.

The Regulation also establishes a register of authorised vessels, which must be updated annually by each Member State. The register includes information on the vessel's EU Fleet Register number, external marking, authorised fishing period, and fishing gears used. Member States must ensure that only authorised vessels are permitted to carry out fishing activities in the designated area and that vessels not on the register are prohibited from fishing, retaining on board, transhipping, or landing fish and shellfish.

Furthermore, Member States must take measures to prevent illegal, unregulated, and unreported fishing, including prohibiting fishing authorisations for vessels with a history of such activities. They must also ensure that their national legislation requires owners of authorised vessels to be nationals or legal entities within the flag Member State and that their vessels comply with all relevant conservation and management measures. Any changes to the list of authorised vessels must be notified to the Commission at least 10 working days before the vessel begins fishing activity. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the sustainable management of fishery resources in the Mediterranean and to prevent illegal fishing activities.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to establish a framework for the management of fishing activities in the GFCM Agreement area, with the aim of ensuring the long-term sustainability of fish stocks and the protection of the marine environment. The act applies to Member States and their fishing vessels, and sets out key obligations and conditions for fishing in the area.

To fish in the area, vessels must be authorised by their Member State and issued with a fishing authorisation in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009. Vessels that do not have records of fishing in the area prior to 31 December 2008 are not eligible for authorisation. Member States must communicate their national legislation regarding fishing activities to the Commission, including rules on the maximum number of hours and days that vessels can engage in fishing activities.

Member States are also required to submit reports to the Commission on fishing activities carried out in the area, including the number of vessels involved, total landings, and transhipments of common dolphinfish. The Commission may adopt implementing acts to specify the format and transmission of these reports. Additionally, Member States must set up a system for collecting and treating fisheries catch and fishing effort data, and report to the Commission on the number of vessels involved in the fishery and the total landings and transhipments of common dolphinfish.

The act also establishes a register of authorised vessels, which must be updated annually by Member States and sent to the Commission. The register includes information on the vessel's EU Fleet Register number, external marking, and fishing gears used. Vessels that are not on the register are not permitted to fish, retain on board, tranship, or land any type of fish or shellfish within the GFCM Agreement area.

Member States must take measures to ensure that only authorised vessels can carry out fishing activities in the area, and that vessels that have engaged in illegal, unregulated, and unreported fishing are not issued with a fishing authorisation. They must also prohibit fishing, retention on board, transhipment, and landing of fish and shellfish caught in the area by vessels that are not on the register.

In terms of inspection and enforcement, Member States must carry out inspections of at least 5% of landing and transhipment operations by third-country fishing vessels each year, and inspect certain vessels in all cases, such as those reported in the framework of a notification made under the Community alert system. Officials in charge of inspections have the right to examine all relevant areas of the vessel and verify compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

Overall, the act aims to promote sustainable and responsible fishing practices in the GFCM Agreement area, and to prevent illegal, unregulated, and unreported fishing activities. It sets out a framework for the management of fishing activities, and establishes key obligations and conditions for Member States and their fishing vessels.

The purpose of this Regulation is to implement certain provisions for fishing in the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) Agreement area, which includes the Mediterranean and the Black Sea and connecting waters. The Regulation aims to promote the development, conservation, rational management, and best utilisation of living marine resources in the GFCM Agreement area at sustainable levels. It applies to all Member States whose fishing vessels operate in the GFCM Agreement area.

Member States are required to authorise vessels to fish in the area, and these vessels must be issued with a fishing authorisation in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009. Vessels that do not have records of fishing in the area prior to 31 December 2008 are not permitted to start fishing there. Member States must also communicate their national legislation regarding fishing activities, such as the maximum number of hours per day a vessel can engage in fishing activity, to the Commission by 16 February 2012.

The Regulation also establishes a system for collecting and treating fisheries catch and fishing effort data, which is essential for scientific advice and management measures. Member States must report to the Commission on the number of vessels involved in the fishery, as well as the total landings and transhipments of common dolphinfish, by 15 January each year. The Commission may adopt implementing acts regarding the format and transmission of these reports.

Furthermore, the Regulation sets out rules for the registration of authorised vessels. Member States must send an updated list of vessels authorised to fish in the GFCM Agreement area to the Commission by 1 December each year, which includes information such as the vessel's EU Fleet Register number, the period during which fishing and/or transhipment is authorised, and the fishing gears used. The Commission will then forward this information to the Executive Secretary of the GFCM.

The Regulation also prohibits fishing, retention on board, transhipment, and landing of fish and shellfish caught in the GFCM Agreement area by vessels that are not on the GFCM register. Member States must take measures to ensure that only authorised vessels are permitted to carry out fishing activities in the GFCM Agreement area and that vessels that have carried out illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing are not issued with a fishing authorisation.

In addition, the Regulation establishes a closed season for dolphinfish fisheries using fish aggregating devices and sets out rules for the use of certain fishing gears, such as trawling activities exploiting demersal stocks in the Black Sea. Member States must submit reports on the list of fishing vessels that conduct such activities and the percentage of vessels that are equipped with certain types of nets.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the sustainable exploitation of fishery resources in the GFCM Agreement area by implementing measures to prevent overfishing, protect sensitive habitats, and combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

The European Union's Regulation No 70/2012 aims to establish a common framework for compiling statistics on the carriage of goods by road within the EU. The regulation requires each Member State to collect statistical data on the carriage of goods by road using goods road transport vehicles registered in that Member State. The data collection covers various areas, including vehicle, journey, and goods-related information. The regulation defines key terms, such as "carriage of goods by road," "road transport vehicle," and "goods road transport vehicle," to ensure consistency in data collection.

The regulation applies to all Member States, except Malta, which is exempt due to its specific geographical situation and limited road network, provided that the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed for international carriage does not exceed 400 vehicles. Member States may also exclude certain vehicles from the scope of the regulation, such as those with a load capacity or maximum permissible weight below a specified limit.

The regulation sets out the statistical variables to be collected, including vehicle-related variables, such as axle configuration, age, and maximum permissible weight, as well as journey-related variables and goods-related variables. The data collection method is left to the discretion of the Member States, but they must refrain from carrying out formalities at frontiers between Member States. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to update the statistical variables and adapt the annexes to take account of economic and technical developments.

The regulation also requires the dissemination of statistical results no later than 12 months after the end of the period to which the results relate. The Commission will adopt rules on the dissemination of statistical results, including the structure and content of the results to be disseminated. The regulation entered into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

This Regulation aims to facilitate and support the activities of national authorities, the private sector, and Union institutions in the fight against infringements of intellectual property rights. The Office for Harmonization in the Internal Market (Trade Marks and Designs) is entrusted with tasks to achieve this goal, including improving understanding of the value of intellectual property, enhancing knowledge of best practices to protect intellectual property rights, and assisting in raising citizens' awareness of the impact of infringements. The Office shall also establish a transparent methodology for collecting and analyzing data on infringements, provide regular assessments and reports, and develop training programs for national officials involved in intellectual property rights protection.

The Office's tasks and activities are carried out in accordance with a work program adopted pursuant to Article 7 and in line with Union law. The Office shall comply with existing provisions of Union law on data protection and shall not participate in individual operations or investigations carried out by competent authorities. The Regulation applies to the Office, national authorities, and private-sector representatives, who are required to cooperate with the Office and provide information on their policies and strategies on intellectual property rights enforcement.

Member States are obliged to inform the Office of their overall policies and strategies on intellectual property rights enforcement, provide statistical data on infringements, and inform the Office of important case-law. This Regulation aims to establish an accelerated phasing-in scheme for the application of double-hull or equivalent design requirements to single-hull oil tankers, as defined in the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973, as amended by the Protocol of 1978 relating thereto. The Regulation also bans the transport of heavy grade oil in single-hull oil tankers to or from ports of the Member States. The scope of the Regulation applies to oil tankers of 5,000 tonnes deadweight and above, which fly the flag of a Member State or enter or leave a port or offshore terminal, or anchor in an area under the jurisdiction of a Member State. However, it does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries, or other ships owned or operated by a State and used for government non-commercial service.

The Regulation defines various terms, including "MARPOL 73/78", "oil tanker", "deadweight", and "heavy grade oil", to ensure clarity and consistency in its application. It also categorizes oil tankers into three categories based on their deadweight and compliance with specific requirements. Single-hull oil tankers that do not comply with the double-hull or equivalent design requirements are subject to specific restrictions and exemptions. For instance, Category 2 or Category 3 oil tankers that are equipped with double bottoms or double sides but do not meet the conditions for exemption may continue to operate until the anniversary of their delivery date in 2015 or when they reach 25 years of age, whichever is sooner.

The Regulation requires oil tankers carrying heavy grade oil to be double-hull tankers, and those operated exclusively in ports and inland navigation may be exempted from this requirement if they are duly certified under inland waterway legislation. Single-hull oil tankers above 15 years of age must comply with the Condition Assessment Scheme to enter or leave ports or offshore terminals under the jurisdiction of a Member State. The Regulation also sets a final date after which certain oil tankers will no longer be allowed to operate or enter ports under the jurisdiction of a Member State.

Member States are required to notify the International Maritime Organization (IMO) of their decisions to deny entry to oil tankers or allow, suspend, withdraw, or decline the operation of certain oil tankers. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to align the references in the Regulation with non-substantial amendments adopted by the IMO. Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the safety and environmental protection of oil tankers and prevent pollution from ships.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish a framework for the registration and protection of designations of origin, geographical indications, and traditional specialities guaranteed. To apply for registration, an applicant group must submit an application that includes the name and address of the applicant group and the authorities or bodies verifying compliance with the product specification, as well as a product specification and a single document setting out the main points of the product specification and the link between the product and its geographical environment. The application must also include proof that the name of the product is protected in its country of origin, if applicable.

The regulation applies to any operator who prepares and stores a product marketed under one of the quality schemes or who places such products on the market. Member States must ensure that these operators are entitled to be covered by the verification of compliance established pursuant to the regulation and that they do not face obstacles to participation that are discriminatory or otherwise not objectively founded.

The Commission has the power to adopt implementing acts to grant transitional periods of up to five years, or in duly justified cases up to 15 years, to enable products that contravene certain provisions to continue to use their designation under certain conditions. During these transitional periods, the indication of country of origin must clearly and visibly appear on the labelling. Additionally, Member States may grant transitional periods of up to 10 years to overcome temporary difficulties with the long-term objective of ensuring that all producers in the area concerned comply with the specification.

Verification of compliance with the product specification must be carried out by competent authorities or control bodies, and the costs of such verification may be borne by the operators subject to those controls. The regulation also sets out criteria for the eligibility of names for registration as traditional specialities guaranteed, including that the name must describe a specific product or foodstuff that results from a mode of production, processing, or composition corresponding to traditional practice.

Overall, the regulation aims to ensure that designations of origin, geographical indications, and traditional specialities guaranteed are protected and that consumers are provided with accurate information about the products they purchase. It establishes a framework for the registration and protection of these designations and sets out rules for their use, as well as requirements for verification of compliance and transitional periods for certain products.

This EU legal act aims to protect designations of origin and geographical indications, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed, by establishing a registration system and rules for their use. To register a designation of origin or geographical indication, an application must include the name and address of the applicant group, the product specification, and a single document setting out the main points of the product specification and the link between the product and its geographical environment. The application dossier must also comprise a declaration by the Member State that the application meets the conditions of the Regulation, and the publication reference of the product specification.

The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts establishing the Union symbols and implementing acts defining their technical characteristics and rules of use. The Commission may also grant transitional periods of up to five years, or in duly justified cases up to 15 years, to enable products that contravene the registered name to continue to use their designation under certain conditions. During these transitional periods, the indication of country of origin must clearly and visibly appear on the labelling.

The act also sets out criteria for the eligibility of names for registration as traditional specialities guaranteed, including that the name describes a specific product or foodstuff resulting from a traditional mode of production, processing, or composition. The decision on registration may provide that the name of the traditional speciality guaranteed is to be accompanied by the claim "made following the tradition of" immediately followed by the name of a country or a region thereof.

Verification of compliance with product specifications is carried out by competent authorities or control bodies, and the costs of such verification may be borne by the operators subject to those controls. The act also defines various terms, including "quality schemes", "group", "traditional", "labelling", "specific character", "generic terms", "production step", and "processed products".

Registered names are protected against any direct or indirect commercial use, misuse, imitation, or evocation, as well as any other false or misleading indication as to the provenance, origin, nature, or essential qualities of the product. The act also sets out rules for the relations between trade marks, designations of origin, and geographical indications, including that the registration of a trade mark that would contravene the protection of a registered designation of origin or geographical indication shall be refused.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs, allowing producers to communicate the characteristics of their products to buyers and consumers under conditions of fair competition. The regulation applies to producers of agricultural products and foodstuffs within the European Union and third countries, and its key obligations include the registration of designations of origin, geographical indications, and traditional specialities guaranteed. 

To register a designation of origin or geographical indication, an application must be submitted including the name and address of the applicant group, the product specification, and a single document setting out the main points of the product specification and the link between the product and its geographical environment. The application dossier must also include a declaration by the Member State that the application meets the conditions of the regulation, as well as the publication reference of the product specification.

The regulation also provides for transitional periods to enable products that do not comply with the new designations to continue to be marketed under their existing names. These transitional periods can be up to five years, and in exceptional cases, up to 15 years, provided that the use of the designation does not jeopardise the existence of an entirely or partly identical name and that the consumer is not misled as to the true origin of the product.

In addition, the regulation establishes criteria for the eligibility of names for registration as traditional specialities guaranteed, including that the name describes a specific product or foodstuff that results from a traditional mode of production, processing, or composition, and that the name has been traditionally used to refer to the specific product. The regulation also provides for the verification of compliance with product specifications, which can be carried out by competent authorities or control bodies, and for the making public of the name and address of these authorities and bodies.

The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated and implementing acts to establish further details of the eligibility criteria, the technical characteristics of Union symbols, and the rules for their use on products marketed under protected designations of origin or protected geographical indications. Overall, the regulation aims to promote the quality and diversity of agricultural products and foodstuffs, to support rural development, and to provide consumers with accurate information about the products they buy.

This EU legal act aims to support the smaller islands in Greece by mitigating the additional costs incurred due to their insularity, small size, and distance from markets. The act seeks to guarantee the supply of essential products for human consumption, processing, and agricultural inputs, as well as preserve and develop agricultural activities in these islands. To achieve these objectives, a support programme will be established, comprising specific supply arrangements and measures to assist local agricultural production. The programme will be prepared by the competent local and regional authorities in Greece and submitted to the Commission for approval.

The support programme will include a forecast supply balance, indicating the products, quantities, and amount of aid for supply from the Union, as well as a draft programme of support for local production. Greece may submit proposals for amendments to the programme, which will be assessed by the Commission to ensure compliance with Union law. The Commission will adopt implementing acts to establish the procedures for assessing and approving these amendments.

The act also establishes requirements for the export of products covered by the specific supply arrangements to third countries or dispatch to the rest of the Union. Additionally, it sets out rules for administrative checks on agricultural products entering or leaving the smaller islands, as well as penalties for non-compliance with the commitments made by operators.

The programme may include measures to support production, processing, marketing, and transport of raw and processed agricultural products in the smaller islands. Each measure may include various actions, and the programme will define the beneficiaries, eligibility conditions, and unit amount of aid for each action. The Commission will adopt delegated acts to establish the conditions for determining the amount of aid awarded for support of marketing and transport of products outside the region where they are produced.

The act also provides for the possibility of State aid to alleviate the specific constraints on farming in the smaller islands, and Greece may grant additional financing for the implementation of the support programme. The Union will finance the measures provided for in the act, up to a maximum annual amount of EUR 23.93 million, with a maximum of EUR 7.11 million allocated annually to finance the specific supply arrangements. The Commission will adopt implementing acts to establish the requirements for amending the allocation of resources to the various products benefiting from the specific supply arrangements.

This EU legal act aims to mitigate the difficulties caused by the insularity, small size, and distance from markets of the smaller Aegean islands, by providing specific measures for agriculture. The act seeks to guarantee the supply of essential products to these islands, while also preserving and developing agricultural activities, including the production, processing, marketing, and transport of local raw and processed products. To achieve these objectives, a support programme is established, which comprises specific supply arrangements and measures to assist local agricultural production. The programme is prepared by the competent local and regional authorities in Greece and submitted to the Commission for approval.

The support programme is financed by the Union, up to a maximum annual amount of EUR 23.93 million, and its implementation is subject to annual evaluation. Based on this evaluation, Greece may submit proposals for amendments to the programme, which are assessed by the Commission to ensure compliance with Union law. The Commission also adopts implementing acts to establish the requirements for the export of products covered by the specific supply arrangements to third countries or their dispatch to the rest of the Union.

The act also establishes controls and penalties to ensure the proper implementation of the support programme. Agricultural products subject to the specific supply arrangements are subject to administrative checks upon entry into the smaller islands and when exported or dispatched. Operators who fail to comply with their commitments may face penalties, including the recovery of advantages granted and the suspension or revocation of their registration.

Furthermore, the act provides for measures to assist local agricultural production, including aid schemes, studies, demonstration projects, training, and technical assistance operations. The programme may include measures to support production, processing, marketing, and transport of raw and processed agricultural products in the smaller islands. The Commission adopts implementing acts to establish the requirements for the provision of aid and delegated acts to establish the conditions for establishing the amount of aid awarded for the support of marketing and transport of products outside the region where they are produced. Overall, the act aims to support the development of agricultural activities in the smaller Aegean islands and ensure the continuity and development of local lines of agricultural production.

This EU regulation aims to mitigate the difficulties caused by the insularity, small size, and distance from markets of the smaller Aegean islands. The specific measures provided for in the regulation are designed to help meet two main objectives: guaranteeing the supply of essential products to the smaller islands, and preserving and developing agricultural activities in these islands. To achieve these objectives, a support programme will be established, comprising specific supply arrangements and measures to assist local agricultural production. The support programme will be prepared by the competent local and regional authorities in Greece and submitted to the Commission for approval.

The regulation applies to the smaller Aegean islands, which are defined as any islands in the Aegean Sea except the islands of Crete and Evia. The Union will finance the measures provided for in the regulation up to a maximum annual amount of EUR 23.93 million. The Commission will adopt implementing acts to establish the requirements for products covered by the specific supply arrangements, including reimbursement of aid received, and to lay down the procedures for assessing and approving amendments to the support programme.

The regulation also provides for administrative checks on agricultural products entering the smaller islands, as well as when they are exported or dispatched. The Commission will adopt implementing acts concerning the minimum characteristics of these checks. In cases of non-compliance with the commitments made by operators, the competent authority may recover the advantage granted, temporarily suspend or revoke the operator's registration, or suspend their entitlement to apply for certificates.

The support programme may be amended based on an annual evaluation of its implementation, and Greece may submit proposals for amendments to the Commission. The Commission will adopt implementing acts to assess and approve these amendments, which will be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. This procedure involves the committee delivering an opinion, and the Commission adopting the draft implementing act if the opinion is positive. If the opinion is negative, the Commission may not adopt the act, and the chair may submit an amended version or refer the matter to the appeal committee. The regulation also provides for the adoption of implementing acts in cases where no opinion is delivered, and for derogations from the standard procedure in specific cases, such as the adoption of definitive anti-dumping or countervailing measures.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish specific measures for agriculture in favour of the smaller Aegean islands, with the aim of guaranteeing supply to these islands and preserving and developing agricultural activities. The regulation sets out to mitigate the additional costs incurred due to the islands' insularity, small size, and distance from markets, which severely handicap the activities of economic operators and producers. To achieve this, a support programme is established, comprising specific supply arrangements and measures to assist local agricultural production. The programme is to be prepared by the competent local and regional authorities designated by Greece and submitted to the Commission for approval.

The support programme includes measures to ensure the supply of agricultural products and the preservation and development of local agricultural production. The programme is financed under a financial allocation, and Greece may submit proposals for amendments to the programme to bring it more into line with the requirements of the smaller islands. The Commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the procedures for assessing and deciding on these amendments. The regulation also establishes rules concerning the operation of the scheme, including the creation of a register of operators and a system of certificates.

The specific supply arrangements aim to guarantee supply to the smaller Aegean islands by compensating for the additional costs arising from their insularity, small size, and distance from markets. Aid is granted for the supply of Union products to the smaller Aegean islands, taking into account the additional cost of transport and, in the case of agricultural inputs and products intended for processing, the additional costs of insularity, small size, and distance from markets. The regulation specifies that the specific supply arrangements may only apply to products of sound, fair, and marketable quality, and that the dispatch or export of these products from the smaller Aegean islands is prohibited, unless the advantage resulting from the specific supply arrangements is reimbursed.

The regulation applies to all Aegean islands except Crete and Evia, and the measures are designed to avoid speculation and ensure that the economic advantages of the specific supply arrangements are reflected in production costs and reduce prices up to the end-user stage. Administrative checks are carried out on the agricultural products subject to the specific supply arrangements, and the Commission adopts implementing acts concerning the minimum characteristics of these checks. In cases of non-compliance, penalties may be applied, including the recovery of the advantage granted to the operator and the temporary suspension or revocation of the operator's registration. Overall, the regulation aims to promote the development of agricultural activities in the smaller Aegean islands and improve the supply of essential products to these islands.

This Regulation aims to facilitate the development and interoperability of trans-European energy infrastructure, specifically priority corridors and areas, by streamlining permit granting processes, enhancing public participation, and providing rules for cross-border cost allocation and risk-related incentives. The Regulation applies to projects of common interest, which are necessary for the implementation of priority corridors and areas, and must meet specific criteria, including being necessary for at least one priority corridor or area, having overall benefits that outweigh costs, and involving at least two Member States or having a significant cross-border impact.

To be considered a project of common interest, a project must contribute significantly to specific criteria, such as market integration, sustainability, and security of supply, depending on the energy infrastructure category. For example, electricity transmission and storage projects must contribute to market integration, sustainability, and security of supply, while gas projects must contribute to market integration, security of supply, competition, and sustainability. The Regulation also sets out specific criteria for electricity smart grid projects, oil transport projects, and carbon dioxide transport projects.

The decision-making body of each Group is responsible for adopting a regional list of proposed projects of common interest, which must be approved by the Member States concerned. The Commission provides advice to ensure a manageable total number of projects. Project promoters must draw up an implementation plan, including a timetable for feasibility and design studies, approval, construction, and commissioning. The Agency and Groups monitor progress and make recommendations to facilitate implementation.

Project promoters must submit annual reports to the competent authority and either the Agency or the respective Group, depending on the project category. The Regulation determines the conditions for eligibility of projects of common interest for Union financial assistance and provides rules for the cross-border allocation of costs and risk-related incentives. Overall, the Regulation aims to facilitate the timely development and implementation of projects of common interest, which are essential for the integration of the European energy market and the achievement of Union energy policy targets.
