The purpose of this Regulation is to establish the rules for the collection and comparison of fingerprint data of applicants for international protection, as well as the data of other individuals, for the purposes of identifying and tracing these individuals. The Central System, which is the central database for storing and comparing fingerprint data, shall ensure that the comparison of fingerprint data covers the data previously transmitted by a Member State, in addition to the data from other Member States, at the request of a Member State.

The Regulation applies to Member States, which are responsible for ensuring that fingerprint data and other data are lawfully transmitted to the Central System, accurate and up-to-date, and lawfully recorded, stored, corrected, and erased. The Agency is responsible for operating the Central System in accordance with the provisions of the Regulation, ensuring the security of the Central System, and adopting measures to ensure that persons working with the Central System process the data recorded therein only in accordance with the purposes of Eurodac.

The Regulation sets out specific obligations for Member States, including the requirement to update data sets recorded in the Central System in certain circumstances, such as when an applicant for international protection arrives in the Member State responsible following a transfer, or when a person concerned leaves the territory of the Member States. Member States are also required to mark data in the Central System when an applicant for international protection is granted international protection, and to unmark or unblock data when the status of the person concerned is revoked or ended.

The Regulation also establishes procedures for accessing, correcting, and erasing data recorded in the Central System. Member States have access to data which they have transmitted and which are recorded in the Central System, but may not conduct searches of data transmitted by another Member State. The authorities of Member States which have access to data recorded in the Central System must be designated by each Member State, and the Agency shall publish a consolidated list of these units.

Individuals whose data are recorded in the Central System have the right to be informed of the purpose for which their data will be processed, the recipients of the data, and their rights of access, correction, and erasure. They must be informed in writing, and where necessary, orally, in a language that they understand or are reasonably supposed to understand.

The Regulation also sets out security measures to be taken by Member States and the Agency to protect the data processed pursuant to the Regulation, including the adoption of a security plan to physically protect the data. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the effective and secure collection, comparison, and transmission of fingerprint data for the purposes of identifying and tracing applicants for international protection and other individuals.

The Eurodac system is established to assist in determining which Member State is responsible for examining an application for international protection lodged in a Member State by a third-country national or a stateless person, and to facilitate the application of Regulation (EU) No 604/2013. The system consists of a computerised central fingerprint database, known as the Central System, and a communication infrastructure between the Central System and Member States. Each Member State has a single National Access Point, and data on persons covered by the system are processed on behalf of the Member State of origin, separated by appropriate technical means.

The Central System records specific data, including fingerprint data, Member State of origin, place and date of the application for international protection, sex, reference number, and dates related to the transmission and storage of the data. Member States are responsible for ensuring that fingerprints are taken lawfully, data are accurate and up-to-date, and results of fingerprint data comparisons are lawfully processed. The Agency is responsible for operating the Central System in accordance with the provisions of the Regulation, ensuring the security of the system, and adopting measures to ensure that persons working with the Central System process data only in accordance with the purposes of Eurodac.

The system also allows for the comparison of fingerprint data with those stored in the Central System for law enforcement purposes, under specific conditions. When an applicant for international protection arrives in a Member State, the Member State responsible updates its data set recorded in the Central System, adding the date of arrival, and in certain cases, the date of departure or removal from the territory. The Central System informs all Member States of origin of the marking of data by another Member State of origin having produced a hit with data which they transmitted, and those Member States of origin shall also mark the corresponding data sets.

Data stored in the Central System are made available for comparison for a period of three years after the date on which the data subject was granted international protection, and are then automatically blocked from being transmitted. The Member State of origin is responsible for unmarking or unblocking data concerning a third-country national or stateless person whose data were previously marked or blocked, if their status is revoked or ended, or the renewal of their status is refused. Overall, the Eurodac system is designed to facilitate the application of Regulation (EU) No 604/2013, while ensuring the security and integrity of the data processed.

The Agency is responsible for operating the Central System in accordance with the provisions of the Regulation, ensuring the security of the Central System, and adopting measures to ensure that persons working with the Central System process the data recorded therein only in accordance with the purposes of Eurodac.

Important conditions and exceptions are outlined in the Regulation, including the marking of data by the Member State of origin when an applicant for international protection is granted international protection, and the blocking of data from being transmitted after a period of three years. The Regulation also provides for the unmarking or unblocking of data if the status of the person concerned is revoked or ended. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the effective and lawful processing of data for the purposes of determining the Member State responsible for examining an application for international protection.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to establish a framework for customs authorities to enforce intellectual property rights, particularly in cases where goods suspected of infringing these rights are identified. To achieve this, applicants must submit an application to the competent customs department, providing detailed information, including details about the applicant, the intellectual property right or rights to be enforced, and specific and technical data on the authentic goods. The application must also include undertakings by the applicant to notify the customs department of any changes to the information provided, to forward and update relevant information, and to assume liability and bear costs under specified conditions.

The customs authorities are required to take action when they identify goods suspected of infringing an intellectual property right covered by a decision granting an application. They may suspend the release of the goods or detain them, and must notify the declarant or the holder of the goods and the holder of the decision of the suspension or detention. The customs authorities may also request information from the holder of the decision or provide them with information about the goods. In cases where the customs authorities identify goods suspected of infringing an intellectual property right before an application has been granted, they may suspend the release of the goods or detain them, and must notify the declarant or the holder of the goods and potential applicants.

The holder of the decision has notification obligations, including immediately notifying the competent customs department of any changes to the intellectual property right or the applicant's entitlement to submit the application. Failure to comply with these obligations may result in the revocation or suspension of the decision granting the application. The customs authorities may also revoke or suspend a decision if the holder of the decision misuses information provided by the customs authorities or fails to initiate proceedings as required.

In certain circumstances, the declarant or the holder of the goods may request the early release of the goods, which may be granted if a guarantee is provided to protect the interests of the holder of the decision, and other conditions are met. The customs authorities must also exchange data with the Commission and other Member States on decisions relating to applications and detentions, including information on the quantity and type of goods, value, and customs procedures. Overall, this legal act aims to provide a framework for effective enforcement of intellectual property rights at the customs level, while also ensuring that the rights of all parties involved are protected.

This EU legal act outlines the procedures for customs authorities to follow when dealing with goods suspected of infringing intellectual property rights. The act applies to applicants who submit an application to the customs authorities to enforce their intellectual property rights. The application must include detailed information about the applicant, the intellectual property right, and the goods in question. The customs authorities will then assess the application and decide whether to grant it, specifying the period during which they will take action, which cannot exceed one year.

Once an application is granted, the customs authorities may suspend the release of or detain goods suspected of infringing the intellectual property right. The holder of the decision must be notified, and they may be provided with information about the goods, including their quantity, nature, and origin. The customs authorities may also request the holder of the decision to provide additional information or to initiate proceedings to determine whether an intellectual property right has been infringed.

The act also sets out the conditions under which goods may be released or their detention ended. For example, if the customs authorities have not identified any person or entity entitled to submit an application, or if they have not received an application, they must release the goods or end their detention. Additionally, if the declarant or holder of the goods provides a guarantee to protect the interests of the holder of the decision, the customs authorities may release the goods or end their detention before the completion of proceedings to determine whether an intellectual property right has been infringed.

The holder of the decision has certain obligations, including notifying the customs authorities of any changes to the information provided in the application, and assuming liability for any damage caused by the suspension of the release or detention of the goods. They must also bear the costs associated with the storage and destruction of the goods. The act also sets out the permitted use of information provided by the customs authorities, which can only be used for specific purposes, such as initiating proceedings to determine whether an intellectual property right has been infringed, or seeking compensation from the infringer.

Overall, the act aims to provide a framework for customs authorities to enforce intellectual property rights, while also protecting the rights of declarants and holders of goods. It sets out clear procedures and conditions for the suspension of the release or detention of goods, and ensures that the holder of the decision is notified and involved throughout the process.

The Regulation also sets out the period during which the customs authorities are to take action, which shall not exceed one year from the day following the date of adoption of the decision granting the application. The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a common framework for the development, production, and dissemination of European statistics on population and vital events. Member States are required to provide the Commission (Eurostat) with data on their usually resident population at the reference time, covering population by age, sex, and region of residence. They must also provide data on vital events, including live births and deaths, with specific variables such as sex, age, and region of residence. The data must be provided annually, with the reference time being either the reference date, which is the end of the reference period, or the reference period, which is the calendar year in which the events occurred.

Member States are also required to provide data on the total population at national level for the purposes of qualified majority voting in the Council. They may estimate the total population from the legally resident or registered population using scientifically-based, well-documented, and publicly available statistical estimation methods. The Commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down uniform conditions for the breakdown of data, deadlines, and revisions of data, which shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure.

The Regulation applies to all Member States, which must ensure the quality of the data transmitted and report to the Commission (Eurostat) on reference metadata, using the European Statistical System standards. Member States must also keep the Commission informed of any changes to the data sources, definitions, and estimation methods used. The Commission shall submit reports to the European Parliament and the Council on the implementation of this Regulation, evaluating the quality of the data transmitted, the data collection methods used, and the comparability of the statistics.

The Regulation also establishes a review clause, which requires the Commission to submit a first report by 31 December 2018 and a second report by 31 December 2023. These reports shall evaluate the implementation of the Regulation and may be accompanied by proposals to further improve the common legal framework for the development, production, and dissemination of European statistics on population and vital events. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonized system for the collection and dissemination of population and vital events statistics, ensuring the quality, comparability, and reliability of the data.

The Regulation also defines specific terms related to agriculture, such as "agricultural area", "economic losses", "adverse climatic event", and "animal diseases", which are essential for understanding the challenges faced by rural areas.

The Regulation applies to Member States, which may include thematic sub-programmes in their rural development programmes to address specific needs, such as supporting young farmers, small farms, mountain areas, short supply chains, women in rural areas, and climate change mitigation and adaptation. These sub-programmes may include a range of measures and operations, as set out in Annex IV, to address the specific needs of each thematic area.

Each rural development programme must include several key elements, such as an ex ante evaluation, a SWOT analysis, and a description of the strategy to achieve the Union priorities for rural development. The programme must also demonstrate how it will address specific needs linked to regional or sub-regional conditions and ensure the availability of sufficient advisory capacity on regulatory requirements and innovation. Furthermore, the programme must contain an assessment of the ex ante conditionalities applicable to the programme and a description of the actions to be taken to fulfill them.

The Regulation also requires Member States to establish a performance framework and an evaluation plan to monitor the progress and impact of the programme. This will enable the effective implementation of the programme and ensure that the Union priorities for rural development are achieved. Overall, the Regulation provides a framework for Member States to develop and implement effective rural development programmes that address the specific needs of their rural areas and contribute to the achievement of the Union priorities for rural development.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish an Instrument that contributes to the achievement of a high level of security within the Union, by supporting actions in Member States and, where relevant, in third countries. The Instrument seeks synergies, consistency, and complementarity with other relevant financial instruments of the Union, such as the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and Horizon 2020, and ensures that actions financed under this Regulation do not receive financial support for the same purpose from other Union financial instruments.

The Instrument has specific objectives, including crime prevention, combating cross-border, serious, and organised crime, including terrorism, and enhancing the capacity of Member States and the Union to manage security-related risks and crises. To achieve these objectives, the Instrument will support actions that promote and develop measures strengthening Member States' capability to prevent crime and combat cross-border, serious, and organised crime, including terrorism. It will also promote and develop administrative and operational coordination, cooperation, and mutual understanding among Member States' law enforcement authorities and other relevant authorities.

The Instrument will support a range of eligible actions under national programmes, including actions improving police cooperation and coordination, projects promoting networking and public-private partnerships, analytical and monitoring activities, awareness-raising and communication activities, and the acquisition and maintenance of IT systems and technical equipment. The Instrument may also support actions in relation to and in third countries, including actions improving police cooperation and coordination, networking, and exchange, training, and education of staff and experts of relevant authorities.

Member States will pursue strategic Union priorities under their national programmes, taking into account the outcome of policy dialogue and ensuring that no more than 8% of their total allocation is used for the maintenance of Union IT systems and national IT systems, and no more than 8% for actions in relation to or in third countries. The achievement of the specific objectives of the Instrument will be evaluated using common indicators and programme-specific indicators, as set out in Annex II to this Regulation and included in national programmes. The Commission and the Member States, together with the European External Action Service, will ensure coordination as regards actions in and in relation to third countries.

The Internal Security Fund, established by this Regulation, aims to provide financial support for police cooperation, preventing and combating crime, and crisis management. The Instrument seeks synergies, consistency, and complementarity with other relevant financial instruments of the Union, such as the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and Horizon 2020, to ensure a cohesive approach to internal security. Actions financed under this Regulation cannot receive financial support for the same purpose from other Union financial instruments, ensuring that funding is targeted and effective.

The Instrument has specific objectives, including crime prevention, combating cross-border, serious, and organised crime, including terrorism, and enhancing the capacity of Member States and the Union to manage security-related risks and crises. To achieve these objectives, the Instrument will support actions such as improving police cooperation and coordination, promoting public-private partnerships, and enhancing training and education for law enforcement authorities. The Instrument will also support measures to protect critical infrastructure, promote early identification and support for victims of crime, and develop comprehensive threat and risk assessments.

The Regulation applies to Member States and sets out the eligible actions that can be supported under the Instrument. These actions include improving police cooperation and coordination, promoting networking and public-private partnerships, and supporting analytical, monitoring, and evaluation activities. The Instrument may also support actions in third countries, such as improving police cooperation and coordination, and promoting mutual confidence and understanding.

The Commission and Member States, together with the European External Action Service, will ensure coordination regarding actions in and related to third countries. The achievement of the specific objectives of the Instrument will be evaluated using common indicators, as set out in Annex II to this Regulation, and programme-specific indicators included in national programmes. Overall, the Regulation provides a framework for the implementation of the Internal Security Fund, ensuring that financial support is targeted, effective, and complementary to other Union initiatives.

Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the security of the Union and its citizens, by supporting actions that prevent and combat crime, and promote cooperation and coordination between law enforcement authorities.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a framework for the implementation of programmes and the use of support provided under the Specific Regulations. Member States and their competent authorities are responsible for implementing these programmes and carrying out their tasks at the appropriate level, in accordance with their institutional, legal, and financial framework, and subject to compliance with this Regulation and the Specific Regulations. The arrangements for the implementation and use of the support provided under the Specific Regulations must take into account the principle of proportionality, reducing the administrative burden and facilitating efficient implementation.

To facilitate the preparation of national programmes, each Member State and the Commission must hold a dialogue at the level of senior officials, focusing on the overall results to be achieved by means of the national programmes and addressing the needs and priorities of the Member States in the areas of intervention covered by the Specific Regulations. The outcome of this dialogue serves as a guide for the preparation and approval of the national programmes.

Each Member State must propose a multiannual national programme, covering the financial years from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2020, which consists of several elements, including a description of the baseline situation, an analysis of requirements, a strategy identifying the objectives to be pursued, and a description of how the objectives of the Specific Regulations are covered. The Commission must examine the proposed national programme before approving it, checking its consistency with the objectives of the Specific Regulations, the distribution of Union funding, and compliance with Union law.

The Commission may make observations on the proposed national programme and invite the Member State to provide additional information or modify the programme. The Commission must approve each national programme within six months of its formal submission, provided that any observations have been adequately taken into account. The Commission must also inform the European Parliament of the overall outcome of the application of the approval procedure.

The measures may include expenditure relating to programme management, audits, evaluations, information, and dissemination, as well as expenditure on the acquisition and maintenance of computerised systems and the reinforcement of administrative capacity. The appropriations for technical assistance may be used to support actions for the reduction of administrative burden and to reinforce the capacity of Member State authorities and beneficiaries to administer and use the support provided under the Specific Regulations.

The purpose of the Fund is to enhance solidarity and responsibility-sharing between Member States, particularly towards those most affected by migration and asylum flows, including through practical cooperation. The Fund's specific objectives will be evaluated using common indicators and programme-specific indicators included in national programmes. 

The Fund shall support actions focusing on third-country nationals who enjoy refugee status or subsidiary protection status, those who have applied for international protection and have not yet received a final decision, those who enjoy temporary protection, and those who are being or have been resettled in or transferred from a Member State. As regards reception conditions and asylum procedures, the Fund shall support actions such as the provision of material aid, support services, health and psychological care, and the setting-up and improvement of administrative structures and systems to ensure effective and easy access to asylum procedures. The Fund may also support integration-related measures, such as those concerning the reception of persons, where deemed appropriate and provided for in the national programme of a Member State.

In addition, the Fund shall support actions related to resettlement of third-country nationals and other humanitarian admission programmes, including the establishment and development of national resettlement programmes and strategies, the establishment of appropriate infrastructure and services, and the setting up of structures and systems to conduct missions to third countries and/or other Member States. The Fund shall also support actions for family reunification purposes, the strengthening of infrastructure and services relevant to migration and asylum, and creating conditions conducive to the integration, autonomy, and self-reliance of resettled refugees on a long-term basis.

The Fund shall also support actions similar to those listed above, where deemed appropriate in the light of policy developments or where the national programme of a Member State makes such provisions, in relation to the transfer of applicants for and/or beneficiaries of international protection, with their consent from the Member State which granted them international protection or is responsible for examining their application. 

The Fund applies to Member States, and its support is subject to the objectives of the national programmes defined in Article 19 of this Regulation. The achievement of the Fund's specific objectives will be evaluated in accordance with Article 55(2) of Regulation (EU) No 514/2014, using common indicators and programme-specific indicators. Overall, the Fund aims to provide support to third-country nationals in need of international protection, and to enhance the reception and asylum systems of Member States, while also promoting the integration of third-country nationals and legal migration.

The purpose of the Fund is to enhance solidarity and responsibility-sharing between Member States, particularly towards those most affected by migration and asylum flows, including through practical cooperation. The Fund aims to achieve specific objectives, which will be evaluated using common indicators and programme-specific indicators. The Fund supports actions focusing on various categories of third-country nationals, including those who enjoy refugee status or subsidiary protection status, those who have applied for international protection and are awaiting a final decision, those who enjoy temporary protection, and those who are being or have been resettled in a Member State.

In the area of reception and asylum systems, the Fund supports actions such as the provision of material aid, including assistance at the border, education, training, support services, health, and psychological care. It also supports the setting-up and improvement of administrative structures, systems, and training for staff and relevant authorities to ensure effective and easy access to asylum procedures. Additionally, the Fund supports the provision of social assistance, information, or help with administrative and/or judicial formalities, as well as the provision of legal assistance and representation. The Fund may also support integration-related measures, such as those concerning the reception of persons, where deemed appropriate and provided for in the national programme of a Member State.

The Fund also supports actions related to resettlement and other humanitarian admission programmes, including the establishment and development of national resettlement programmes and strategies, the establishment of appropriate infrastructure and services, and the setting up of structures, systems, and training of staff to conduct missions to third countries and/or other Member States. The Fund supports pre-departure health assessments and medical treatment, pre-departure material provisions, pre-departure information and integration measures, and travel arrangements, including the provision of medical escort services. It also supports information and assistance upon arrival, actions for family reunification purposes, and the strengthening of infrastructure and services relevant to migration and asylum in countries designated for the implementation of Regional Protection Programmes.

The Fund applies to Member States and supports actions that are in line with the objectives of the national programmes defined in Article 19 of the Regulation. The support provided by the Fund is subject to certain conditions, including the outcome of the policy dialogue as provided for in Article 13 of Regulation (EU) No 514/2014, and the objectives of the national programmes. The Fund may also support actions similar to those listed, where deemed appropriate in the light of policy developments within the implementation period of the Fund or where the national programme of a Member State makes such provisions.

The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure the independence and quality of statutory audits of public-interest entities, such as banks and insurance companies. To achieve this, statutory auditors and audit firms are required to assess and document potential threats to their independence before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit. They must also confirm annually in writing to the audit committee that they are independent from the audited entity and discuss any threats to their independence and the safeguards applied to mitigate those threats.

The Regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities. These entities must have a duty to report promptly to the competent authorities any information that may indicate a material breach of laws or regulations, a material threat to the continuous functioning of the entity, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion on the financial statements. The competent authorities are responsible for supervising the activities of statutory auditors and audit firms and may delegate tasks to other authorities or bodies.

The Regulation also establishes a system of audit quality assurance, which includes quality assurance reviews of statutory auditors and audit firms carried out by the competent authorities. These reviews must be carried out on the basis of an analysis of the risk and at least every three years for certain entities. The competent authorities must also regularly monitor the developments in the market for providing statutory audit services to public-interest entities and assess the risks arising from high incidence of quality deficiencies.

In addition, the Regulation requires audit reports to be prepared in accordance with the provisions of Directive 2006/43/EC and to include certain information, such as a description of the most significant assessed risks of material misstatement and a summary of the auditor's response to those risks. The Regulation also provides for the establishment of colleges to facilitate the exercise of tasks related to the quality assurance system and investigations.

Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the independence and quality of statutory audits of public-interest entities, thereby contributing to the stability of the financial sector. It imposes various obligations on statutory auditors and audit firms, including the requirement to assess and document potential threats to their independence, to confirm their independence annually, and to report promptly to the competent authorities any information that may indicate a material breach of laws or regulations. The Regulation also establishes a system of audit quality assurance and provides for the regular monitoring of the market for providing statutory audit services to public-interest entities.

This Regulation aims to ensure the independence and integrity of statutory auditors and audit firms when carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities. To achieve this, statutory auditors and audit firms must assess and document their independence before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit, including compliance with specific requirements and the integrity of the public-interest entity's management bodies. They must also confirm their independence annually in writing to the audit committee and discuss any threats to their independence and the safeguards applied to mitigate those threats.

The Regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, as well as to the public-interest entities themselves. However, Member States may decide that certain provisions do not apply to the statutory audit of specific entities, such as cooperatives or savings banks, provided that the principles of independence are complied with.

Statutory auditors and audit firms have a duty to report promptly to the competent authorities any information concerning the public-interest entity that may indicate a material breach of laws or regulations, a material threat to the entity's continuous functioning, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion. They must also provide annual information to the competent authorities on the revenues generated from their audited public-interest entities.

The Regulation designates competent authorities responsible for ensuring that its provisions are applied, which may include authorities responsible for financial market supervision or audit oversight. These authorities have powers to access data, obtain information, carry out on-site inspections, and impose sanctions. The Regulation also requires audited entities to demonstrate, upon request, that their selection procedure for statutory auditors was conducted in a fair manner.

Audit reports must be prepared in accordance with specific provisions, including a description of the most significant assessed risks of material misstatement, a summary of the auditor's response to those risks, and a declaration that the prohibited non-audit services were not provided. The Regulation also requires statutory auditors and audit firms to disclose any services provided to the audited entity in addition to the statutory audit.

Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the independence and integrity of statutory auditors and audit firms, ensuring that they carry out their duties in a fair and transparent manner, and that public-interest entities are subject to effective and reliable audits.

The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure the independence and integrity of statutory auditors and audit firms when carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities. To achieve this, statutory auditors and audit firms are required to assess and document their independence and the threats to their independence before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit. They must also confirm annually in writing to the audit committee that they are independent from the audited entity and discuss with the audit committee the threats to their independence and the safeguards applied to mitigate those threats.

The Regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, which include entities such as banks, insurance companies, and listed companies. These entities are required to have their financial statements audited by a statutory auditor or an audit firm to ensure the accuracy and reliability of their financial reporting.

Statutory auditors and audit firms have a duty to report promptly to the competent authorities any information that may indicate a material breach of laws or regulations, a material threat to the continuous functioning of the public-interest entity, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion on the financial statements. They must also provide an audit report that includes, among other things, a description of the most significant assessed risks of material misstatement, a summary of the auditor's response to those risks, and a declaration that the prohibited non-audit services were not provided and that the statutory auditor or the audit firm remained independent of the audited entity.

The Regulation also establishes the powers of the competent authorities to supervise the activities of statutory auditors and audit firms. These powers include the power to access data related to the statutory audit, obtain information related to the statutory audit, carry out on-site inspections, and impose administrative measures and sanctions. The competent authorities may use these powers in relation to statutory auditors and audit firms, persons involved in their activities, audited public-interest entities, and third parties related to the statutory auditors and audit firms.

Furthermore, the Regulation requires the audited entity to demonstrate, upon request, that the selection procedure for the statutory auditor or audit firm was conducted in a fair manner. The audit committee is responsible for the selection procedure, and the competent authority must make public a list of the statutory auditors and audit firms concerned, which is updated on an annual basis.

In addition, the Regulation provides for the issuance of guidelines and recommendations by the Authority to establish consistent, efficient, and effective supervisory practices within the European Supervisory Framework. The competent authorities and financial institutions must make every effort to comply with these guidelines and recommendations, and the Authority may publish the fact that a competent authority does not comply or does not intend to comply with a guideline or recommendation.

The Regulation aims to enhance the quality and reliability of statutory audits of public-interest entities, such as credit institutions, insurance undertakings, and issuers of securities admitted to trading on a regulated market. To achieve this, statutory auditors and audit firms are required to assess and document their independence and the integrity of the members of the supervisory, administrative, and management bodies of the public-interest entity before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit. They must also confirm annually in writing to the audit committee that they are independent from the audited entity and discuss with the audit committee the threats to their independence and the safeguards applied to mitigate those threats.

The Regulation sets out specific requirements for the content of the audit report, including a description of the most significant assessed risks of material misstatement, a summary of the auditor's response to those risks, and a declaration that the prohibited non-audit services were not provided and that the statutory auditor or the audit firm remained independent of the audited entity in conducting the audit. The audit report must also indicate any services, in addition to the statutory audit, which were provided by the statutory auditor or the audit firm to the audited entity and its controlled undertakings.

Statutory auditors and audit firms have a duty to report promptly to the competent authorities any information concerning the public-interest entity that may bring about a material breach of laws, regulations, or administrative provisions, a material threat or doubt concerning the continuous functioning of the public-interest entity, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion on the financial statements or the issuing of an adverse or qualified opinion. The Regulation also requires Member States to designate competent authorities to oversee the activities of statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, and to lay down rules for the selection procedure of statutory auditors and audit firms.

The competent authorities have powers to access data related to the statutory audit, obtain information related to the statutory audit, carry out on-site inspections, refer matters for criminal prosecution, and impose administrative measures and sanctions. These powers can only be used in relation to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, persons involved in their activities, audited public-interest entities, and third parties to whom the statutory auditors and audit firms have outsourced certain functions or activities. Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the quality and reliability of statutory audits, contributing to the integrity and efficiency of financial statements and the orderly functioning of markets.

This Regulation sets out rules and procedures for the European Union to effectively and timely exercise its rights to suspend or withdraw concessions or other obligations under international trade agreements. The purpose of this Regulation is to respond to breaches by third countries of international trade rules that affect the Union's interests, and to rebalance concessions or other obligations in trade relations with third countries when the treatment accorded to goods from the Union is altered. The Regulation applies in various scenarios, including after the adjudication of trade disputes under the World Trade Organization (WTO) Dispute Settlement Understanding, under other international trade agreements, and in cases of modification of concessions by a WTO member.

The Commission is responsible for adopting implementing acts to determine the appropriate commercial policy measures, which shall meet certain conditions, such as not exceeding the level authorised by the WTO Dispute Settlement Body or the level of nullification or impairment. The measures shall be determined based on criteria such as effectiveness, potential to provide relief to economic operators, availability of alternative sources of supply, and avoidance of disproportionate administrative complexity and costs. The commercial policy measures that may be enacted include the suspension of tariff concessions, introduction of quantitative restrictions, and suspension of concessions regarding goods, services, or suppliers in the area of public procurement.

The Regulation also provides for the suspension or repeal of implementing acts in certain circumstances, such as when a third country accords adequate and proportionate compensation to the Union or brings itself into compliance with international trade rules. The Commission shall repeal an implementing act when a mutually satisfactory solution has been reached or when a safeguard measure is withdrawn or expires. The Regulation aims to ensure that the Union's actions are substantially equivalent to the level of concessions or other obligations affected by the third country's measures, and that the measures are fair and do not disproportionately affect downstream industries, contracting authorities, or final consumers within the Union.

This Regulation sets out rules and procedures to ensure the effective and timely exercise of the Union's rights to suspend or withdraw concessions or other obligations under international trade agreements. The aim is to respond to breaches by third countries of international trade rules that affect the Union's interests, and to rebalance concessions or other obligations in trade relations with third countries when the treatment accorded to goods from the Union is altered. The Regulation applies in various situations, including after the adjudication of trade disputes under the WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding or other international trade agreements, and in cases of modification of concessions by a WTO member without compensatory adjustments.

The Commission is responsible for adopting implementing acts to determine the appropriate commercial policy measures, which must meet certain conditions. The commercial policy measures that may be enacted include the suspension of tariff concessions, the introduction or increase of quantitative restrictions on imports or exports of goods, and the suspension of concessions regarding goods, services, or suppliers in the area of public procurement.

This EU legal act outlines the procedures for sea operations conducted by participating units to prevent the smuggling of migrants by sea and to protect the lives of persons at risk. During these operations, the participating units are required to approach vessels suspected of carrying persons intending to circumvent checks at border crossing points or engaged in the smuggling of migrants by sea, and to survey them at a prudent distance while collecting and reporting information about the vessel and its passengers. 

The participating units may take measures such as requesting information and documentation, stopping and searching the vessel, and questioning persons on board, subject to the authorisation of the flag State and in accordance with national and international law. If evidence confirms the suspicion, the participating units may seize the vessel, apprehend persons on board, or conduct the vessel to a third country or a Member State. 

In cases where the vessel is stateless or its nationality is uncertain, the participating units shall verify the vessel's right to fly its flag and may take further measures if the suspicions prove to be founded. The act also emphasizes the obligation of Member States to render assistance to any vessel or person in distress at sea and to ensure that their participating units comply with this obligation during sea operations. 

The act applies to participating units from Member States engaged in sea operations, and the measures taken shall be proportionate and not exceed what is necessary to achieve the objectives of the act. The International Coordination Centre plays a key role in facilitating communications between the participating units and the relevant authorities of the Member States, and in transmitting information about vessels suspected of being engaged in the smuggling of migrants by sea. 

In the event of search and rescue situations, Member States shall observe their obligation to render assistance to any vessel or person in distress at sea, in accordance with international law and respect for fundamental rights. The act also requires the participating units to identify intercepted or rescued persons, assess their personal circumstances, and inform them of their destination, while also giving them an opportunity to express any reasons for believing that disembarkation in the proposed place would be in violation of the principle of non-refoulement. 

Overall, the act aims to prevent the smuggling of migrants by sea while protecting the lives and fundamental rights of persons at risk, and to ensure that sea operations are conducted in accordance with national and international law.

This Regulation applies to border surveillance operations carried out by Member States at their external sea borders, with the aim of preventing the smuggling of migrants by sea. During a sea operation, participating units are required to take certain measures when they suspect that a vessel is carrying persons intending to circumvent checks at border crossing points or is engaged in the smuggling of migrants. When a vessel is detected, the participating units shall approach it to observe its identity and nationality, and survey it at a prudent distance, taking all due precautions. They shall collect and report information about the vessel, including the situation of persons on board, to the International Coordination Centre.

If there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a vessel is engaged in the smuggling of migrants, the participating units may take measures such as requesting information and documentation, stopping, boarding, and searching the vessel, and questioning persons on board. They may also seize the vessel and apprehend persons on board, or order the vessel to alter its course. These measures must be taken subject to the authorisation of the flag State and in accordance with national and international law.

The Regulation also sets out procedures for the interception of vessels on the high seas, including the requirement for participating units to verify the nationality of a vessel and to obtain the authorisation of the flag State before taking any measures. If a vessel is found to be stateless, the participating unit may board and search it to verify its statelessness, and the host Member State may take further measures in accordance with national and international law.

Before disembarking intercepted or rescued persons in a third country, the participating units must use all means to identify them, assess their personal circumstances, and inform them of their destination in a way that they can understand. The units must also give them an opportunity to express any reasons for believing that disembarkation in the proposed place would be in violation of the principle of non-refoulement. The operational plan must include further details on these procedures, including the availability of shore-based medical staff, interpreters, and legal advisers.

The Regulation is coordinated by the European Agency for the Management of Operational Cooperation at the External Borders of the Member States of the European Union, and applies to joint operations, pilot projects, or rapid interventions carried out by Member States for the surveillance of their external sea borders. The host Member State is responsible for instructing the participating units and for facilitating communications with the relevant authorities, and the International Coordination Centre plays a key role in transmitting information and coordinating the response to suspected cases of migrant smuggling.

On the high seas, the participating units shall take measures subject to the authorisation of the flag State, in accordance with the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants and national and international law. These measures may include requesting information and documentation, stopping and searching the vessel, or seizing the vessel and apprehending persons on board. The participating units shall also verify the vessel's right to fly its flag and may take further measures if the suspicions regarding the nationality of the vessel prove to be founded.

The Regulation also sets out procedures for situations where the vessel is stateless or where the flag State is unwilling or unable to take action. In such cases, the participating unit may board and search the vessel, or the host Member State may take further measures in accordance with national and international law. The International Coordination Centre shall facilitate communications with the relevant authorities and inform the National Coordination Centre of the Member States towards which the vessel is directed. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that border surveillance operations are carried out in a way that respects the rights of individuals and prevents the smuggling of migrants by sea.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish rules for the surveillance of the external sea borders in the context of operational cooperation coordinated by the European Agency for the Management of Operational Cooperation at the External Borders of the Member States of the European Union. The Regulation applies to the surveillance of the external sea borders of the Member States, with the aim of preventing the smuggling of migrants by sea and ensuring the safety of persons on board vessels. 

The participating units, which are part of the operational cooperation, shall take measures to detect and prevent the smuggling of migrants by sea. When a vessel is suspected of carrying persons intending to circumvent checks at border crossing points or is engaged in the smuggling of migrants by sea, the participating units shall approach the vessel, observe its identity and nationality, and survey it at a prudent distance, taking all due precautions. They shall collect and report information about the vessel, including the situation of persons on board, to the International Coordination Centre, which shall transmit the information to the National Coordination Centre of the host Member State.

In the territorial sea of the host Member State or a neighbouring participating Member State, the host Member State or the neighbouring participating Member State may authorise the participating units to take measures such as requesting information and documentation, stopping, boarding, and searching the vessel, and questioning persons on board. If evidence confirming the suspicion is found, the host Member State or the neighbouring participating Member State may authorise the participating units to take further measures, including seizing the vessel and apprehending persons on board, ordering the vessel to alter its course, or conducting the vessel or persons on board to the coastal Member State.

On the high seas, the participating units shall take measures to detect and prevent the smuggling of migrants by sea, subject to the authorisation of the flag State and in accordance with the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants and national and international law. The participating units may request information and documentation, stop, board, and search the vessel, and question persons on board. If evidence confirming the suspicion is found, the participating units may take further measures, including seizing the vessel and apprehending persons on board, warning and ordering the vessel not to enter the territorial sea or the contiguous zone, or conducting the vessel or persons on board to a third country or the host Member State.

Before disembarking intercepted or rescued persons in a third country, the participating units shall identify the persons, assess their personal circumstances, inform them of their destination, and give them an opportunity to express any reasons for believing that disembarkation in the proposed place would be in violation of the principle of non-refoulement. The operational plan shall include further details on the procedures for disembarkation in third countries, and the report on the operation shall include information on cases of disembarkation in third countries and how the procedures were applied to ensure compliance with the principle of non-refoulement.

The Regulation also establishes procedures for the verification of the right of a vessel to fly its flag and for the taking of measures against stateless vessels. The host Member State or the participating Member State shall instruct the participating unit appropriately through the International Coordination Centre, and the national official representing the host Member State or a participating Member State at the International Coordination Centre shall be responsible for facilitating communications with the relevant authorities. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the efficient monitoring of the external sea borders, prevent the smuggling of migrants by sea, and protect the safety and rights of persons on board vessels, while also ensuring compliance with international law and the principle of non-refoulement.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a framework for the authorisation and supervision of Central Securities Depositories (CSDs) in the European Union. CSDs are entities that operate securities settlement systems, which are critical to the functioning of financial markets. The Regulation applies to CSDs that operate in the EU and sets out the conditions for their authorisation and supervision.

The relevant authorities involved in the authorisation and supervision of CSDs include the authority responsible for the oversight of the securities settlement system, central banks issuing relevant currencies, and the central bank in whose books the cash leg of a securities settlement system is settled. The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) plays a key role in the supervision of CSDs and is responsible for developing regulatory technical standards and guidelines.

To be authorised, a CSD must demonstrate its ability to comply with the requirements of the Regulation, including the provision of services listed in the Annex. The competent authority must consult with other relevant authorities, including those in other Member States, before granting authorisation. Once authorised, a CSD's activities are limited to the provision of services covered by its authorisation, and it may only operate a securities settlement system if it is authorised to do so.

A CSD may provide banking-type ancillary services, but only if it is authorised as a credit institution and meets specific prudential requirements. In such cases, the CSD must submit an application containing all necessary information, including a programme of operations and a structural organisation of its relations with designated credit institutions. The competent authority must transmit this information to relevant authorities, including ESMA and the European Banking Authority (EBA).

The Regulation also sets out conditions for the recognition of third-country CSDs, which may provide services in the EU if they meet certain conditions, including effective authorisation, supervision, and oversight in their home country. The competent authorities in the host Member State may request information from the responsible third-country authorities on the activities of the recognised CSD.

The competent authority of a CSD must regularly review and evaluate the CSD's arrangements to ensure that it meets its obligations under the Regulation. This includes reviewing the CSD's access to necessary information from designated credit institutions and reporting any infringements to the competent authority and other relevant authorities. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and efficient operation of CSDs in the EU, and to protect the stability of financial markets and the interests of investors.

This Regulation aims to promote safe, efficient, and smooth settlement of financial instruments in the Union by laying down uniform requirements for central securities depositories (CSDs). A CSD is defined as a legal person that operates a securities settlement system and provides at least one other core service. The Regulation applies to the settlement of all financial instruments and activities of CSDs, unless otherwise specified. 

The Regulation involves various authorities in the authorisation and supervision of CSDs, including the authority responsible for the oversight of the securities settlement system, central banks issuing relevant currencies, and the central bank in whose books the cash leg of a securities settlement system is settled. The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is responsible for publishing the list of relevant authorities and developing draft regulatory technical standards for the conditions under which Union currencies are considered most relevant and for the consultation of relevant authorities.

To be authorised, a CSD must limit its activities to the provision of services covered by its authorisation or notification. Securities settlement systems may only be operated by authorised CSDs, including central banks acting as CSDs. An authorised CSD may have participation in a legal person whose activities are limited to the provision of services listed in the Annex, unless such participation is approved by its competent authority on the basis that it does not significantly increase the risk profile of the CSD.

The Regulation also sets out conditions for the recognition of third-country CSDs, which must be subject to effective authorisation, supervision, and oversight, and have cooperation arrangements with ESMA and the responsible authorities in the third country. The competent authorities of the Member States in which the third-country CSD provides CSD services may request the responsible third-country authorities to report periodically on the third-country CSD's activities and communicate the identity of the issuers and participants in the securities settlement systems operated by the third-country CSD.

In addition, the Regulation sets out specific requirements for CSDs that seek to provide banking-type ancillary services, including the need for authorisation as a credit institution, compliance with prudential requirements, and the submission of an adequate recovery plan to ensure continuity of critical operations. The Regulation also clarifies that in cases of conflicting provisions, the CSD must comply with the stricter requirements on prudential supervision.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and efficient operation of CSDs in the Union, while also providing a framework for the recognition of third-country CSDs and the provision of banking-type ancillary services.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish a framework for the authorisation and supervision of Central Securities Depositories (CSDs) in the European Union. CSDs are entities that hold and settle securities transactions, and this Regulation aims to ensure their stability and soundness. The Regulation applies to CSDs established in the EU, as well as to third-country CSDs that provide services in the EU. 

The Regulation sets out the conditions for authorisation, which include the requirement for CSDs to be established in the EU and to have a sufficient level of capital and resources. The competent authority in the Member State where the CSD is established is responsible for granting authorisation, and must consult with other relevant authorities, such as the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the central banks in the Union. 

CSDs are limited to providing services that are covered by their authorisation, and may only operate securities settlement systems if they are authorised to do so. They may also provide non-banking-type ancillary services, such as data processing and property management, but only if these services are explicitly listed in the Annex to the Regulation. If a CSD intends to provide banking-type ancillary services, such as credit facilities, it must be authorised as a credit institution and meet additional prudential requirements. 

The Regulation also sets out conditions for the recognition of third-country CSDs, which must be subject to effective authorisation, supervision, and oversight in their home country, and must cooperate with ESMA and the relevant authorities in the EU. Recognised third-country CSDs may provide services in the EU, but must comply with EU law and regulations. 

In addition, the Regulation requires CSDs to have in place adequate risk management systems, including systems for managing credit and liquidity risk, and to report regularly to the competent authority on their activities and risk exposure. They must also have an adequate recovery plan in place to ensure continuity of their critical operations in the event of a crisis. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the stability and soundness of CSDs, and to protect investors and the financial system as a whole. It establishes a framework for the authorisation and supervision of CSDs, and sets out conditions for their operation, including the provision of ancillary services and the management of risk.

The Regulation aims to improve securities settlement in the European Union by establishing a set of common requirements for central securities depositories (CSDs) operating securities settlement systems. CSDs play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of financial markets, and their activities are considered systemic for the functioning of securities markets. The Regulation applies to CSDs, which are entities that operate securities settlement systems, and to other authorities involved in the authorisation and supervision of CSDs, such as the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), national competent authorities, and central banks.

The Regulation sets out various obligations for CSDs, including the requirement to obtain authorisation from the relevant competent authority before providing services. The authorisation process involves the transmission of information to other authorities, such as those responsible for overseeing securities markets, and consultation with these authorities on the CSD's ability to comply with relevant requirements. The Regulation also limits the activities of authorised CSDs to the provision of services covered by their authorisation or notification, and prohibits them from operating securities settlement systems unless they are authorised to do so.

In addition, the Regulation establishes conditions for the recognition of third-country CSDs, which are CSDs established outside the European Union. To be recognised, a third-country CSD must be subject to effective authorisation, supervision, and oversight in its home country, and must have established cooperation arrangements with ESMA and the relevant authorities in the European Union. The Regulation also requires third-country CSDs to take measures to allow their users to comply with relevant national law in the European Union, and to report periodically on their activities in the European Union.

The Regulation also sets out rules for CSDs that seek to provide banking-type ancillary services, such as intra-day credit. These CSDs must be authorised as credit institutions and meet specific prudential requirements, including the requirement to hold additional capital to cover the risks associated with the provision of such services. The Regulation also requires CSDs to submit recovery plans to ensure continuity of their critical operations in situations where liquidity or credit risk crystallises.

Overall, the Regulation aims to promote the safety, efficiency, and competition of securities settlement systems in the European Union, and to remove obstacles to the functioning of the internal market. By establishing a set of common requirements for CSDs and promoting cooperation between authorities, the Regulation seeks to increase confidence in the integrity of financial markets and to facilitate cross-border investment in the European Union.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to facilitate the coordination of insolvency proceedings concerning the same debtor, particularly in cases involving groups of companies. To achieve this, the act sets out key obligations for courts and insolvency practitioners. Courts with jurisdiction over insolvency proceedings are required to cooperate with other courts that have opened or are pending proceedings concerning the same debtor, to the extent that such cooperation is not incompatible with the rules applicable to each of the proceedings. This cooperation may involve the coordination of the appointment of insolvency practitioners, communication of information, and coordination of the administration and supervision of the debtor's assets and affairs.

Insolvency practitioners appointed by a court with jurisdiction may exercise their powers in another Member State, as long as no other insolvency proceedings have been opened there and no preservation measure to the contrary has been taken. They are also required to make certain information publicly available, including the date of the opening of insolvency proceedings, the court that opened the proceedings, and the type of proceedings. This information is crucial for facilitating the coordination of insolvency proceedings and ensuring that all relevant parties are informed.

In cases where insolvency proceedings relate to two or more members of a group of companies, courts are required to cooperate to facilitate the effective administration of the proceedings. This cooperation may involve the coordination of the appointment of insolvency practitioners, communication of information, and coordination of the administration and supervision of the assets and affairs of the group members. Insolvency practitioners are also required to communicate with each other and consider possibilities for coordinating the administration and supervision of the group members' affairs, as well as restructuring possibilities.

The act also provides for the opening of group coordination proceedings, which aim to facilitate the effective administration of insolvency proceedings relating to different group members. The court seised of a request to open such proceedings must give notice to the insolvency practitioners appointed in relation to the group members and must be satisfied that the opening of such proceedings is appropriate and will not financially disadvantage any creditor. Insolvency practitioners may also request the inclusion of their proceedings in the group coordination proceedings after the court decision, and the coordinator may accede to such a request after consulting the involved insolvency practitioners.

Overall, the act applies to courts and insolvency practitioners involved in insolvency proceedings in EU Member States, and its key obligations and conditions are designed to facilitate the coordination of such proceedings and ensure that they are administered effectively and fairly.

This Regulation aims to provide a framework for the coordination of insolvency proceedings within the European Union, ensuring that the rights of debtors and creditors are protected and that the administration of insolvency proceedings is carried out in an efficient and effective manner. The Regulation applies to public collective proceedings, including interim proceedings, which are based on laws relating to insolvency and have the purpose of rescue, adjustment of debt, reorganisation, or liquidation. It does not apply to proceedings concerning insurance undertakings, credit institutions, investment firms, and collective investment undertakings.

The Regulation establishes the jurisdiction of courts to open insolvency proceedings, with the centre of the debtor's main interests being the primary factor in determining jurisdiction. The courts of the Member State where the centre of the debtor's main interests is situated have jurisdiction to open main insolvency proceedings, while the courts of another Member State may have jurisdiction to open territorial insolvency proceedings if the debtor has an establishment within that Member State.

Insolvency practitioners appointed by a court with jurisdiction may exercise their powers in another Member State, as long as no other insolvency proceedings have been opened there and no preservation measure to the contrary has been taken. They may remove the debtor's assets from the territory of the Member State in which they are situated, subject to certain conditions. The Regulation also requires the public disclosure of certain information, including the date of the opening of insolvency proceedings, the court opening the proceedings, and the type of proceedings opened.

To facilitate the coordination of insolvency proceedings, courts and insolvency practitioners are required to cooperate with each other, including the communication of information, coordination of the administration and supervision of the debtor's assets and affairs, and coordination of the conduct of hearings. This cooperation may be implemented by any means considered appropriate by the court, including the appointment of an independent person or body to act on its instructions.

In cases where insolvency proceedings relate to two or more members of a group of companies, the Regulation requires courts to cooperate with each other to facilitate the effective administration of the proceedings. This cooperation may include the coordination of the appointment of insolvency practitioners, communication of information, and coordination of the administration and supervision of the assets and affairs of the members of the group.

Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a framework for the coordination of insolvency proceedings within the European Union, ensuring that the rights of debtors and creditors are protected and that the administration of insolvency proceedings is carried out in an efficient and effective manner.

The purpose of this Regulation is to provide a framework for the efficient and effective administration of cross-border insolvency proceedings within the European Union. It aims to avoid forum shopping, where parties transfer assets or judicial proceedings from one Member State to another to obtain a more favorable legal position, and to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market. The Regulation applies to insolvency proceedings that meet the conditions set out in it, regardless of whether the debtor is a natural person or a legal person, and includes proceedings that promote the rescue of economically viable but distressed businesses, as well as those that provide for restructuring, debt discharge, or debt adjustment.

The Regulation sets out rules on jurisdiction, recognition, and applicable law, and provides for the coordination of insolvency proceedings that relate to the same debtor or to several members of the same group of companies. It requires courts to cooperate with each other to facilitate the effective administration of proceedings, and allows for the appointment of an independent person or body to act on their instructions. Insolvency practitioners are also required to cooperate with each other, communicate relevant information, and consider possibilities for coordinating the administration and supervision of the debtor's assets and affairs.

The Regulation applies to collective proceedings that include all or a significant part of the creditors to whom a debtor owes outstanding debts, and ensures that the claims of creditors who are not involved in such proceedings remain unaffected. It excludes confidential insolvency proceedings, as their nature makes it impossible for creditors or courts in other Member States to know that such proceedings have been opened. The Regulation also sets out rules on the information that must be made publicly available, including the date of the opening of insolvency proceedings, the court that opened the proceedings, and the type of proceedings that were opened.

Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a comprehensive framework for the administration of cross-border insolvency proceedings, and to ensure that such proceedings operate efficiently and effectively throughout the European Union. It applies to a wide range of insolvency proceedings, including those that promote the rescue of distressed businesses, and provides for the coordination and cooperation of courts and insolvency practitioners to achieve this goal.

The purpose of this regulation is to ensure the safety and conformity of subsystems and safety components of cableway installations with the essential requirements set out in Annex II. Manufacturers of these subsystems and safety components have several key obligations, including designing and manufacturing them in accordance with the essential requirements, drawing up technical documentation, and carrying out conformity assessment procedures. They must also affix the CE marking to the subsystem or safety component and provide instructions and safety information in a language easily understood by users. The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and to ensure the free movement of personal data within the Union. Controllers are responsible for ensuring that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation, and they must implement measures such as data protection policies and maintain a record of processing activities. 

The legal basis for processing personal data must be laid down by Union law or Member State law to which the controller is subject, and the purpose of the processing must be determined in that legal basis. The Regulation also requires controllers to provide data subjects with certain information, such as the period for which the personal data will be stored, the existence of the right to request access to and rectification or erasure of personal data, and the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. 

In addition, the Regulation sets out rules for the transfer of personal data to third countries or international organisations, including the requirement for the Commission to assess the adequacy of the level of protection in the third country or international organisation. The Regulation also establishes the European Data Protection Board, which is responsible for ensuring the consistent application of the Regulation and for issuing guidelines, recommendations, and best practices on various aspects of the Regulation. 

The Regulation also sets out rules for the use of automated decision-making, including profiling, and requires controllers to provide meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject. Overall, the Regulation aims to protect the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data, and to ensure that personal data is processed in a lawful, fair, and transparent manner. 

Controllers and processors must adhere to the principles of data protection by design and by default, and they must implement measures to ensure the security and confidentiality of personal data. The Regulation also sets out rules for the notification of personal data breaches and for the implementation of data protection by design and by default. 

In summary, the Regulation sets out a comprehensive framework for the protection of personal data, and its key obligations include the implementation of technical and organisational measures to ensure compliance, the provision of information to data subjects, and the establishment of rules for the transfer of personal data to third countries or international organisations. The Regulation aims to protect the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data, and to ensure that personal data is processed in a lawful, fair, and transparent manner.

The purpose of this Regulation is to lay down rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the free movement of personal data.
