Controllers are responsible for ensuring that personal data is processed lawfully, fairly, and in a transparent manner, and that it is collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes. Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage.

When processing personal data, controllers must provide data subjects with certain information, including the period for which the personal data will be stored, the existence of the right to request access to and rectification or erasure of personal data, and the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. Controllers must also inform data subjects about the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, and provide meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing.

The basis for processing personal data must be laid down by Union law or Member State law to which the controller is subject, and the purpose of the processing must be determined in that legal basis. The legal basis may contain specific provisions to adapt the application of rules of this Regulation, including the general conditions governing the lawfulness of processing, the types of data subject to processing, and the entities to which personal data may be disclosed.

Controllers and processors may adhere to approved codes of conduct or certification mechanisms to demonstrate compliance with the obligations of the controller. The Regulation also provides for the maintenance of a record of processing activities, which must contain information such as the name and contact details of the controller, the purposes of the processing, and the categories of data subjects and personal data.

Overall, the Regulation aims to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular their right to the protection of personal data, and to ensure the free movement of personal data within the Union.

This Regulation aims to determine the existence, degree, and effect of alleged injurious pricing of vessels sold to the Union. To achieve this, the normal value of a vessel is determined based on the price or constructed value in a market-economy third country, or the price from such a third country to other countries, including the Union. The selection of an appropriate market-economy third country is made in a not unreasonable manner, taking into account reliable information and time limits, and the parties to the investigation are informed of the selected country and given 10 days to comment.

The determination of injury to the Union industry is based on positive evidence and involves an objective examination of the effect of the sale at less than normal value on prices in the Union market and the consequent impact on the Union industry. The examination considers factors such as price undercutting, depression of prices, and prevention of price increases, as well as the impact on the Union industry's sales, profits, output, market share, productivity, and return on investments. The Regulation also requires an evaluation of all relevant economic factors and indices having a bearing on the state of the industry.

The investigation is initiated upon a written complaint by any natural or legal person, or any association, acting on behalf of the Union industry. The complaint must include evidence of injurious pricing, injury, and a causal link between the injuriously priced sale and the alleged injury. The complaint must also demonstrate that the complainant was capable of building the vessel concerned and made demonstrable efforts to conclude a sale with the buyer consistent with the bid specifications.

The Commission examines the accuracy and adequacy of the evidence provided in the complaint to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify the initiation of an investigation. An investigation is not initiated unless the complaint has been made by, or on behalf of, the Union industry, which is defined as those Union producers whose collective capacity to produce the like vessel constitutes more than 50% of the total capacity of that portion of the Union industry expressing either support for, or opposition to, the complaint. However, no investigation is initiated where Union producers expressly supporting the complaint account for less than 25% of the total capacity of the Union producers capable of producing the like vessel.

The Regulation also provides for the assessment of the effect of the sale at less than normal value on the production of the Union industry of like vessels, and the determination of a threat of material injury, which must be based on facts and not merely on allegation, conjecture, or remote possibility. The change in circumstances that would create a situation in which the sale at less than normal value would cause injury must have been clearly foreseen and must be imminent. Overall, the Regulation aims to protect the Union industry from injurious pricing practices while ensuring that investigations are initiated and conducted in a fair and transparent manner.

The examination considers factors such as price undercutting, depression of prices, and prevention of price increases. The effects of sales from more than one country are cumulatively assessed if the margin of injurious pricing is more than de minimis and a cumulative assessment is appropriate.

The investigation is initiated upon a written complaint by any natural or legal person or association acting on behalf of the Union industry. The complaint must include evidence of injurious pricing, injury, and a causal link between the injuriously priced sale and the alleged injury. The complaint must also demonstrate that the complainant was capable of building the vessel and made efforts to conclude a sale with the buyer. The Commission examines the accuracy and adequacy of the evidence provided in the complaint to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify the initiation of an investigation.

The Regulation also sets out the conditions for initiating an investigation, including the requirement that the complaint has been made by, or on behalf of, the Union industry, which is defined as those Union producers whose collective capacity to produce the like vessel constitutes more than 50% of the total capacity of that portion of the Union industry expressing either support for, or opposition to, the complaint. However, no investigation is initiated where Union producers expressly supporting the complaint account for less than 25% of the total capacity of the Union producers capable of producing the like vessel. The authorities must avoid publicizing the complaint unless a decision has been taken to initiate an investigation.

The purpose of this regulation is to establish procedures for accepting and monitoring voluntary undertaking offers submitted by exporters to revise their prices or cease exports at dumped prices, in order to eliminate the injurious effect of dumping. The Commission may accept such undertakings if it is satisfied that the injurious effect of the dumping is thereby eliminated, and provisional or definitive duties shall not apply to the relevant imports of the product concerned manufactured by the companies referred to in the Commission decision accepting undertakings. 

The regulation applies to exporters who submit voluntary undertaking offers, as well as to the Commission, which is responsible for accepting and monitoring these undertakings. The Commission may suggest undertakings, but exporters are not obliged to enter into such an undertaking, and the fact that they do not offer such undertakings or do not accept an invitation to do so shall not prejudice consideration of the case. 

In the case of breach or withdrawal of undertakings, the acceptance of the undertaking shall be withdrawn by Commission Decision or Commission Regulation, and the provisional or definitive duty shall automatically apply, provided that the exporter concerned has been given an opportunity to comment. The Commission may request the assistance of the competent authorities of the Member States in the monitoring of undertakings, and any interested party or Member State may submit information showing prima facie evidence of a breach of an undertaking. 

Reviews of the undertakings may be carried out, and the relevant provisions of the regulation with regard to procedures and the conduct of investigations shall apply to such reviews. These reviews shall be carried out expeditiously, and shall normally be concluded within a specified timeframe, which varies depending on the type of review. If the investigation is not completed within the deadlines specified, the measures shall either expire or remain unchanged, and a notice announcing the actual expiry or maintenance of the measures shall be published in the Official Journal of the European Union. 

The regulation also provides for the possibility of parallel reviews, and in such cases, the review pursuant to one paragraph shall be concluded at the same time as the review pursuant to another paragraph. The deadlines for completing the reviews are strict, and the regulation provides for the consequences of not meeting these deadlines. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a framework for the acceptance and monitoring of voluntary undertaking offers, and to ensure that the undertakings are effective in eliminating the injurious effect of dumping.

The act also sets out procedures for reviews carried out pursuant to certain paragraphs, which shall be carried out expeditiously and concluded within specified time limits. If a review is not completed within the deadlines, the measures shall either expire or remain unchanged, depending on the type of investigation. A notice announcing the actual expiry or maintenance of the measures shall be published in the Official Journal of the European Union. The relevant provisions of the Regulation with regard to procedures and the conduct of investigations shall apply to any review carried out, excluding those relating to time limits.

This Regulation aims to protect the European Union against dumped imports from countries that are not members of the EU. It sets out detailed rules for the calculation of dumping, procedures for initiating and pursuing an investigation, and the imposition of anti-dumping duties. The Regulation applies to all imports from non-EU countries, and its key obligations include the requirement for exporters to sell products at a fair price, and for importers to pay duties on dumped products. The Regulation also establishes procedures for investigating complaints of dumping, and for imposing provisional and definitive measures to counteract the effects of dumping. 

The Regulation defines a product as being dumped if its export price to the Union is less than a comparable price for a like product in the ordinary course of trade, as established for the exporting country. It also sets out rules for determining the normal value of a product, including the use of representative sales in the ordinary course of trade, and the allocation of costs and profit margins. In cases where the exporting country is not a market economy, the Regulation provides for the use of a third country as a reference point for determining normal value.

The Regulation also establishes procedures for accepting undertakings from exporters to eliminate dumping and injury, and for imposing provisional duties in cases where there is a risk of injury to the EU industry. It provides for the termination of investigations and the imposition of measures, including the use of sampling in cases where the number of parties or transactions is large. The Regulation also sets out rules for the treatment of confidential information, and for the disclosure of essential facts and considerations to parties involved in an investigation.

In terms of conditions and exceptions, the Regulation provides for the exemption of certain imports from anti-dumping duties, and for the suspension of measures in cases where there is a temporary change in market conditions. It also provides for the retroactive collection of provisional duties in certain circumstances, and for the lapse of measures after a certain period of time. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a fair and transparent system for protecting the EU against dumped imports, while also ensuring that the rules are applied in a way that is consistent with the EU's international obligations.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to establish a framework for the management of bluefin tuna fishing in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The act applies to Member States and sets out key obligations for the submission of records, catch reporting, and transfer authorisation. Each Member State is required to submit electronically to the Commission a list of catching vessels and other fishing vessels authorised to fish for bluefin tuna, as well as a list of vessels that have been prevented from participating due to legitimate operational reasons or force majeure. The lists must be submitted one month before the start of the fishing season and must contain the vessel's name and Union fleet register number.

Masters of catching vessels and trap operators are required to send daily catch reports to the authorities of the flag Member State, including information on the weight and number of bluefin tuna caught, as well as zero catches. The reports must be transmitted electronically in a specified format and must be sent on a daily basis for purse seiners and vessels over 24 metres, and on a weekly basis for other catching vessels. The Commission may adopt implementing acts to lay down detailed rules for the recording and reporting of vessel and trap activities.

Member States are also required to inform the Commission of the quantities of bluefin tuna caught, landed, transhipped, trapped, or caged during the preceding month, and to submit detailed information on bluefin tuna catches in the preceding fishing year. This information must include the name and ICCAT number of each catching vessel, the period of authorisation, and the total catches of each catching vessel. The Commission shall transmit this information to the ICCAT Secretariat.

In addition, the act sets out rules for transfer authorisation, which requires the master of a catching vessel or the operator of a farm or trap to send a prior notification of transfer to the competent authorities of the relevant Member State. The notification must include information on the estimated time of transfer, the quantity of bluefin tuna to be transferred, and the position where the transfer will take place. The Member State responsible for the catching vessel, farm, or trap shall decide whether to grant authorisation for the transfer operation, and shall assign a unique identification number to each transfer operation.

The act also provides for verification by ICCAT regional observers and the launching of investigations in cases where there is a difference of more than 10% in the number of bluefin tuna between the estimates made by the ICCAT regional observer and the relevant control authorities. The Member State responsible for the farm shall launch an investigation in cooperation with the Member State or CPC responsible for the catching vessel or trap, and shall use other information at their disposal to conclude the investigation. The results of the investigation shall be communicated to the Commission, which shall transmit them to the ICCAT Secretariat.

Overall, the act aims to ensure the sustainable management of bluefin tuna fishing in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and to prevent overfishing and protect the marine environment. It sets out a framework for the submission of records, catch reporting, and transfer authorisation, and provides for verification and investigation in cases of non-compliance.

The European Union's legal act aims to regulate the fishing and farming of bluefin tuna in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Each Member State is required to submit annual lists of authorized fishing vessels to the Commission, which will then forward the information to the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) Secretariat. The lists must include the vessel's name and Union fleet register number, and no retroactive submissions are allowed. Member States must also inform the Commission of any changes to the lists during the calendar year, providing full details and justifying the reasons for the replacement.

Masters of catching vessels and trap operators are obligated to send daily catch reports to their flag Member State authorities, including information on the weight and number of bluefin tuna caught, as well as zero catches. The reports must be transmitted electronically in a specified format, and the Commission may adopt implementing acts to lay down detailed rules for recording and reporting vessel and trap activities.

Member States are also required to submit detailed information on bluefin tuna catches to the Commission on a yearly basis, including the name and ICCAT number of each catching vessel, the period of authorization, and the total catches. The Commission will then transmit this information to the ICCAT Secretariat.

In addition, the act regulates the transfer of bluefin tuna between vessels, farms, or traps, requiring prior notification and authorization from the relevant Member State. ICCAT regional observers are responsible for verifying the transfer operations and estimating the catches transferred. In cases of discrepancies, Member States must launch an investigation, which must be concluded within a specified timeframe.

The act also establishes measures and programs to estimate the number and weight of bluefin tuna to be caged, including the use of stereoscopic camera systems or alternative techniques. The results of these programs must be communicated to the Commission and the ICCAT Secretariat, and any discrepancies must be investigated. Overall, the act aims to ensure the sustainable management of bluefin tuna fisheries and the accuracy of catch reporting, while also preventing illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing activities.

The Regulation establishes a multiannual recovery plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, with the objective of ensuring the sustainable exploitation of this species. Each Member State must submit to the Commission, on an annual basis, lists of catching vessels and other fishing vessels flying its flag that are authorised to fish for bluefin tuna in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Prior to any transfer operation, the master of the catching vessel or the operator of the farm or trap must send a prior notification of transfer to the competent authorities of the relevant Member State, including information on the estimated time of transfer, the quantity of bluefin tuna to be transferred, and the position where the transfer will take place.

ICCAT regional observers are responsible for verifying the transfer operations and estimating the catches transferred. In cases where there is a significant difference between the estimates made by the ICCAT regional observer and the relevant control authorities or the master of the catching vessel, an investigation must be launched, and caging shall not be authorised pending the results of the investigation.

The Regulation applies to all Member States and fishing operators that engage in fishing activities for bluefin tuna in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It is essential for ensuring the long-term sustainability of bluefin tuna stocks and for complying with the Union's international obligations under the International Convention for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas.

The purpose of this Regulation is to ensure that products placed on the market are accompanied by accurate and informative labels, providing consumers with the necessary information to make informed decisions about their energy efficiency. Suppliers have a key role to play in this regard, as they are responsible for ensuring that their products are labelled correctly and that the information provided is accurate. 

Suppliers must provide each unit of a product with a printed label and a product information sheet, free of charge, and must ensure that the information provided is accurate and up-to-date. They must also deliver these labels and sheets to dealers upon request, within a specified timeframe. Furthermore, suppliers are prohibited from placing products on the market that have been designed to alter their performance in test conditions, with the aim of achieving a more favourable energy efficiency rating. 

In addition to these general obligations, suppliers must also obtain explicit consent from customers before introducing any changes to a product's energy efficiency parameters through updates, and must provide customers with the option to refuse such updates without suffering avoidable loss of functionality. Suppliers and dealers are also required to cooperate with market surveillance authorities and take immediate action to remedy any cases of non-compliance with the Regulation's requirements.

The Regulation also imposes obligations on Member States, which must not impede the placing on the market of products that comply with the Regulation and must ensure that incentives provided for products are aimed at the highest energy efficiency classes. Member States must also lay down rules on penalties and enforcement mechanisms for infringements of the Regulation and must notify the Commission of these rules.

Market surveillance authorities have the right to recover costs from suppliers in cases of non-compliance and must take all appropriate measures to ensure that products presenting a risk are withdrawn from the market or recalled. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to establish detailed requirements for labels for specific product groups and to review and rescale labels as necessary to ensure that they remain effective in promoting energy efficiency. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to promote energy efficiency and provide consumers with accurate and reliable information about the energy efficiency of products, while also ensuring that suppliers and dealers comply with the requirements and that Member States take effective enforcement measures to prevent non-compliance.

This Regulation aims to provide a framework for the labelling and provision of standard product information for energy-related products, enabling customers to make informed choices and reduce their energy consumption. The Regulation applies to energy-related products placed on the market or put into service, with certain exceptions, such as second-hand products and means of transport for persons or goods. Suppliers are obligated to ensure that products are accompanied by accurate printed labels and product information sheets, free of charge, and to deliver these to dealers promptly upon request. Suppliers must also ensure the accuracy of the labels and product information sheets and produce technical documentation to support this. Additionally, suppliers must request explicit consent from customers before introducing updates that would be detrimental to the product's energy efficiency label. Suppliers and dealers are also required to cooperate with market surveillance authorities and take immediate action to remedy any cases of non-compliance. Member States are responsible for ensuring that products comply with the Regulation and for laying down rules on penalties and enforcement mechanisms. The Regulation also provides for Union market surveillance and control of products entering the Union market, with the Commission encouraging cooperation and the exchange of information between national authorities. In cases where a product presents a risk, market surveillance authorities may require the supplier or dealer to take corrective action, and Member States may take provisional measures to prohibit or restrict the availability of the product. The Commission may also review and rescale labels to reflect technological developments and changes in the market. Overall, the Regulation seeks to promote the availability of energy-efficient products and to provide customers with accurate and reliable information to make informed choices.

These labels and sheets must be provided in accordance with this Regulation and relevant delegated acts. Suppliers must also deliver printed labels and product information sheets to dealers upon request, within five working days.

Suppliers are prohibited from placing on the market products that have been designed to alter their performance in test conditions, with the objective of reaching a more favourable level for any of the parameters specified in the relevant delegated act. They must not provide or display labels, marks, symbols, or inscriptions that do not comply with the requirements of this Regulation, if doing so would be likely to mislead or confuse customers.

Member States have an obligation to ensure that products which comply with this Regulation are not impeded from being placed on the market or put into service within their territories. They must also provide incentives for products that achieve high levels of energy efficiency and ensure that the introduction of labels and rescaling of labels is accompanied by educational and promotional information campaigns.

In cases where a product presents a risk to public interest protection, market surveillance authorities must carry out an evaluation and require the supplier or dealer to take corrective action to bring the product into compliance. The Commission and other Member States must be informed of the results of the evaluation and any action taken, and Member States must ensure that appropriate restrictive measures are taken in respect of non-compliant products.

The Regulation also establishes a framework for Union market surveillance and control of products entering the Union market, with the Commission encouraging and supporting cooperation and the exchange of information between national authorities and the Commission. Market surveillance authorities have the right to recover costs from suppliers in cases of non-compliance, and the Commission must elaborate guidelines for the enforcement of this Regulation. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that products placed on the market are accurate, informative, and compliant with the requirements set out, and that suppliers, dealers, and Member States cooperate to achieve this goal.

This Directive establishes a common framework for conducting proportionality assessments when introducing new or amending existing legislative, regulatory, or administrative provisions that restrict access to or the pursuit of regulated professions. The aim is to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market while maintaining a high level of consumer protection. The Directive applies to provisions of Member States that restrict access to a regulated profession or its pursuit, including the use of professional titles and activities allowed under such titles, as defined in Directive 2005/36/EC.

Member States are required to undertake a proportionality assessment before introducing new or amending existing provisions, considering factors such as the nature of the risks related to public interest objectives, the suitability of the provision, and its impact on the free movement of persons and services within the Union. They must also assess whether less restrictive means can achieve the public interest objective and consider the effect of new or amended provisions when combined with other requirements.

The Directive emphasizes the need for Member States to ensure that provisions are justified by public interest objectives and are proportionate, meaning they do not go beyond what is necessary to attain the objective. In assessing proportionality, Member States must consider various elements, including the connection between the scope of activities and professional qualifications, the possibility of obtaining qualifications through alternative routes, and the impact of organizational and supervision arrangements.

Additionally, Member States must monitor the compliance of new or amended provisions with the principle of proportionality after their adoption, taking into account any developments that have occurred since the provisions were adopted. They are also required to make information available to citizens and other stakeholders before introducing new or amending existing provisions.

The Directive further stipulates that Member States must ensure compliance with the principle of proportionality for specific requirements related to temporary or occasional provision of services. They must also record the reasons for considering provisions justified and proportionate in a database and make this information publicly available.

Overall, the Directive aims to strike a balance between the need to regulate professions to protect public interests and the need to avoid unnecessary restrictions that could hinder the internal market's functioning and consumer choice. It encourages Member States to adopt a proportionate approach to regulating professions, ensuring that any restrictions are necessary, suitable, and do not excessively limit access to or the pursuit of regulated professions.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to promote the use of renewable energy sources in the transport sector and to increase the share of renewable energy in the final consumption of energy in the transport sector. To achieve this, each Member State is required to set an obligation on fuel suppliers to ensure that the share of renewable energy within the final consumption of energy in the transport sector is at least 14% by 2030. This obligation may be met through various measures, including the use of biofuels, biogas, renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin, and recycled carbon fuels.

The calculation of the minimum share of renewable energy in the transport sector is based on the energy content of road and rail transport fuels supplied for consumption or use on the market, including petrol, diesel, natural gas, biofuels, biogas, and renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin. The energy content of these fuels is taken into account, and Member States may also take into account recycled carbon fuels. However, the share of biofuels and biogas produced from certain feedstocks is limited to 1.7% of the energy content of transport fuels supplied for consumption or use on the market, except in Cyprus and Malta.

Member States are also required to ensure that any national rules concerning the authorization, certification, and licensing procedures for plants and associated transmission and distribution networks for the production of electricity, heating, or cooling from renewable sources are proportionate and necessary. These rules should be objective, transparent, and non-discriminatory, and should take into account the particularities of individual renewable energy technologies. Administrative procedures should be streamlined and expedited, and administrative charges should be transparent and cost-related.

The act applies to all Member States, which are required to set their own obligations on fuel suppliers to achieve the minimum share of renewable energy in the transport sector. Member States may exempt or distinguish between different fuel suppliers and energy carriers when setting these obligations, taking into account the varying degrees of maturity and cost of different technologies. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend the act and to establish a Union methodology for calculating the minimum shares of renewable energy in the transport sector. Overall, the act aims to promote the use of renewable energy sources in the transport sector and to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, in line with the EU's international commitments for decarbonization.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to promote the use of renewable energy sources in the transport sector and to increase the share of renewable energy in the final consumption of energy. To achieve this, each Member State is required to set an obligation on fuel suppliers to ensure that the share of renewable energy within the final consumption of energy in the transport sector is at least 14% by 2030. This obligation may be met through various measures, including the use of biofuels, biogas, renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin, and recycled carbon fuels.

The calculation of the minimum share of renewable energy in the transport sector is based on the energy content of road and rail transport fuels supplied for consumption or use on the market, including petrol, diesel, natural gas, biofuels, biogas, and renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin. The energy content of these fuels is taken into account, and Member States may also consider recycled carbon fuels. However, the share of biofuels and biogas produced from certain feedstocks is limited to 1.7% of the energy content of transport fuels supplied for consumption or use on the market, except in Cyprus and Malta.

Member States are also required to ensure that any national rules concerning the authorization, certification, and licensing procedures for plants and associated transmission and distribution networks for the production of electricity, heating, or cooling from renewable sources are proportionate and necessary. These rules should be objective, transparent, and non-discriminatory, and should take into account the particularities of individual renewable energy technologies. Administrative procedures should be streamlined and expedited, and administrative charges should be transparent and cost-related.

In addition, Member States may exempt fuel suppliers supplying fuel in the form of electricity or renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin from the requirement to comply with the minimum share of advanced biofuels and biogas produced from certain feedstocks. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend the Directive and to establish a Union methodology for calculating the minimum shares of renewable energy in the transport sector.

Overall, this legal act aims to increase the use of renewable energy sources in the transport sector, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and promote sustainable transportation. The purpose of this Regulation is to establish common statistical standards for the collection of data on goods transport by inland waterways, with the aim of achieving the fullest practicable comparability between transport modes. This Regulation applies to Member States where inland waterways transport exists, and its scope is limited to the collection of data on goods transport, excluding certain types of vessels such as those used for passenger transport, ferrying purposes, or non-commercial purposes. 

Member States are required to transmit data relating to inland waterways transport on their national territory to the Commission (Eurostat), with the specific data to be collected determined by the volume of goods transported annually. Member States with a total volume of goods transported exceeding 1,000,000 tonnes are required to supply more detailed data, while those with lower volumes are subject to less stringent requirements. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend the threshold for statistical coverage and to adapt definitions and annexes to reflect changes in coding and nomenclature at international level or in relevant Union legislative acts.

The data collection process is outlined in Article 4, which requires data to be collected in accordance with specific tables set out in annexes to the Regulation. The Commission is also required to develop a methodology for compiling statistics on passenger transport by inland waterways, including by cross-border transport services, and to conduct pilot studies on the availability of statistical data relating to passenger transport. The results of these pilot studies will be reported to the European Parliament and the Council, and may lead to a legislative proposal to amend the Regulation.

The Regulation also establishes requirements for the quality of the data transmitted, including the adoption of implementing acts laying down methodological requirements and criteria designed to ensure data quality. Member States are required to take measures to ensure the quality of the data transmitted, and the Commission (Eurostat) is responsible for assessing the quality of the data. The Commission is also required to adopt implementing acts laying down arrangements for transmitting data and disseminating results, and to submit reports on the implementation of the Regulation and future developments. 

Overall, this Regulation aims to provide a framework for the collection of harmonized data on goods transport by inland waterways, which will enable the Commission to monitor and develop the common transport policy, as well as the transport elements of policies on regions and trans-European networks. The Regulation's provisions are designed to ensure the quality and comparability of the data collected, and to minimize the burden on Member States and respondents.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish common statistical standards for the collection of data on goods transport by inland waterways, with the aim of achieving the fullest practicable comparability between transport modes. This Regulation applies to Member States where inland waterways transport exists, and requires them to transmit data relating to inland waterways transport on their national territory to the Commission (Eurostat). The scope of the Regulation is limited to Member States where the total volume of goods transported annually by inland waterways exceeds 1,000,000 tonnes, although certain exemptions apply, such as the carriage of goods by vessels of less than 50 deadweight tonnes or vessels used principally for the carriage of passengers.

Member States are required to collect data in accordance with the tables set out in the Annexes to the Regulation, and to classify goods in accordance with the classification system set out in Annex VI. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend the Annexes to reflect changes in coding and nomenclature at international level or in relevant Union legislative acts, and to raise the threshold for statistical coverage of inland waterways transport. When exercising this power, the Commission must ensure that the delegated acts do not impose a significant additional burden on the Member States or on the respondents, and must duly justify the statistical actions using a cost-effectiveness analysis.

The Regulation also requires the Commission to adopt implementing acts laying down the arrangements for transmitting data to the Commission (Eurostat) and for disseminating results, which shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. The Commission is also required to arrange for pilot studies to be conducted on the availability of statistical data relating to passenger transport by inland waterways, and to submit a report to the European Parliament and to the Council on the results of these pilot studies. Depending on the results of the report, the Commission may submit a legislative proposal to amend the Regulation with regard to statistics on passenger transport by inland waterways. The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the Commission for a period of five years, and may be revoked at any time by the European Parliament or by the Council.

The Commission must submit a report on the results of these pilot studies and may subsequently submit a legislative proposal to amend the Regulation regarding statistics on passenger transport by inland waterways.

The Commission has the power to adopt implementing acts laying down arrangements for transmitting data, including data interchange standards, which must be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. This procedure involves the Commission submitting a draft implementing act to a committee, which delivers an opinion, and the Commission then adopts the act if the opinion is positive. If the opinion is negative, the Commission may not adopt the act, but may submit an amended version to the committee or to an appeal committee for further deliberation. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a framework for the collection of harmonized data on goods transport by inland waterways, which will contribute to the development of the common transport policy and the monitoring of its objectives.

This EU legal act aims to regulate the declaration and disclosure of cash entering or leaving the Union, with the purpose of preventing and combating money laundering and terrorist financing. The act applies to natural and legal persons who transport or send cash, and to competent authorities responsible for controlling and verifying compliance with the declaration and disclosure obligations. 

The declaration and disclosure obligations require providing detailed information about the declarant, the owner, sender, and recipient of the cash, as well as the nature, amount, economic provenance, and intended use of the cash. The competent authorities have the power to carry out controls on natural persons, their luggage, and means of transport, as well as on consignments, receptacles, or means of transport that may contain unaccompanied cash, in accordance with national law and based primarily on risk analysis.

If the declaration or disclosure obligations are not fulfilled, the competent authorities may compose an ex officio declaration containing the required details. The competent authorities must exchange information with each other and with the Commission, including ex officio declarations, information obtained during controls, and declarations related to criminal activity. This information must be transmitted electronically and in accordance with technical rules and using a specified form.

The act also provides for the exchange of information with third countries, subject to written authorization and compliance with national and Union law on the transfer of personal data. Member States must notify the Commission of any transmission of information to third countries. The Commission must annually publish information on the application of the act, including the list of competent authorities and anonymized statistical information.

The act is subject to evaluation by the Commission every five years, which will assess the effectiveness of the disclosure procedure, the threshold for unaccompanied cash, and the penalties introduced by Member States. The evaluation will also consider whether other assets should be included within the scope of the act and whether the information flows between competent authorities and with the Commission are effective. The report will include information received from Member States regarding cash related to criminal activities and exchange of information with third countries.

This Regulation establishes a system of controls for cash entering or leaving the European Union, complementing the legal framework for preventing money laundering and terrorist financing. The Regulation applies to carriers who transport cash of EUR 10,000 or more, as well as to senders and recipients of unaccompanied cash of the same value. Carriers are required to declare the cash to the competent authorities of the Member State through which they are entering or leaving the Union, providing details such as their identity, the owner of the cash, the intended recipient, the nature and amount of the cash, its economic provenance, and intended use. Similarly, senders or recipients of unaccompanied cash may be required to make a disclosure declaration within 30 days, providing the same information. 

The competent authorities have the power to carry out controls on natural persons, their luggage, and means of transport, as well as on consignments, receptacles, or means of transport that may contain unaccompanied cash. If the obligation to declare or disclose cash is not fulfilled, the competent authorities may compose an ex officio declaration containing the required details. The controls are based on risk analysis, aiming to identify and evaluate risks and develop countermeasures. The competent authorities are also required to exchange information with other Member States and, in certain cases, with the Commission, the European Public Prosecutor's Office, and Europol, regarding ex officio declarations, information obtained during controls, and declarations related to criminal activity. Additionally, Member States may transmit information to third countries, subject to certain conditions and authorizations. Overall, the Regulation aims to prevent and combat money laundering and terrorist financing by ensuring the transparency and traceability of cash movements within and outside the European Union.

To achieve this, individuals are required to declare accompanied cash, providing details such as their full name, contact information, date and place of birth, nationality, and identification document number, as well as information about the owner, sender, and recipient of the cash, the nature and amount of the cash, its economic provenance, and intended use. 

Competent authorities have the power to carry out controls on natural persons, their luggage, and means of transport to verify compliance with the declaration obligation, and may also control consignments, receptacles, or means of transport that may contain unaccompanied cash. The Regulation also establishes a framework for the exchange of information between competent authorities and with the Commission. Member States must transmit certain information, such as ex officio declarations, information obtained during controls, and declarations related to criminal activity, to the competent authorities of other Member States and, in some cases, to the Commission, the European Public Prosecutor's Office, and Europol. This information must be transmitted electronically, using a specific form, and within a specified timeframe. Additionally, Member States may transmit information to third countries, subject to certain conditions and authorizations, to facilitate international cooperation in combating money laundering and terrorist financing.

The Regulation applies to all Member States and is intended to complement existing Union legislation on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, such as Directive (EU) 2015/849. It does not affect the ability of Member States to provide additional national controls on movements of cash within the Union, as long as these controls are in accordance with the Union's fundamental freedoms. Overall, the Regulation aims to contribute to the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, while also facilitating the prevention, detection, and investigation of related criminal activities.

The purpose of Eurojust is to enhance the coordination of investigations and prosecutions among the Member States, with a focus on serious and organized crime. In carrying out its tasks, Eurojust is required to take into account requests from competent authorities of Member States, information provided by Union authorities, and information collected by Eurojust itself. It must also facilitate the execution of requests for judicial cooperation, including those based on instruments that give effect to the principle of mutual recognition. Eurojust's key obligations include informing Member States of investigations and prosecutions with repercussions at Union level, assisting in the coordination of investigations and prosecutions, and providing operational, technical, and financial support to Member States' cross-border operations and investigations.

Eurojust applies to the Member States and their competent authorities, as well as to Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. The agency is required to cooperate closely with the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) and other Union institutions, and to support Member States' action in combating serious crime. In terms of information exchange, Eurojust may receive and process personal data, but only in accordance with applicable data protection rules. The agency must maintain a record of all categories of processing activities under its responsibility and ensure that data subjects are informed of their rights.

The competent authorities of the Member States are required to exchange with Eurojust all information necessary for the performance of its tasks, including information on joint investigation teams, requests for judicial cooperation, and cases with serious cross-border dimensions. However, Member States are not obliged to supply information if it would harm essential national security interests or jeopardize the safety of individuals. Eurojust must also ensure that the processing of personal data is carried out in accordance with the data protection provisions of the Regulation and other relevant Union or national data protection provisions.

In terms of data protection, Eurojust has established a Data Protection Officer who is responsible for ensuring compliance with data protection provisions, informing and advising Eurojust and staff of their obligations, and cooperating with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS). The EDPS has duties under the Regulation, including hearing and investigating complaints, conducting inquiries, and advising Eurojust on matters concerning the processing of operational personal data. Data subjects have the right to access their personal data processed by Eurojust, and may make a request to Eurojust or to the national supervisory authority in their Member State of choice. Overall, Eurojust plays a crucial role in enhancing the coordination of investigations and prosecutions among the Member States, while ensuring the protection of personal data and fundamental rights and freedoms.

It facilitates the execution of requests for and decisions on judicial cooperation, including those based on instruments giving effect to the principle of mutual recognition. Eurojust informs the competent authorities of Member States about investigations and prosecutions with repercussions at Union level or affecting multiple Member States, and assists in coordinating these investigations and prosecutions.

Eurojust cooperates closely with the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) on matters relating to its competence, and provides operational, technical, and financial support to Member States' cross-border operations and investigations. It also supports the development of Union centres of specialised expertise and cooperates with Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, as well as networks established in the area of freedom, security, and justice. Furthermore, Eurojust supports Member States' action in combating forms of serious crime, such as trafficking in human beings, sexual abuse, and corruption.

This includes information about joint investigation teams, cases affecting at least three Member States, and cases with serious cross-border dimensions. However, Member States are not obliged to supply information if it would harm essential national security interests or jeopardise the safety of individuals.

Eurojust may process operational personal data, including data on persons suspected of committing or having committed a criminal offence, in order to carry out its operational functions. Data subjects have the right to access their operational personal data processed by Eurojust, and may make a request to Eurojust or to the national supervisory authority in their Member State of choice. Eurojust is required to maintain a record of all categories of processing activities under its responsibility, including the purposes of the processing, the categories of data subjects, and the categories of recipients to whom the data have been disclosed.

In exercising its operational functions, Eurojust acts either through one or more of its national members or as a College, and may take a proactive role in coordinating cases and supporting national authorities in their investigations and prosecutions. The forms of serious crime affecting two or more Member States for which Eurojust is competent are clearly laid down, and Eurojust may also be involved in cases affecting only one Member State and a third country, or cases with repercussions at Union level. Overall, Eurojust plays a crucial role in enhancing the coordination of investigations and prosecutions between Member States, and its operational functions are strengthened by its cooperation with other Union institutions and bodies.

This Regulation aims to harmonise the rules for the visa requirement for nationals of third countries when crossing the external borders of the European Union. It lists the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of a visa and those whose nationals are exempt from this requirement. The lists are based on a considered assessment of various criteria, including the situation of human rights in the third countries concerned, and are subject to periodic review. The Regulation also provides for exemptions from the visa requirement for certain categories of persons, such as recognised refugees, stateless persons, and school pupils travelling on school excursions, where they reside in a third country that is included in the list of countries whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement.

The Regulation introduces a mechanism for the temporary suspension of the exemption from the visa requirement in emergency situations, where an urgent response is needed to solve difficulties faced by at least one Member State. This suspension mechanism can be triggered by the Commission on its own initiative or by a Member State, and it allows for a fast procedure with short reference periods and deadlines. The Commission is also empowered to adopt implementing acts to determine the categories of nationals of the third country concerned who should be subject to a temporary suspension of the exemption from the visa requirement.

The Regulation also provides for a reciprocity mechanism, which enables the Union to respond as an act of solidarity if a third country included in the list of countries whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement decides to make the nationals of one or more Member States subject to a visa requirement. The Commission is delegated the power to adopt acts in respect of certain elements of the reciprocity mechanism, and it must carry out appropriate consultations during its preparatory work.

The Regulation applies to all Member States and third countries listed in its Annexes. It is intended to ensure the efficient application of the visa requirement and exemption rules, while also providing for flexibility and solidarity among Member States in their relations with third countries. The Commission is required to monitor the situation in third countries concerned and to report regularly to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of the Regulation.

This Regulation aims to harmonise the rules for the visa requirement for nationals of third countries when crossing the external borders of the European Union. It lists the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of a visa and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement. The grounds for suspension include a decrease in cooperation on readmission, a substantial increase in risks to public policy or internal security, and an increase in migratory pressure.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to ensure the interoperability of electronic toll systems (EETS) across the European Union, allowing for seamless payment of road tolls by users. To achieve this, Member States are required to take measures to ensure that toll chargers, responsible for managing EETS domains, cooperate with EETS providers to identify suspected offenders who fail to pay road fees. EETS providers must provide toll chargers with data relating to vehicles and their owners or holders, instantly and no later than two days after receiving a request, depending on the circumstances. This data can only be used for the purpose of identifying suspected offenders or complying with tax authorities' obligations, and toll chargers must not disclose it to other toll service providers.

Toll chargers are also obligated to develop and maintain an EETS domain statement, which sets out the general conditions for EETS providers to access their EETS domains. This statement must be published with sufficient notice to allow EETS providers to adapt to new requirements and obtain re-accreditation. Member States must ensure that toll chargers accept any EETS provider that requests to provide EETS on their domains, on a non-discriminatory basis, as long as the provider complies with the obligations and general conditions set out in the EETS domain statement.

In addition, toll chargers must accept operational on-board equipment (OBE) from EETS providers with whom they have contractual relationships, as long as the OBE has been certified and does not appear on a list of invalidated OBE. In the event of an EETS dysfunction, toll chargers must provide a degraded mode of service to enable vehicles to circulate safely. The act also sets out rules for the classification of vehicles for toll purposes, the payment of tolls, and the communication of substantiated toll declarations between toll chargers and EETS providers.

The act applies to Member States, toll chargers, and EETS providers, and its provisions aim to ensure the efficient and secure collection of road tolls, while also protecting the rights of EETS users. The Commission is tasked with adopting implementing and delegated acts to lay down the minimum content of the EETS domain statement, the details for the classification of vehicles, and the specifications of electronic interfaces between toll chargers, EETS providers, and EETS users. Overall, the act seeks to promote the development of interoperable EETS across the EU, facilitating the free movement of goods and people while ensuring the efficient collection of road tolls.

The purpose of this Directive is to facilitate the wider dissemination of television and radio programmes across the European Union, promoting cultural and linguistic diversity, social cohesion, and access to information. To achieve this, the Directive lays down rules on the exercise of copyright and related rights applicable to certain online transmissions of broadcasting organisations and retransmissions of television and radio programmes. The Directive applies to broadcasting organisations that offer online services ancillary to their broadcasts, such as simulcasting and catch-up services, as well as to operators of retransmission services that aggregate broadcasts of television and radio programmes into packages and provide them to users simultaneously with the initial transmission. 

The key obligation of the Directive is to establish the country of origin principle, which means that the exercise of copyright and related rights relevant for acts that occur in the course of the provision of, the access to or the use of an ancillary online service is governed by the law of the Member State in which the broadcasting organisation has its principal establishment. This principle covers the clearance of all rights necessary for a broadcasting organisation to communicate to the public or make available to the public its programmes when providing ancillary online services, including the clearance of any copyright and related rights in the works or other protected subject matter used in the programmes. However, the country of origin principle is limited to certain types of programmes, such as news and current affairs programmes, and a broadcasting organisation's own productions that are exclusively financed by it.

The Directive also ensures that the amount of payment for the rights in question takes into account all aspects of the ancillary online service, including the features of the service, the audience, and the language versions provided. Nevertheless, it remains possible to use specific methods for calculating the amount of payment for the rights subject to the country of origin principle, such as methods based on the revenues of the broadcasting organisation generated by the online service. The principle of contractual freedom is maintained, allowing parties to limit the exploitation of the rights affected by the country of origin principle, provided that any such limitation is in compliance with Union law.

The Directive does not result in any obligation for broadcasting organisations to communicate or make available to the public programmes in their ancillary online services, or to provide such ancillary online services in a Member State other than the Member State of their principal establishment. Additionally, the country of origin principle does not affect the freedom of rightholders and broadcasting organisations to agree on limitations, including territorial limitations, to the exploitation of their rights. Overall, the Directive aims to facilitate the clearance of rights for the provision of ancillary online services across borders, while ensuring that rightholders receive appropriate remuneration for the retransmission of their works and other protected subject matter.

This Directive aims to achieve equality between men and women in the labour market by facilitating the reconciliation of work and family life for workers who are parents or carers. It provides for individual rights related to paternity leave, parental leave, and carers' leave, as well as flexible working arrangements for workers who are parents or carers. The Directive defines these terms, with paternity leave referring to leave for fathers or equivalent second parents to care for a newborn, parental leave referring to leave for parents to care for a child, and carers' leave referring to leave for workers to care for a relative or person in need of significant care or support.

Member States must ensure that each worker has an individual right to parental leave of at least four months, which can be taken before the child reaches the age of eight. Two months of parental leave cannot be transferred, and workers must provide reasonable notice to their employers before taking parental leave. Member States may make the right to parental leave subject to a period of work qualification or length of service qualification, which cannot exceed one year. Employers may postpone parental leave for a reasonable period if it would seriously disrupt the business, but must provide written reasons for doing so.

Workers also have the right to request flexible working arrangements, such as remote working or reduced hours, for caring purposes. Employers must consider and respond to these requests, taking into account the needs of both the employer and the worker. The duration of flexible working arrangements may be subject to reasonable limitation, and workers have the right to return to their original working pattern at the end of the agreed period.

Member States must ensure that workers who exercise their right to leave receive a payment or allowance, with the amount and conditions to be determined by national law or collective agreements. The payment or allowance for paternity leave must guarantee an income at least equivalent to that which the worker would receive in the event of a break in their activities due to health reasons. For parental leave, the payment or allowance must be defined by the Member State or social partners and set in a way that facilitates the take-up of parental leave by both parents.

The Directive applies to all workers, including those with successive fixed-term contracts, and Member States must bring into force the necessary laws and regulations to comply with the Directive by specified deadlines. Member States may entrust the social partners with the implementation of the Directive, provided that the results sought by the Directive are guaranteed at all times. Overall, the Directive aims to promote equality and work-life balance for workers who are parents or carers, and to support the reconciliation of work and family life.

This Regulation establishes special provisions for the EU type-approval and the placing on the market of vehicles, systems, components, and separate technical units that have been type-approved by the type-approval authority of the United Kingdom. The Regulation applies to these products that fall within the scope of certain EU directives and regulations, and have been approved by the UK type-approval authority on the basis of those acts. 

Manufacturers holding a valid UK type-approval may submit an application to a Union type-approval authority for a Union type-approval of the same type, until the Union type-approval legislation ceases to apply to and in the United Kingdom. To be approved, the type must comply with the requirements applicable for the placing on the market, registration, or entry into service of new vehicles, systems, components, or separate technical units at the time when the Union type-approval takes effect. The manufacturer is liable to pay adequate fees for any costs resulting from the exercise of the powers and the fulfilment of the obligations of the Union type-approval authority.

The Union type-approval authority may grant a Union type-approval if the type meets the applicable requirements, and may request the repetition of specific tests. The type-approval certificate will include the number of the latest amending act containing requirements for type-approval, and for vehicles, will contain a mention of the previous UK type-approval. The Union type-approval shall take effect on the day of its granting or on a later date determined therein, and the UK type-approval shall become invalid on the day preceding the day on which the Union type-approval takes effect.

A Union type-approval is considered to be an EC type-approval or an EU type-approval within the meaning of the relevant directives and regulations, and all provisions of those acts not derogated from in this Regulation shall continue to apply. The Union type-approval authority shall take full responsibility for the obligations stemming from the Union type-approval, and shall exercise all the powers and fulfil all the obligations of the UK type-approval authority with respect to vehicles, systems, components, or separate technical units produced on the basis of the UK type-approval. Vehicles, systems, components, or separate technical units produced on the basis of a UK type-approval which has become invalid as a result of the granting of a Union type-approval may be placed on the market, registered, and entered into service in the Union until the Union type-approval legislation ceases to apply to and in the United Kingdom.

This Regulation establishes special provisions for the EU type-approval and the placing on the market of vehicles, systems, components, and separate technical units that have been type-approved by the type-approval authority of the United Kingdom. The Regulation applies to these products that fall within the scope of certain EU directives and regulations, and have been approved by the UK type-approval authority on the basis of those acts. 

Manufacturers holding a valid UK type-approval may submit an application to a Union type-approval authority for a Union type-approval of the same type, until the Union type-approval legislation ceases to apply to and in the United Kingdom. To be approved, the type must comply with the requirements applicable for the placing on the market, registration, or entry into service of new vehicles, systems, components, or separate technical units at the time when the Union type-approval takes effect. The manufacturer is liable to pay adequate fees for any costs resulting from the exercise of the powers and the fulfilment of the obligations of the Union type-approval authority.

For vehicles, manufacturers must indicate the Union type-approval number in a supplement to the certificate of conformity before placing them on the market, registering, or entering them into service in the Union. This Regulation aims to strengthen the functioning of the internal market by improving the application of the principle of mutual recognition and removing unjustified barriers to trade. It lays down rules and procedures concerning the application of this principle in individual cases, particularly in relation to goods lawfully marketed in another Member State. The Regulation applies to goods subject to Article 34 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and has regard to Article 36 TFEU and relevant case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

When a competent authority in a Member State intends to assess goods to determine whether they are lawfully marketed in another Member State, it must contact the economic operator concerned without delay. The authority must inform the operator of the assessment, specify the applicable national technical rule or prior authorization procedure, and indicate the possibility of supplying a mutual recognition declaration. If such a declaration is provided, it will be accepted as sufficient to demonstrate that the goods are lawfully marketed in another Member State, and no additional information will be required.

If no mutual recognition declaration is supplied, the competent authority may request documentation and information necessary for the assessment, concerning the characteristics of the goods and their lawful marketing in another Member State. The economic operator has at least 15 working days to submit the requested documents and information. The competent authority may also contact the competent authorities or Product Contact Points in the Member State where the economic operator claims to be lawfully marketing its goods to verify the information provided.

The Regulation also provides for the establishment and maintenance of Product Contact Points in Member States, which will provide information online, including details on the principle of mutual recognition, contact information for competent authorities, and available remedies in case of disputes. The Commission will facilitate cooperation among competent authorities and Product Contact Points, supporting the exchange of information and best practices, and enhancing cross-border cooperation.

In the event of an administrative decision being taken by a competent authority, it must be notified to the economic operator, the Commission, and other Member States within 20 working days. The decision must set out the reasons for it in a detailed and reasoned manner, including the national technical rule on which it is based, the legitimate public interest grounds justifying its application, and the technical or scientific evidence considered. The decision must also specify the available remedies under national law and the time limits applicable to them. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the smooth functioning of the internal market by facilitating the free movement of goods and promoting cooperation among Member States.

The purpose of this Regulation is to harmonise the calculation of Gross National Income (GNI) at market prices across the European Union, ensuring that GNI data is comparable, reliable, and exhaustive. To achieve this, the Regulation sets out rules for the calculation and transmission of GNI data by Member States. Each year, before 1 October, Member States must provide the Commission (Eurostat) with figures for GNI aggregates and their components, along with a report on the quality of the data, including the methodology used and any significant changes to sources and methods. The Commission is responsible for verifying the quality of GNI data, using a verification model based on peer review and cost-effectiveness, and for establishing specific measures to improve the comparability, reliability, and exhaustiveness of GNI data.

The Regulation applies to all Member States, which must comply with the definitions and accounting rules of the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) when calculating GNI. The Commission has the power to adopt implementing acts to establish the structure and detailed arrangements of an inventory of sources and methods used to produce GNI data, as well as the timetable for its updating and transmission. The Commission must also adopt delegated acts to define the list of issues to be addressed in every verification cycle to ensure the reliability, exhaustiveness, and comparability of GNI data.

To facilitate the verification process, the Commission may carry out GNI information visits in Member States, with the purposes of verifying the quality of GNI aggregates and their components and ensuring compliance with ESA 2010. The Regulation repeals previous directives and regulations, including Council Directive 89/130/EEC and Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1287/2003, and establishes a new framework for the verification and assessment of GNI data. The European Statistical System Committee (ESSC) is given an advisory role in assisting the Commission in exercising its implementing powers, and a formal expert group is established to assist the Commission in other functions related to GNI data. Overall, the Regulation aims to improve the quality and comparability of GNI data, which is essential for the calculation of own resources and for the coordination of national economic policies.

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish the rules and procedures for the management and administration of the .eu top-level domain (TLD). The Registry, designated by the Commission, is responsible for the operational functions of the .eu TLD and may reserve or register domain names necessary for its functions. The Commission may also instruct the Registry to reserve or register domain names for use by Union institutions and bodies. Member States may notify the Commission of domain names that are not to be registered or may only be registered at the second-level by the Member States, and the Commission shall adopt these lists by means of implementing acts.

The Registry has several key obligations, including promoting the .eu TLD, complying with Union data protection law, and ensuring the availability and integrity of the databases of domain names. The Registry must also implement the lists of reserved domain names, provide for the delegation of the .eu TLD code, and perform the registration of domain names for eligible parties. Additionally, the Registry is required to ensure the possibility for Registrars and registrants to resolve contractual disputes through alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and to publish the principles and procedures on the functioning of the .eu TLD in all official languages of the Union institutions.

The Commission has the authority to supervise the organisation, administration, and management of the .eu TLD by the Registry, and the contract between the Commission and the Registry shall reflect the obligations of the Registry. The contract shall be limited in time and renewable once without the need for a new selection procedure. The Commission shall also establish a .eu Multistakeholder Advisory Group to advise on the implementation of this Regulation and to issue opinions on strategic matters relating to the management of the .eu TLD.

The Regulation also provides for the evaluation and review of the .eu TLD, with the Commission assessing its implementation, effectiveness, and functioning every three years. The Commission shall also assess the possibility of extending the criteria for registration and may propose further measures to combat speculative and abusive registrations of domain names. Transitional provisions are established to ensure the continuity of existing domain name registrations and to provide for the designation of a new Registry and the entry into a new contract.

The framework includes several interoperability components, such as a European search portal, a shared biometric matching service, a common identity repository (CIR), and a multiple-identity detector (MID). The CIR stores data from the different information systems, logically separated according to the system from which the data originated.

The Regulation also lays down provisions on data quality requirements, a universal message format, and a central repository for reporting and statistics. It adapts the procedures and conditions for designated authorities and the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) to access the EES, VIS, ETIAS, and Eurodac for the purposes of preventing, detecting, or investigating terrorist offences or other serious criminal offences.
