This Regulation aims to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market while achieving a high level of cybersecurity, cyber resilience, and trust within the Union. It establishes the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and sets out its objectives, tasks, and organizational matters. ENISA is tasked with assisting Member States in improving their cybersecurity capabilities, as well as supporting the development and implementation of Union policy on cybersecurity certification of ICT products, services, and processes. The Agency will also cooperate with Union institutions, bodies, and agencies to address common concerns and establish practical arrangements for specific tasks.

The Regulation lays down a framework for the establishment of European cybersecurity certification schemes, which will ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity for ICT products, services, and processes in the Union. The framework applies without prejudice to specific provisions in other Union legal acts regarding voluntary or mandatory certification. ENISA will support and promote the development and implementation of Union policy on cybersecurity certification by monitoring developments in standardization, preparing candidate European cybersecurity certification schemes, and evaluating adopted schemes.

The Management Board of ENISA will establish the general direction of the Agency's operation, ensure consistency with Member States' activities, and adopt the annual budget. The Board will also establish an Advisory Group composed of recognized experts representing relevant stakeholders, such as the ICT industry, consumer groups, and academic experts. The Stakeholder Cybersecurity Certification Group will advise the Commission on strategic issues regarding the European cybersecurity certification framework and assist ENISA on general and strategic matters.

National cybersecurity certification authorities will have powers to request information, carry out investigations, and take measures to ensure compliance with the Regulation or European cybersecurity certification schemes. They will also have the power to withdraw or impose penalties on European cybersecurity certificates that do not comply with the Regulation or schemes. Peer review will assess the activities of national cybersecurity certification authorities, including their separation from supervisory activities and their procedures for supervising and enforcing rules.

The Commission, based on candidate schemes prepared by ENISA, may adopt implementing acts providing for European cybersecurity certification schemes, which will meet the requirements set out in the Regulation. The Regulation applies to ENISA, Member States, and national cybersecurity certification authorities, and its provisions are without prejudice to the competences of Member States regarding public security, defense, national security, and criminal law. Overall, the Regulation aims to promote a high level of cybersecurity, cyber resilience, and trust within the Union, while ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market.

The purpose of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 is to ensure that products placed on the EU market comply with Union harmonisation legislation, providing a high level of protection for public interests such as health and safety, consumer protection, and environmental protection. To achieve this, the Regulation establishes a framework for market surveillance and compliance, which applies to economic operators throughout the entire supply chain, including manufacturers, importers, distributors, and fulfilment service providers. These operators are expected to act responsibly and in accordance with the legal requirements applicable when placing or making products available on the market, with the manufacturer retaining ultimate responsibility for compliance.

The Regulation covers products subject to Union harmonisation legislation, excluding food, feed, medicinal products, living plants and animals, and products of human origin. It introduces a systematic approach to market surveillance, requiring Member States to establish effective enforcement measures, including risk assessment methodologies and peer review systems. The Regulation also clarifies the responsibilities of economic operators, including those involved in online sales, and introduces measures to prevent non-compliant products from entering the EU market.

In cases where products are offered for sale online or through other means of distance sales, the product is considered to have been made available on the market if the offer is targeted at end users in the EU. A case-by-case analysis is required to establish whether an offer is targeted at end users, taking into account factors such as geographical areas, languages, and means of payment. The Regulation also addresses the role of information society service providers, such as online platforms, which are not required to monitor or actively seek out non-compliant products, but may be required to remove or restrict access to such products.

The Regulation does not deal with the protection of intellectual property rights, but notes that counterfeit products often do not comply with Union harmonisation legislation and can pose risks to health and safety. Member States are encouraged to take effective measures to prevent counterfeit products from entering the EU market. Overall, the Regulation aims to create a fairer single market, ensuring equal conditions for competition and protection against unfair competition, while also protecting the health and safety of consumers and the environment.

This Regulation aims to strengthen the security standards applicable to identity cards issued by Member States to their nationals and to residence documents issued to Union citizens and their family members. The Regulation applies to identity cards, registration certificates, and residence cards issued to Union citizens and their family members, but does not apply to identification documents issued on a provisional basis with a period of validity of less than six months. 

Identity cards must be produced in ID-1 format, contain a machine-readable zone, and comply with the specifications and minimum security standards set out in ICAO Document 9303. They must also include a highly secure storage medium containing a facial image and two fingerprints in interoperable digital formats, with certain exemptions for children and individuals for whom fingerprinting is physically impossible. The storage medium must have sufficient capacity and capability to guarantee the integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of the data. 

Residence documents issued to Union citizens must indicate the title of the document, a clear reference that the document is issued to a Union citizen, the document number, the name and date of birth of the holder, and the issuing authority. They must also contain the two-letter country code of the Member State issuing the document, printed in negative in a blue rectangle and encircled by twelve yellow stars. 

The collection of biometric identifiers, such as fingerprints, must be carried out by qualified and duly authorised staff, and the applicant must appear in person at least once during the issuance process. The biometric identifiers must be stored in a highly secure manner and only until the date of collection of the document, and then immediately erased or destroyed. 

Member States are responsible for ensuring the security, integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of the data collected and stored, and must designate a body responsible for printing identity cards and residence cards. The Commission may establish additional technical specifications to ensure compliance with future minimum security standards, and must carry out an evaluation of the Regulation every six years to assess its impact on fundamental rights, mobility of Union citizens, and the effectiveness of biometric verification. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the security and integrity of identity cards and residence documents, while also protecting the fundamental rights of individuals and ensuring the free movement of Union citizens.

The biometric identifiers must be stored in a highly secure manner and only until the date of collection of the document, and then immediately erased or destroyed.

The Regulation also provides for the phasing out of existing residence cards that do not meet the new security standards, with a deadline of 3 August 2026 for most cards and 3 August 2023 for cards that do not meet the minimum security standards or do not include a functional MRZ. The storage medium must have sufficient capacity to guarantee the integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of the data, and the data stored must be accessible in contactless form and secured. 

Residence documents issued to Union citizens must indicate the title of the document, a clear reference that it is issued to a Union citizen, the document number, the name and date of birth of the holder, and the issuing authority. They must also contain the two-letter country code of the Member State issuing the document, printed in negative in a blue rectangle and encircled by 12 yellow stars. 

The collection of biometric identifiers, such as fingerprints, must be done solely by qualified and authorized staff, and the applicant must appear in person at least once during the issuance process. The biometric identifiers stored for the purpose of personalization of identity cards or residence documents must be kept in a highly secure manner and erased or destroyed after 90 days from the date of issue. 

Member States are responsible for ensuring the security, integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of the data collected and stored, and must comply with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The authorities responsible for issuing identity cards and residence documents are considered the controllers of personal data and must have responsibility for the processing of personal data. Supervisory authorities must have access to all personal data and necessary information to fully exercise their tasks. 

Overall, this Regulation aims to enhance the security of identity cards and residence documents, reduce the risk of falsification and document fraud, and facilitate the exercise of the right to free movement for Union citizens and their family members.

The purpose of this regulation is to outline the tasks and responsibilities of immigration liaison officers, who are deployed by the European Union to third countries to manage migration effectively. These officers carry out their tasks within the framework of their responsibilities determined by the deploying authorities and in accordance with Union and national laws, as well as international agreements. They must respect fundamental rights and international law, with particular consideration for vulnerable persons and the gender dimension of migration flows.

Immigration liaison officers are responsible for collecting information on various issues, including European integrated border management, migratory flows, routes used by migrants, and the existence of criminal organisations involved in smuggling and trafficking. They must also establish and maintain direct contacts with the competent authorities of third countries and relevant organisations, and coordinate among themselves and with stakeholders to provide capacity-building activities. Additionally, they may render assistance in establishing the identity and nationality of third-country nationals, facilitating their return, and confirming the identity of persons in need of international protection.

The regulation also provides for the creation of local or regional networks of immigration liaison officers, who shall cooperate with each other and with liaison officers deployed by non-Member States. These networks shall meet regularly, exchange information and practical experience, and coordinate positions to be adopted in contacts with commercial carriers. The Steering Board, established by the regulation, shall oversee the activities of the immigration liaison officers and networks, and carry out tasks such as establishing priorities, planning activities, and reviewing the implementation of its activities.

The regulation applies to immigration liaison officers deployed by the European Union to third countries, as well as to the Member States and Union agencies. It is essential that these officers carry out their tasks in accordance with the provisions of the regulation, respecting fundamental rights and international law, and with particular consideration for vulnerable persons. The regulation also requires the Steering Board to transmit certain documents to the European Parliament, ensuring transparency and accountability in the management of migration. Overall, the regulation aims to ensure effective management of migration, while respecting the rights and dignity of migrants.

The European Union has established a military crisis management operation, named EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, to contribute to preventing arms trafficking and the illicit export of petroleum from Libya, as well as to disrupt human smuggling and trafficking networks. The operation will gather and share information on arms trafficking with relevant partners and agencies, and will carry out inspections of vessels on the high seas off the coast of Libya where there are reasonable grounds to believe that they are carrying arms or related materiel in violation of the UN arms embargo. The operation will also assist in the development of the capacities and training of the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy in law enforcement tasks at sea.

The operation will be carried out in accordance with relevant UN Security Council Resolutions, including UNSCR 1970 (2011), UNSCR 2292 (2016), and UNSCR 2473 (2019), and will be subject to the political control and strategic direction of the EU's Political and Security Committee. The Committee will exercise its control through the EU Operation Commander and the EU Force Commander, and will receive regular reports on the conduct of the operation. The operation will also be subject to regular review and assessment, and its authorisation will be reconfirmed every four months.

The operation will collect and store information, including personal data, on individuals involved in arms trafficking and human smuggling, and will share this information with relevant law enforcement authorities and competent Union bodies. The operation will also collect and store medical information and biometric data on trainees, with their consent. The EU will release information to designated third states, the International Criminal Court, and INTERPOL, as appropriate and in accordance with operational needs, and will handle classified information in accordance with EU rules and procedures.

The operation's tasks will be carried out on the high seas in the agreed Area of Operation, and may also be carried out in the territory of Libya or a host third state neighbouring Libya, with the consent of the relevant authorities. The operation will transmit information gathered on suspected incidents of non-compliance with the UN arms embargo and measures to prevent illicit exports of petroleum to the UN, and will release information to legitimate Libyan authorities as necessary. Overall, the operation aims to contribute to the implementation of UN measures and the prevention of arms trafficking and human smuggling, while also supporting the development of the capacities of the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy.

EUNAVFOR MED IRINI will also assist in the development of the capacities and training of the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy in law enforcement tasks at sea. The operation will be carried out in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council Resolutions, including UNSCR 1970, 2146, 2292, 2473, 2509, and 2510, and will be subject to the political control and strategic direction of the EU's Political and Security Committee. The operation's Area of Operation and Area of Interest will be defined in relevant planning documents, and the operation will be authorized to collect, store, and exchange information, including personal data, with relevant authorities and agencies. The EU's High Representative will be authorized to release classified and non-classified information to designated third states, the International Criminal Court, and other relevant entities, in accordance with operational needs and the principles of reciprocity and inclusiveness. The operation will be regularly reviewed and assessed, and its authorization will be reconfirmed every four months, unless it is determined that the operation is having a pull effect on migration.

The European Security and Defence College (ESDC) is established to organise and conduct training and education activities in the field of the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) within the wider context of the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP). The ESDC's main tasks include providing basic and advanced level courses, leadership development, and training directly supporting CSDP Missions and Operations, as well as promoting EU partnerships and supporting civilian and military training. The ESDC will also develop and produce training materials, support exchange programmes, and maintain relationships with relevant actors in the field of Freedom, Security, and Justice, and with International Organisations.

The ESDC's structure consists of a Steering Committee, an Executive Academic Board, a Head, and a Secretariat. The Steering Committee is responsible for the overall coordination and direction of the ESDC's training and education activities, including approving the annual academic programme, selecting and prioritising training activities, and adopting curricula. The Executive Academic Board ensures the quality and coherence of the ESDC's training and education activities, implements the agreed annual academic programme, and develops curricula. The Head is the sole legal representative of the ESDC, responsible for the financial and administrative management, and advises the Steering Committee and the Board. The Secretariat assists the Head, provides support to the Steering Committee and the Board, and ensures the overall quality and coherence of the ESDC's training and education activities.

The ESDC's activities are guided by the need to support the development of the CSDP, and to promote the exchange of best practices and experience among Member States' training and educational institutes. The ESDC will also support the management of training and education in areas such as conflict prevention, civilian crisis management, and Security Sector Reform initiatives. The ESDC's work is overseen by the Steering Committee, which evaluates the performance of the Head and contributes to the selection process of the Head. The ESDC's budget is approved by the Steering Committee, and the Head is responsible for the financial and administrative management of the ESDC. Overall, the ESDC plays a crucial role in promoting the development of the CSDP, and in supporting the training and education needs of Member States' personnel involved in CSDP activities.

The European Year of Rail, designated as the year 2021, aims to encourage and support efforts to increase the share of passengers and freight moving by rail. The general objective is to promote rail as a sustainable, innovative, and interconnected mode of transport, highlighting its role in achieving the Union's climate neutrality objective by 2050. Specific objectives include promoting rail as a game changer, a pillar of an efficient logistic network, and a transport mode that reaches out to the wider public, especially the young. The European Year also seeks to enhance the contribution of rail to the Union's economy, industry, and society, and to promote rail as an important element in relations between the Union and its neighbouring countries.

To achieve these objectives, measures will be taken at Union, national, regional, and local levels, including initiatives and events to promote debate, build a positive image, and raise awareness about rail transport. These measures will be closely coordinated with ongoing activities promoting rail transport and will include informative exhibitions, educational campaigns, and the use of demonstration and information trains. The Commission will consider initiating studies on the feasibility of creating a European label to promote goods and products transported by rail and introducing a rail connectivity index to categorise the level of integration achieved through the use of services on the rail network.

The Commission will regularly convene meetings of national contact persons to coordinate the running of the European Year and will also convene regular meetings of stakeholders and representatives of organisations active in the field of rail transport. The Commission may organise calls for proposals and projects that can receive support for their outstanding contribution to the objectives of the European Year, if the budget allows. The European Year will be promoted through various channels, including the media, social networks, and other online communities, and its visual identity may be used by Union institutions and bodies, as well as Member States, to promote the activities referred to in the European Year. Overall, the European Year of Rail aims to promote rail as a sustainable, innovative, and interconnected mode of transport, and to increase its share of passengers and freight, thereby contributing to the Union's climate neutrality objective and enhancing the contribution of rail to the Union's economy, industry, and society.

This Regulation establishes total allowable catches (TACs) for various fish species in different zones. The TACs are allocated among the Union, Norway, and other countries, with specific quotas for each member state. The Regulation applies to fisheries in Union waters and international waters, with some special conditions and exceptions. For example, in Norwegian waters south of 62° N, the Union is allowed to catch up to 50,000 tonnes of herring, while Sweden is allowed to catch up to 948 tonnes. Similarly, in zone 4, the Union is allowed to catch up to 10,618 tonnes of cod, while Norway is allowed to catch up to 2,502 tonnes.

The Regulation also sets out special conditions for by-catches, which are catches of non-target species. For instance, by-catches of cod, haddock, and whiting are to be counted against the quota for those species. Additionally, some quotas are exclusively for by-catches, and no directed fisheries are permitted under those quotas. The Regulation also provides for transfers of quotas between member states, with advance notification to the Commission.

The Regulation covers various fish species, including herring, cod, haddock, mackerel, and common sole, among others. It also sets out specific zones and areas where fishing is permitted or restricted. For example, in zone 6a, the Union is allowed to catch up to 14,453 tonnes of mackerel, while in zone 3a, Denmark is allowed to catch up to 447 tonnes of common sole.

Overall, the Regulation aims to manage fisheries in a sustainable way, ensuring the long-term conservation of fish stocks while also providing for the economic and social needs of the fishing industry. The European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency, known as SURE, has been established to address the impact of the COVID-19 outbreak and respond to its socio-economic consequences. This instrument enables the Union to provide financial assistance to Member States experiencing a severe economic disturbance caused by the COVID-19 outbreak, primarily for the financing of short-time work schemes or similar measures aimed at protecting employees and the self-employed, as well as for the financing of some health-related measures. The financial assistance takes the form of a loan granted by the Union to the Member State concerned, which is financed by recourse to international capital markets. 

To be eligible for financial assistance, a Member State must demonstrate a sudden and severe increase in actual and possibly also planned public expenditure due to national measures directly related to short-time work schemes and similar measures, as well as, where applicable, to relevant health-related measures. The Commission verifies the compliance of the Member State with the conditions set out in the regulation and assesses the existing and expected needs of the requesting Member State, as well as requests for financial assistance from other Member States, applying the principles of equal treatment, solidarity, proportionality, and transparency.

The borrowing and lending operations under the instrument are carried out in euros, and the characteristics of the loan are agreed upon in a loan agreement between the beneficiary Member State and the Commission. The Commission may refinance or restructure the loan at the request of the beneficiary Member State, where circumstances permit an improvement in the interest rate. The Economic and Financial Committee is kept informed of any refinancing or restructuring.

The instrument is of a temporary nature, and the Commission assesses every six months whether the exceptional circumstances causing the severe economic disturbances in Member States still exist. The availability of the instrument is limited in time, and the Council may extend its period of availability if the exceptional occurrences that justify its application continue to exist. The United Kingdom does not participate in the financial assistance under this regulation, as any contingent financial liability of the Union arising from financial assistance would be subsequent to the date of entry into force of the Withdrawal Agreement. 

The Union's borrowing and lending operations under the instrument are supported by guarantees provided by the Member States, which are irrevocable, unconditional, and on demand. The Commission draws on the margin available under the own-resources ceiling for payment appropriations before calling on the guarantees provided by Member States. The need for guarantees may be reviewed if an agreement on a revised own-resources ceiling is reached. The additional safeguards to enhance the robustness of the system consist of conservative financial management, a maximum annual exposure, and sufficient diversification of the loan portfolio. 

In order to make the contingent liability arising from loans granted under the instrument compatible with the applicable multiannual financial framework and own-resources ceilings, prudential rules are laid down, including on the possibility of rolling over the borrowings contracted on behalf of the Union. Decisions to grant financial assistance require the exercise of implementing powers, which are conferred on the Council. The Council, on a proposal from the Commission, considers the existing and expected needs of the requesting Member State, as well as requests for financial assistance from other Member States, having regard to the principles of equal treatment, solidarity, proportionality, and transparency.

The European Union Recovery Instrument, established by Council Regulation (EU) 2020/2094, aims to support the recovery in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis. The Instrument is designed to address the significant disturbances to economic activity, employment, and social conditions caused by the crisis, which have had a disproportionate impact on certain sectors, such as travel and tourism, and on small and medium-sized enterprises. The Regulation recognizes that the crisis has spread quickly across the Union, posing a risk to the single market, social and territorial cohesion, and the financial situation of many businesses.

To mitigate these effects, the Instrument will provide substantial amounts of public and private investment to set the Union on a path towards a sustainable and resilient recovery, creating high-quality jobs, supporting social inclusion, and repairing the immediate damage caused by the crisis. The support provided under the Instrument will focus on measures to restore labour markets and social protection, as well as healthcare systems, and will also support businesses affected by the crisis, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises. Additionally, the Instrument will support investment in activities essential for strengthening sustainable growth in the Union, including direct financial investment in enterprises, research and innovation, and capacity building at Union level to enhance future crisis preparedness.

The Instrument will be financed up to an amount of EUR 750 000 million in 2018 prices, with the amount allocated as follows: up to EUR 384 400 million in non-repayable support and repayable support through financial instruments, and up to EUR 360 000 million in loans to Member States. The allocation of financial resources will reflect the extent to which the programmes are capable of contributing to the objectives of the Instrument. The Regulation also provides for the use of established mechanisms of spending through Union programmes under the multiannual financial framework, with support to be provided in the form of non-repayable support, loans, and provisioning for budgetary guarantees.

The Instrument's implementation will be subject to strict compliance with its objectives, which are linked to supporting recovery in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis. The Commission will prepare a report by 31 October 2022 to review the progress achieved in the implementation of the Instrument and the use of the support allocated. Overall, the European Union Recovery Instrument is an exceptional and coordinated programme of economic and social support, designed to prevent further deterioration of the economy, employment, and social cohesion, and to boost a sustainable and resilient recovery of economic activity, in a spirit of solidarity between Member States.

The European Parliament and the Council have adopted a Decision on the Strategic Innovation Agenda of the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) for the period 2021-2027. The Agenda aims to boost the innovation talent and capacity of Europe, and it repeals Decision No 1312/2013/EU. The EIT's Strategic Innovation Agenda should set out priority fields and strategies, establish key actions, and include an assessment of the EIT's expected social, economic, and environmental impact. The Agenda should also take into account the strategic planning of Horizon Europe, the Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, and ensure consistency with Union priorities and commitments, such as the European Green Deal and the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030.

The Decision highlights the importance of innovation in areas such as marine and freshwater ecosystem degradation, and the circular and sustainable blue economy. It notes that the global market for goods and services to measure and mitigate degradation is growing and highly competitive, and that innovation can enhance, restore, and recover marine, coastal, and freshwater capital. The Decision also emphasizes the need for a Knowledge and Innovation Community (KIC) on Water, Marine, and Maritime (WMM) to address the challenges in these areas, and to establish synergies with relevant Union policy initiatives and international initiatives.

The KIC on WMM should reduce the fragmentation of the water, maritime, and marine sectors' innovation landscape, promote an integrated and multidisciplinary approach, connect actors and networks across sectors and disciplines, train and develop the next generation of innovators and entrepreneurs, and contribute to the development of the appropriate framework conditions to transform ideas into new technological developments and social innovation. The KIC should also establish synergies with other European Partnerships, missions, the European Innovation Council (EIC), the European Investment Bank (EIB), and BlueInvest, to scale up innovations and increase the market deployment and societal acceptance of innovative solutions.

The Decision applies to the EIT and its Knowledge and Innovation Communities, including the KIC on WMM, and it enters into force with retroactive effect from 1 January 2021. The Decision is necessary to ensure the continuity of the activities of the EIT and the KICs, and it is in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity and proportionality. Overall, the Decision aims to strengthen the innovation ecosystems throughout Europe, tackle water-related challenges, and promote the blue economy vision, thereby contributing to the competitiveness of Union businesses and supporting jobs and growth across the Union.

The purpose of this Agreement is to establish a mandatory transparency register for organisations and self-employed individuals engaged in EU policy-making and policy implementation. The register is managed by a joint operational structure, known as the Secretariat, which is composed of heads of unit from each signatory institution and their respective staff. The Secretariat is responsible for monitoring registrations, evaluating registrants' ongoing eligibility, and ensuring compliance with the code of conduct.

Registrants, including organisations and self-employed individuals, are required to provide accurate and up-to-date information about their activities, interests, and financial resources. They must also operate in accordance with the code of conduct, which sets out principles for transparency, honesty, and integrity in their relations with the EU institutions. The code of conduct requires registrants to identify themselves, declare their interests and objectives, and avoid any behaviour that could damage the reputation of the register or the EU institutions.

The Secretariat has the power to investigate and apply measures in cases of non-compliance, and registrants are required to cooperate sincerely and constructively with the Secretariat. The Agreement also provides for the voluntary involvement of Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, as well as Member States' permanent representations, which can notify the Management Board of measures they take to make certain activities conditional upon registration in the register.

The signatory institutions, which include the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission, are committed to financing the maintenance, development, and promotion of the register. The Agreement enters into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union, and it replaces the 2014 Agreement. Registrants who were already entered in the register before the date of entry into force of this Agreement have six months to amend their registration to satisfy the new requirements. Any investigations opened under the 2014 Agreement will be carried out in accordance with the procedure laid down in that Agreement.

This Agreement establishes a framework for transparent and ethical interest representation, aiming to coordinate the approach of signatory institutions in this regard. The Agreement covers activities carried out by interest representatives to influence policy or legislation formulation, implementation, or decision-making processes of Union institutions. These activities include meetings, consultations, communication campaigns, and preparation of policy papers, among others. To ensure transparency, a register is maintained, and registrants must provide accurate information and cooperate with the Secretariat, a joint operational structure set up to manage the register's functioning. The Secretariat, composed of heads of unit from signatory institutions, is responsible for monitoring registrations, evaluating registrants' ongoing eligibility, and providing helpdesk support. It also carries out investigations, establishes guidelines, and undertakes communication and awareness-raising actions. The Management Board oversees the Agreement's implementation, determines priorities and budget estimates, and issues instructions to the Secretariat. Signatory institutions are responsible for financing the register's maintenance, development, and promotion. This Agreement establishes a framework for transparent and ethical interest representation, aiming to coordinate the approach of signatory institutions in this regard. The Interinstitutional Agreement between the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union, and the European Commission establishes a mandatory transparency register for interest representatives. The EU's health programme aims to improve human health throughout the Union and ensure a high level of protection of human health in all Union policies and activities. To achieve this, the programme pursues several general objectives, including improving and fostering health in the Union, protecting people from serious cross-border threats to health, and improving the availability and accessibility of medicinal products and medical devices. The programme also seeks to strengthen health systems by improving their resilience and resource efficiency, particularly through supporting integrated and coordinated work between Member States, promoting the implementation of best practices, and advancing digital transformation.

The programme applies to the Member States, and its implementation is supported by the EU4Health Steering Group, which ensures consistency and complementarity between the Member States' health policies and the programme. The group also follows up on the implementation of the programme and proposes necessary adjustments based on evaluations. In terms of funding, costs incurred prior to the submission of a grant application may be eligible for funding under certain conditions, such as when implementing the objective of protecting people from serious cross-border threats to health. Additionally, costs incurred by entities established in non-associated countries may be considered eligible in exceptional cases during a health crisis.

The programme's progress is monitored through a set of indicators, including preparedness and response planning for serious cross-border threats to health, access to centrally authorised medicinal products, and the number of actions contributing to the reduction of avoidable mortality in the area of non-communicable diseases. Other indicators include vaccination coverage, EU laboratory capacity, age-standardised five-year net survival rate for paediatric cancer, and screening coverage for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer screening programmes. These indicators help to assess the programme's impact and identify areas for improvement, ensuring that the programme is effective in achieving its objectives and improving the health of people in the Union.

The InvestEU Regulation establishes the InvestEU Fund, which provides an EU guarantee to support financing and investment operations carried out by implementing partners that contribute to the Union's internal policies. The Regulation also sets up an advisory support mechanism, known as the InvestEU Advisory Hub, to help develop investable projects and provide access to financing, as well as a database, the InvestEU Portal, to give visibility to projects seeking financing and provide investors with information on investment opportunities. The InvestEU Programme has a budget and an EU guarantee amount for the period 2021 to 2027, with specific forms of Union funding and rules for providing such funding.

The Regulation applies to Member States, which may allocate amounts on a voluntary basis to support the provisioning of the EU guarantee under the Member State compartment. These amounts can be used to cover financing and investment operations in the Member State concerned or to contribute to the InvestEU Advisory Hub. The allocation of these amounts is subject to the conclusion of a contribution agreement between the Member State and the Commission, which must contain certain elements, including the overall amount of the EU guarantee, the provisioning rate, and the amount of the contribution from funds under shared management.

The contribution agreement must also include the Member State strategy, consisting of the financial products and their minimum leverage, geographical coverage, types of projects, and investment period. The agreement must also provide for the obligations to provide annual reports to the Member State, including reporting on relevant indicators related to policy objectives. The Commission and the EIB Group form a partnership to support the implementation of the InvestEU Programme, with the EIB Group implementing the portion of the EU guarantee specified in the Regulation and supporting the implementation of the EU compartment of the InvestEU Fund.

The provisioning rate for the EU guarantee under the Member State compartment is set at 40% and may be adjusted downwards or upwards in each contribution agreement to take account of the risks attached to the financial products intended to be used. The contribution agreement must be implemented by the Commission through guarantee agreements concluded with implementing partners, and any unused amount of provisioning must be re-used in accordance with the relevant Regulations or paid back to the Member State. The Regulation also sets out rules for the management of annual surpluses and replenishments after the constitution phase, including the obligation for the Member State to provide up to 5% of the initial provisioning to the common provisioning fund if the level of provisions falls below 10% of the initial provisioning.

In particular, it applies to entities such as national statistical institutes, non-profit making entities, and bodies operating in the field of statistics. Third countries may also be eligible for funding for certain actions, such as protection measures taken in the case of a direct threat to the health status of the Union. However, in principle, third countries that are not associated with the Programme should finance their own participation in such actions.

Important conditions and exceptions apply to the eligibility criteria. For example, actions must not constitute activities that are already funded under other Union programmes, and entities must not have conflicts of interests. Additionally, certain entities, such as the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group and the Bureau Européen des Unions de Consommateurs, may be designated as beneficiaries without a call for proposals, provided they meet specific conditions. The Commission is also empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend certain annexes, where necessary, to take account of new animal diseases and zoonoses. Overall, the act aims to support the development of a strong and competitive internal market, while also ensuring the protection of consumers and the environment.

The Programme aims to support and accelerate the digital transformation of the European economy, industry, and society, bringing its benefits to citizens, public administrations, and businesses across the Union. The Programme has five interrelated specific objectives: High Performance Computing, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Trust, Advanced Digital Skills, and Deployment and Best Use of Digital Capacities and Interoperability. The Programme shall be implemented in close coordination with other Union programmes and aims to strengthen and promote Europe's capacities in key digital technology areas, as well as widen the diffusion and uptake of these technologies in the private sector and areas of public interest.

The financial contribution from the Union under Specific Objective 2 – Artificial Intelligence shall pursue operational objectives such as building up and strengthening core AI capacities, making these capacities accessible to businesses and civil society, and reinforcing AI testing and experimentation facilities. Similarly, the financial contribution under Specific Objective 3 – Cybersecurity and Trust shall support the building-up of advanced cybersecurity equipment and knowledge, ensure a wide deployment of effective cybersecurity solutions, and improve resilience against cyberattacks.

The Programme also supports the development of advanced digital skills, particularly in areas such as high-performance computing, big data analytics, and cybersecurity, with a focus on increasing Europe's talent pool and bridging the digital divide. The financial contribution under Specific Objective 4 – Advanced Digital Skills shall support the design and delivery of high-quality training and courses, as well as on-the-job training and work placements.

Specific Objective 5 – Deployment and Best Use of Digital Capacities and Interoperability aims to support the public sector and areas of public interest in effectively deploying and accessing state-of-the-art digital technologies, as well as deploying trans-European interoperable digital service infrastructures. The Programme shall also facilitate the development and use of solutions and frameworks by public administrations, businesses, and citizens, and support the uptake of advanced digital technologies by SMEs and start-ups.

The Programme applies to the European Union and its Member States, with each Member State designating candidate entities to form a network of European Digital Innovation Hubs. The selection of these entities shall be based on criteria such as appropriate competences, management capacity, and financial viability. The Commission shall adopt decisions on the selection of entities through implementing acts, taking into account the examination procedure and the utmost account of the selection criteria. Overall, the Programme seeks to improve the competitiveness of Europe in the global digital economy, contribute to bridging the digital divide, and reinforce the Union's strategic autonomy.

The purpose of this EU legal act is to establish the rules and conditions for the participation of third countries and international organisations in Union programmes, such as Galileo, EGNOS, Copernicus, GOVSATCOM, and the Secure Communication Services (SWE and NEO sub-components). The act applies to these programmes and sets out the conditions for third country participation, including the requirement for a specific agreement to be concluded in accordance with Article 218 TFEU. This agreement must ensure a fair balance of contributions and benefits, lay down conditions of participation, and guarantee the rights of the Union to ensure sound financial management and protect its financial interests.

The act also sets out the eligibility and participation conditions for procurement, grants, or prizes under this Title, which the Commission may apply if necessary to preserve the security, integrity, and resilience of the operational Union systems. The Commission must inform the Programme committee and take into account the views of the Member States before applying these conditions. In certain circumstances, the Commission may waive these conditions for a particular legal entity, provided that specific criteria are met, including the availability of substitutes in the Member States and the implementation of sufficient measures to ensure the protection of European Union Classified Information (EUCI).

The act establishes the tasks and responsibilities of the Agency, which include ensuring the security accreditation of all the Programme's components, performing tasks related to the development of downstream applications, and undertaking communication, market development, and promotion activities. The Commission may entrust the implementation of certain tasks to entities other than the Agency, such as the European Space Agency (ESA), and may conclude a Framework Partnership Agreement (FFPA) with ESA, which sets out the roles, responsibilities, and obligations of the parties.

The act also sets out the conditions for Member States wishing to participate in the provision of Space Surveillance and Tracking (SST) services, which include demonstrating compliance with specific criteria, such as ownership of or access to adequate SST sensors and human resources to operate them. The act establishes the Administrative Board, which is responsible for adopting the Agency's work programme, performing budgetary functions, and overseeing the operation of the Galileo Security Monitoring Centre.

Overall, the act aims to ensure the security, integrity, and resilience of the Union's space programmes, while also promoting the Union's strategic autonomy and open economy. It sets out a framework for the participation of third countries and international organisations, and establishes the tasks and responsibilities of the Agency and other entities involved in the implementation of the programmes.

The Union Space Programme, established for the duration of the Multiannual Financial Framework 2021-2027, aims to achieve specific objectives through various components, including Galileo, EGNOS, Copernicus, GOVSATCOM, and the Space Situational Awareness (SSA) programme. The programme is open to participation from third countries and international organisations under specific agreements that ensure a fair balance of contributions and benefits, and guarantee the protection of the Union's financial interests. These agreements must be concluded in accordance with Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and must lay down conditions for participation, including the calculation of financial contributions and administrative costs.

The Commission has the authority to apply eligibility and participation conditions to procurement, grants, or prizes under the programme to preserve the security, integrity, and resilience of the operational Union systems. The Commission may waive certain conditions for a particular legal entity if specific criteria are met, such as the availability of substitutes in the Member States or the implementation of sufficient measures to protect the European Union's classified information.

The European Union Agency for the Space Programme has various tasks, including ensuring the security accreditation of the programme's components, performing communication and market development activities, and providing expertise to the Commission. The Commission may entrust tasks to entities other than the Agency, such as the European Space Agency (ESA), which must apply Union security rules and manage funds in accordance with the Financial Regulation.

The programme's implementation is subject to monitoring and control measures, including a cost forecast system, systematic provision of information on costs and schedule, and corrective action in case of discrepancies. The Commission may establish principles for the remuneration of ESA, which must be commensurate with the conditions under which the actions are implemented. Overall, the Union Space Programme aims to promote the Union's strategic autonomy, particularly in terms of technology, while preserving an open economy and ensuring the protection of the Union's financial interests.

This Regulation aims to provide effective protection for passengers and encourage rail travel by establishing rules applicable to rail transport. The Regulation covers various aspects, including non-discrimination between passengers, liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage, passengers' rights in the event of accidents or disruptions, and minimum information to be provided to passengers. Railway undertakings are liable for passengers and their luggage, subject to the provisions of the Regulation and applicable national law. In the event of cancellation or delay, passengers may be entitled to compensation, and railway undertakings may allow passengers to conclude contracts with other providers of transport services to reach their final destination under comparable conditions. The Regulation also sets out rules for the exclusion of liability, such as when a passenger does not conform to formalities required by customs or other administrative authorities. Passengers are liable to the carrier for any loss or damage resulting from their failure to fulfil obligations or caused by articles and animals they bring with them, unless they can prove that the loss or damage was caused by circumstances beyond their control. Carriers who have paid compensation may have a right of recourse against other carriers who have taken part in the carriage. The Regulation also requires railway undertakings to provide minimum information to passengers, including pre-journey information, information during the journey, and information on operations regarding reservation systems. Additionally, the Regulation sets out minimum service quality standards, including punctuality of services, delays, cancellations, cleanliness of rolling stock and station facilities, and complaint handling. Overall, the Regulation applies to railway undertakings and aims to ensure that passengers are protected and informed throughout their journey.

The liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage is governed by specific chapters and titles of Annex I, and railway undertakings must be adequately insured or have adequate guarantees to cover their liabilities. In the event of cancellation, delay, or missed connections, passengers may be entitled to compensation, including reimbursement for costs incurred in reaching their final destination under comparable conditions. Railway undertakings may also be required to make advance payments to meet immediate economic needs of passengers who are killed or injured. The Regulation applies to international and domestic rail journeys and services throughout the Union, provided by licensed railway undertakings, although Member States may exempt certain services, such as those operated for historical or touristic use, from its application. Exemptions may also be granted for urban, suburban, and regional rail passenger services, as well as international rail passenger services with a significant part operated outside the Union. However, certain provisions, including those related to liability and insurance, continue to apply even in cases of exemption. Overall, the Regulation seeks to ensure that passengers are protected and have access to necessary information and compensation in the event of disruptions or accidents, while also providing a framework for railway undertakings to operate in a fair and non-discriminatory manner.

This Regulation aims to provide effective protection for passengers and encourage rail travel by establishing rules applicable to rail transport. The Regulation applies to international and domestic rail journeys and services throughout the Union, provided by one or more railway undertakings licensed in accordance with Directive 2012/34/EU. However, Member States may exempt certain services from the application of this Regulation, such as services operated strictly for historical or touristic use, urban, suburban, and regional rail passenger services, and international rail passenger services with a significant part operated outside the Union.

The Regulation sets out rules on the liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage, including in the event of an accident, disruption, or cancellation. Railway undertakings are liable for loss or damage resulting from the fact that a journey cannot be continued on the same day due to cancellation, late running of a train, or a missed connection. Passengers are also entitled to reimbursement for reasonable costs incurred in reaching their final destination under comparable conditions if the railway undertaking fails to provide available re-routing options within 100 minutes from the scheduled departure time.

The Regulation also requires railway undertakings to be adequately insured or have adequate guarantees to cover their liabilities. In the event of a passenger being killed or injured, the railway undertaking must make advance payments to meet immediate economic needs, without delay and not later than 15 days after the establishment of the identity of the natural person entitled to compensation. The advance payment shall not be less than EUR 21,000 per passenger in the event of death and shall not constitute recognition of liability.

Furthermore, the Regulation sets out rules on the provision of information to passengers, including minimum and accurate information on the issuing of tickets, to be provided in an accessible format and in a timely manner. Infrastructure managers must distribute real-time data relating to the arrival and departure of trains to railway undertakings, ticket vendors, tour operators, and station managers. Railway undertakings must also provide other railway undertakings, ticket vendors, and tour operators with access to minimum travel information and operations on reservation systems.

Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a high level of protection for passengers and ensure that railway undertakings are liable for any loss or damage resulting from their services. The Regulation also promotes transparency and accessibility of information, which is essential for passengers to make informed decisions about their travel.

This Regulation aims to provide effective protection for rail passengers and encourage rail travel within the European Union. It establishes rules applicable to rail transport, including non-discrimination between passengers, liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage, and passengers' rights in the event of accidents or disruptions. The Regulation also sets out rules for the provision of information to passengers, assistance for persons with disabilities and reduced mobility, and the handling of complaints. Railway undertakings are liable for loss or damage resulting from the cancellation or late running of a train, or a missed connection, and must reimburse passengers for reasonable costs incurred in continuing their journey. The Regulation applies to all rail passenger services, although Member States may grant exemptions for certain services, such as those operated strictly for historic or touristic use, or urban, suburban, and regional rail passenger services. However, such exemptions must not apply to essential rules, including non-discriminatory conditions of transport contracts, liability in respect of passengers and their luggage, and requirements for adequate insurance and personal security measures. The Regulation also promotes the use of bicycles in combination with train journeys, and requires railway undertakings to provide access to real-time travel information and facilitate the distribution of such information among operators. Overall, the Regulation seeks to improve rail passenger services, increase the share of rail transport, and safeguard users' rights, while allowing for certain exemptions and flexibility in its application.

This Regulation aims to prevent the misuse of hosting services for disseminating terrorist content online, while ensuring the protection of fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression and information. It applies to hosting service providers offering services in the Union, regardless of their place of main establishment, and sets out uniform rules for the removal of terrorist content. The Regulation does not apply to material disseminated for educational, journalistic, artistic, or research purposes, or for preventing or countering terrorism, as long as the true purpose of the dissemination is assessed and found to be legitimate.

Hosting service providers have a duty of care to address the dissemination of terrorist content through their services, and must ensure the expeditious removal of or disabling of access to such content. The Regulation establishes a procedure for issuing removal orders, which can be issued by the competent authority of each Member State. The removal order must contain specific elements, including the identification of the competent authority, a statement of reasons, and information about the redress available to the hosting service provider and the content provider.

The hosting service provider must remove the terrorist content or disable access to it within one hour of receiving the removal order, and must inform the competent authority of the removal or disabling without undue delay. If the hosting service provider cannot comply with the removal order due to force majeure or technical reasons, it must inform the competent authority of the grounds for non-compliance. The removal order becomes final upon the expiry of the deadline for appeal, and the competent authority must inform the competent authority of the Member State where the hosting service provider has its main establishment of the final removal order.

In cases where the hosting service provider does not have its main establishment in the Member State of the competent authority that issued the removal order, the competent authority must submit a copy of the removal order to the competent authority of the Member State where the hosting service provider has its main establishment. The hosting service provider and the content provider have the right to request the competent authority to scrutinize the removal order to determine whether it infringes the Regulation or fundamental rights and freedoms. If the competent authority finds an infringement, the removal order ceases to have legal effects, and the hosting service provider must reinstate the content or access thereto.

Hosting service providers must also preserve removed terrorist content and related data for administrative or judicial review proceedings, or for the prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of terrorist offenses. Additionally, hosting service providers must set out clearly in their terms and conditions their policy for addressing the dissemination of terrorist content, including the use of automated tools, and must provide meaningful explanations of their specific measures. Overall, the Regulation seeks to balance the need to prevent the dissemination of terrorist content online with the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, and establishes a framework for cooperation among Member States, hosting service providers, and competent authorities to achieve this goal.

The Instrument aims to uphold and promote the Union's values, principles, and fundamental interests worldwide, while contributing to the reduction of poverty, promotion of democracy, and respect for human rights. It seeks to achieve these objectives by supporting and fostering dialogue and cooperation with third countries and regions, developing special partnerships with European Neighbourhood Policy countries, and promoting multilateralism. The Instrument's specific objectives include protecting and promoting democracy, the rule of law, and human rights, as well as supporting civil society organisations and addressing global challenges such as climate change and migration.

The Instrument applies to the Union and its Member States, who are required to coordinate their policies and consult each other on their assistance programmes. The Union shall foster inclusiveness in the implementation of the Instrument and collaborate with Member States to maximise added value and reinforce shared interests, values, and common goals. The Instrument also provides for thematic programmes, including Human Rights and Democracy, Civil Society Organisations, Peace, Stability and Conflict Prevention, and Global Challenges, which shall cover areas such as advancing fundamental values of democracy, supporting inclusive and participatory civil society, and addressing health, education, and environmental challenges.

The European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) aims to support Member States and regions in achieving high employment levels, fair social protection, and a skilled and resilient workforce, as well as promoting inclusive and cohesive societies. The ESF+ has several specific objectives, including improving access to employment and activation measures, modernising labour market institutions, promoting a gender-balanced labour market, and enhancing equal access to quality education and training. The fund also aims to promote social inclusion, reduce poverty, and support the socio-economic integration of marginalised communities, such as Roma people and third-country nationals.

The ESF+ is implemented under shared management, with Member States responsible for programming their resources to address challenges identified in the European Semester and relevant country-specific recommendations. Member States must allocate an appropriate amount of their resources to address these challenges and to implement the Child Guarantee, which aims to tackle child poverty. In particular, Member States with high rates of child poverty must allocate at least 5% of their ESF+ resources to targeted actions and structural reforms to address this issue.

The ESF+ also supports actions to promote gender equality, equal opportunities, and non-discrimination, including ensuring accessibility for persons with disabilities and promoting the transition from residential or institutional care to family and community-based care. The fund aims to increase the participation of women in employment, combat the feminisation of poverty, and reduce gender discrimination in the labour market and education and training.

In exceptional or unusual circumstances, the ESF+ may provide temporary additional support, such as financing short-time work schemes or access to healthcare, for a limited period of 18 months. The Commission monitors the implementation of this support and assesses whether it is sufficient to facilitate the use of ESF+ resources in response to these circumstances. Overall, the ESF+ plays a crucial role in promoting social inclusion, reducing poverty, and supporting the development of a skilled and resilient workforce in the European Union.

The Integrated Border Management Fund, established by this Regulation, aims to support the customs union and customs authorities in protecting the financial and economic interests of the Union and its Member States, ensuring security and safety, and facilitating legitimate business activity. The Fund has a specific objective to contribute to adequate and equivalent results of customs controls through the purchase, maintenance, and upgrading of state-of-the-art customs control equipment. The Instrument, which is part of the Fund, provides financial support for these purposes and is implemented under direct management in accordance with the Financial Regulation. 

The Instrument may provide funding in various forms, including grants, and the Commission is responsible for setting up a coordination mechanism to ensure the interoperability of customs control equipment purchased with Union support. To be eligible for funding, actions must implement the objectives set out in Article 3 and support the purchase, maintenance, or upgrading of customs control equipment, including innovative detection technology equipment, with specific customs control purposes such as non-intrusive inspection, radiation detection, and analysis of samples. 

The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend the indicative list of customs control equipment and to establish a monitoring and evaluation framework. The performance reporting system ensures that data for monitoring the implementation and results of the Instrument are collected efficiently, and proportionate reporting requirements are imposed on recipients of Union funds. The Instrument is implemented through work programmes that aim to achieve the objectives set out in Article 3, and the preparation of these work programmes is supported by an assessment of the needs of the customs authorities, which is updated regularly. 

The assessment of needs is based on a common categorisation of border crossing points, a comprehensive description of available customs control equipment, and an estimate of financial needs. The work programmes set out the total amount of the financing plan for all actions and include details such as objectives, expected results, and implementation timetables. The Commission encourages the joint procurement and joint testing of customs control equipment by two or more Member States, and customs control equipment financed under the Instrument should be used primarily for customs controls but may also be used for additional purposes, including support of national border management authorities and investigation. 

The Regulation also establishes indicators for reporting on the progress of the Instrument in achieving its general and specific objectives, including the availability of customs control equipment meeting agreed standards at different types of border crossing points. These indicators are used to ensure the effective assessment of the Instrument's progress towards its objectives, and the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend these indicators as necessary. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the efficient and effective operation of the customs union and to support the customs authorities in their mission to protect the interests of the Union.

The Integrated Border Management Fund, established by this Regulation, aims to support the customs union and customs authorities in protecting the financial and economic interests of the Union and its Member States, ensuring security and safety within the Union, and facilitating legitimate business activity. The Fund will provide financial support for the purchase, maintenance, and upgrading of customs control equipment, with a focus on state-of-the-art technology that is secure, safe, and environmentally friendly. The Commission will set up a coordination mechanism to ensure the interoperability of customs control equipment purchased with Union support. In exceptional cases, costs incurred before the grant application was submitted may be considered eligible for funding, provided they were incurred on or after 1 January 2021.

The customs control equipment financed under this Instrument should be used primarily for customs controls but may also be used for additional purposes, including support of national border management authorities and investigation. The Commission will encourage joint procurement and joint testing of customs control equipment by two or more Member States. The Regulation also defines key terms related to customs authorities, customs legislation, and customs controls, which are essential for understanding the scope and application of the Fund. 

The Regulation applies to the period from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2027, and its duration is aligned with the multiannual financial framework. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to update the indicative list of customs control equipment, ensuring that the Fund remains effective in supporting the customs union and customs authorities. Overall, the Regulation aims to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of customs controls, facilitating legitimate trade while protecting the Union's interests and ensuring the safety and security of its citizens.

The specific objective is to contribute to adequate and equivalent results of customs controls through the transparent purchase, maintenance, and upgrading of relevant and reliable state-of-the-art customs control equipment.

The Commission will set up a coordination mechanism to ensure the interoperability of customs control equipment purchased with Union support.
